latestRelease.notes:
# Hermes Agent v0.20.4 (v2026.8.18)

**Release Date:** August 18, 2026

> Patch release. This tag rolls up the ~74 PRs merged since v0.20.3 into a stable tagged release for downstream consumers (Docker images, hosted deployments, fresh installs).

---

## About this release

Since v0.20.3 (v2026.8.16.2, tagged August 17), this window landed **~146 commits** across **~265 files** (+21,697 / −2,217) — **~74 merged PRs** including the desktop glass/translucency surface work (matte glass, frost picker, macOS pre-select), the tabbed SESSIONS|BOTS sidebar with per-bot hide/unhide, Bot Mode group-chat fixes (long-running member turns, Markdown rendering, cross-machine routing), NVIDIA SkillEvaluator Tier 1 advisory scanning on skill installs (license + security checks), cron media-send hardening (configurable timeout, manual-run attachments, missed-fire surfacing), SessionDB event-loop-thread and contention fixes, `hermes update` parked-branch honesty, and kanban native OS notifications.

**Full curated release notes for this window will ship with v0.21.0**, which will document everything from v0.20.0 onward — highlights, feature areas, and complete contributor credits. Nothing in this window is skipped.

## Updating

- `hermes update` from an existing install
- Fresh install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash`

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/compare/v2026.8.16.2...v2026.8.18

signals.title: [Feature]: Named/resumable sessions for cron jobs
signals.text: ### Problem or Use Case Every cron job invocation creates a brand-new session (auto-named with timestamp + hash, e.g. 20260421_135634_d8fa8a14). For recurring jobs that run every N minutes, this generates massive session bloat: - A job running every 20 minutes creates 72 new sessions per day - A job running every hour creates 24 new sessions per day - Over a month, a single cron job accumulates ~2,160 sessions These sessions are meaningless monitoring/health-check sessions that carry no conversation history worth preserving. They pollute the session directory, consume disk space, and slow down session enumeration. Expected Behavior Cron jobs should support a session parameter that allows specifying a named session to reuse across invocations. For example: yaml job: name: "Gateway Health Monitor" session: "gateway_health_monitor" # Reuse this session each run schedule: "every 20m" With this, each run of the job appends to the same conversation thread instead of creating a new session. The session would still exist but remain lean — just a short log of each cron run rather than a full isolated conversation. Benefits 1. Massive session reduction — 72 sessions/day → 1 session forever 2. Cleaner session directory — monitoring jobs no longer pollute session lists 3. Persistent short-term context — if the health check needs to remember the last state (e.g., "gateway was down 3 minutes ago"), it can without creating new sessions 4. Easier debugging — all health check runs are in one place, easy to review timeline of issues Implementation Notes - The session name should be a simple string identifier (no special characters) - If the session doesn't exist on first run, create it - The session could have a special marker/type to indicate it's a cron-reused session (for session cleanup/rotation logic) - Optional: support a max_session_history to keep the reused session from growing unbounded ### Proposed Solution cron job yaml file has session parameter that will append log data upon cron execution. ### Alternatives Considered deleting prior sessions that match a string. ### Feature Type Gateway / messaging improvement ### Scope Small (single file, < 50 lines) ### Contribution - [ ] I'd like to implement this myself and submit a PR ### Debug Report (optional) ```shell ```

signals.title: Desktop sessions miss configured MCP tools and uvx servers can fail under macOS GUI PATH
signals.text: ## Bug description Configured MCP servers can be discoverable from the Hermes CLI but still be missing from Hermes Desktop sessions. I hit this with a native MCP server configured like this: ```yaml mcp_servers: linkedin: command: uvx args: - linkedin-scraper-mcp ``` The server itself was installed and healthy. Running the Hermes MCP diagnostic from the Hermes venv connected and discovered tools: ```bash /Users/dpearson/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3 /Users/dpearson/.hermes/hermes-agent/hermes mcp test linkedin ``` Result: ```text ✓ Connected ✓ Tools discovered: 17 ``` But the active Hermes Desktop/API session did not expose any `mcp_linkedin_*` tools, so the agent had to fall back to a manual FastMCP client path. There appear to be two separate issues here: 1. Desktop/dashboard WebSocket sessions do not start MCP discovery, so agents created from that path can snapshot tools before configured MCP servers are registered. 2. On macOS, Desktop/launchd processes can inherit a minimal PATH like `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`. That PATH does not include `~/.local/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin`, or `/usr/local/bin`, so an MCP server configured as `command: uvx` can fail from Desktop even though it works from an interactive terminal. ## Steps to reproduce 1. On macOS, install/configure an MCP server using `uvx`, for example: ```yaml mcp_servers: linkedin: command: uvx args: - linkedin-scraper-mcp ``` 2. Verify it works from the Hermes CLI: ```bash hermes mcp test linkedin ``` 3. Start Hermes Desktop from the macOS app/GUI path. 4. Open a new Desktop/API session and ask the agent to use the configured MCP server. 5. Inspect the available tool schema or try to call the expected `mcp_<server>_*` tools. ## Expected behavior MCP servers configured in `config.yaml` should be discovered and registered for Hermes Desktop/API sessions the same way they are for CLI/TUI sessions. For `uvx` MCP servers, Desktop should either resolve `uvx` reliably under the macOS GUI environment or surface a clear startup/config error that explains the PATH problem. ## Actual behavior The MCP server was configured and reachable through Hermes MCP diagnostics, but the Desktop/API agent session did not expose the MCP tools. In my case, the server was `linkedin-scraper-mcp`; the missing tools were the expected LinkedIn MCP tools such as `mcp_linkedin_*`. ## Local mitigation applied I mitigated this locally with a small code patch: - Moved the background MCP discovery state out of `tui_gateway/entry.py` and into `tui_gateway/server.py`, which is imported by both the stdio TUI path and the Desktop/dashboard WebSocket path. - Updated `tui_gateway/entry.py` to call the shared `server.start_mcp_discovery_background()`. - Updated `tui_gateway/ws.py` to call `server.start_mcp_discovery_background()` before the Desktop/WebSocket session reports readiness. - Updated `_make_agent()` in `tui_gateway/server.py` to briefly wait for MCP discovery before snapshotting the agent's tool list, with a bounded timeout so slow/dead MCP servers do not block startup indefinitely. - Extended `tools/mcp_tool.py::_resolve_stdio_command()` to resolve `uv` and `uvx` under GUI-style PATHs, using these fallback locations: - `~/.local/bin/{uv,uvx}` - `/opt/homebrew/bin/{uv,uvx}` - `/usr/local/bin/{uv,uvx}` I also added a regression test for the Desktop/WebSocket startup path and kept the existing MCP command resolver tests passing. Local verification after the mitigation: ```text uvx -> /Users/dpearson/.local/bin/uvx uv -> /Users/dpearson/.local/bin/uv npx -> /Users/dpearson/.hermes/node/bin/npx ``` Test results: ```text tests/tools/test_mcp_tool_issue_948.py: 5 passed tests/tui_gateway/test_mcp_discovery_startup.py + MCP resolver tests: 8 passed py_compile over modified files: exit 0 ``` ## Environment - OS: macOS 26.5.1 - Hermes Agent: v0.15.1 (2026.5.29) - Repo: NousResearch/hermes-agent - Commit tested locally: `b34ee8074` - Python: 3.11.15 ## Notes This is not specific to LinkedIn. LinkedIn was just the MCP server that made the bug visible. Any Desktop-launched MCP server using `uvx` can hit the PATH issue, and any configured MCP server can be missed if the Desktop/WebSocket path does not start MCP discovery before the agent snapshots tools.

signals.title: Desktop: mic fails with "runtime does not support microphone recording" when UI is loaded over HTTP (DEV_SERVER / remote dist)
signals.text: ## Summary Pressing the desktop voice/mic control shows: > This runtime does not support microphone recording. This happens when the desktop renderer is loaded from a **non-secure HTTP origin** (e.g. `HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER` pointing at a remote/Tailscale host serving `apps/desktop/dist` over plain HTTP). It is **not** tied to a specific model/provider, and it happens even when voice/STT are enabled in settings. ## Environment - Hermes Desktop (Electron) with renderer loaded from remote HTTP dev/dist server - Also reproducible by opening the same desktop `dist/` in a normal browser over `http://<host>:<port>` (non-localhost) - Voice/STT enabled in config - OS: macOS client + remote Linux host serving the UI (also applies to any HTTP origin) ## Steps to reproduce 1. Serve `apps/desktop/dist` over plain HTTP on a non-localhost address (e.g. LAN/Tailscale IP). 2. Point Electron at that URL via `HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER` (or open the URL in a browser). 3. Open a chat and press the mic / voice control. ## Expected - Mic capture works on the **client** machine (getUserMedia in the renderer), or - UI disables the control with a clear message: "Microphone requires a secure context (HTTPS/localhost) or the native desktop app." ## Actual ```ts // apps/desktop/src/app/chat/composer/hooks/use-mic-recorder.ts if (!navigator.mediaDevices?.getUserMedia || typeof MediaRecorder === 'undefined') { throw new Error(copy.microphoneUnsupported) } ``` On insecure HTTP, Chromium leaves `navigator.mediaDevices` / `getUserMedia` unavailable, so the generic "runtime does not support…" string is thrown. Permission handlers in `electron/main.ts` never run because the API is missing at the document origin. ## Why this matters Remote-agent setups commonly load the desktop UI from a headless host over Tailscale HTTP. Chat works; voice looks enabled in settings but is dead. The error reads like a missing binary feature rather than a secure-context / packaging issue. ## Suggested fix (product) 1. **Detect insecure context** before start: `!window.isSecureContext` or missing `mediaDevices`, and show a specific i18n string (HTTPS / native app / localhost), not "runtime does not support." 2. **Docs**: state that desktop mic requires native package, `file://`, localhost, or HTTPS — plain remote HTTP will never get getUserMedia. 3. Optional: for `HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER` remote workflows, document HTTPS or SSH/local port-forward to `http://127.0.0.1`. 4. Related: browser-side voice capture work in #20765 / #54352. ## Workaround - Use the packaged native desktop app (local renderer), or - Load the UI from `https://` or `http://127.0.0.1` (port-forward), or - Use gateway voice messages (e.g. Telegram) for STT.

signals.title: [Feature Request] Desktop notification sound volume control
signals.text: ## Problem The desktop app plays notification sounds (message received, task complete, etc.) at a fixed volume. There is no way to adjust or mute the notification sound volume independently from the system volume. ## Use Case - Users in shared/office environments need quieter notifications - Users with hearing impairments may need louder notifications - Night-time usage requires low-volume or silent notifications - Current workaround: modify the ASAR package to patch the audio volume in source code, which is lost on every update ## Proposed Solution Add a volume slider in the desktop app settings (e.g., Settings > Sound > Notification Volume, 0%-100%) that controls the notification sound playback volume independently. The volume setting should persist across app restarts. ## Environment - Hermes Agent: v0.20.1 - Desktop: Electron (Linux/Windows/macOS) - Install method: pip (source build)

signals.title: [Bug] Desktop v0.20.4: registered remote Bot handle is absent from composer autocomplete
signals.text: ## Summary Hermes Desktop v0.20.4 can discover a profile on a registered remote gateway and render its source-qualified Bot Mode row, but the qualified remote handle is absent from the normal composer `@` autocomplete. The row itself instructs the user to stay in the current chat and invoke that handle, so the advertised invocation path cannot be completed. ## Environment - Windows 11 Hermes Desktop, packaged build - WSL2 Linux remote gateway on the same machine, reached over loopback HTTP - Desktop and remote Hermes Agent: v0.20.4, commit `8911e2e0ed` - Connection registry: local app-managed gateway remains primary; one token-authenticated remote gateway is added No credentials, session tokens, private paths, or real profile display names are included below. ## Steps to reproduce 1. In **Settings -> Gateways**, keep **This device** as Primary. 2. Add a token-authenticated **Remote gateway** with a synthetic label such as `Lab Agent`. 3. Open **BOTS**. 4. Confirm the remote default profile appears exactly once as a source-qualified row, e.g.: ```text Lab Agent @default-lab-agent ``` The local row also remains exactly once, e.g. `Hermes @default-this-device`. 5. Click the remote row. 6. Observe Bot Mode's instruction to stay in the current chat and invoke `@default-lab-agent`. 7. Open a clean local chat and type a true lone `@`. 8. Inspect the entire scrollable autocomplete list, including its final entries. 9. Type the full qualified handle as an additional check. ## Expected behavior The remote source-qualified handle appears in autocomplete and can be selected as a genuine structured mention. Selecting it routes the turn to the registered remote gateway/profile and returns the remote agent's reply in the current chat. This is also the behavior described by #88060: the composer completion set should use the union agent roster, including `@name-device` handles for duplicate profile names across registered connections. ## Actual behavior - Discovery and deduplication pass: the local and remote Bot rows each appear exactly once. - The complete autocomplete list contains project references and local profile handles only. - The qualified remote handle is absent. - Typing the full handle reports no matching result. - A plain prompt sent after clicking the remote row remains on the current local profile, as expected for an unmentioned message; the remote agent is never invoked. ## Why this is a bug rather than a feature request The installed Bot Mode code deliberately treats `remoteSource` rows as mention-only entry points and tells the user to use the qualified handle. The same handle is then unavailable from the completion surface intended to provide Bot Mode handles. ## Impact A registered remote gateway looks healthy and its agents appear in BOTS, but users cannot exercise the supported cross-gateway invocation flow. Roster visibility can therefore be mistaken for end-to-end connectivity. ## Acceptance criteria - A lone `@` offers every invokable source-qualified remote Bot handle from the union roster. - Selecting the row creates a structured mention carrying connection + profile provenance. - The turn is written to the remote source's session database and the visible reply comes from that remote agent. - Local and remote profiles with the same name remain deduplicated and source-qualified. - Behavior survives Desktop restart and connection-registry reload. - An unreachable remote source surfaces a clear error instead of silently falling back to the active local profile. ## Related - #88060 — composer `@` autocomplete should offer Bot Mode agents (closed/implemented for the general case) - #88680 — preserve connection x profile route identity end to end - #89206 — adjacent non-primary Bot Mode chat/navigation failures

signals.title: [Architecture]: make false success a first-class defect class with typed completion proofs
signals.text: ## Summary Hermes has a recurring cross-system defect class that is broader than any one protocol, UI, updater, or delivery path: > **An earlier lifecycle event is promoted into proof of a later one.** A payload exists. A function returned. A promise resolved. An event was emitted. Source moved. One fan-out target succeeded. A protocol turn ended. All of those can be true while the operation the caller actually cares about **did not complete**. This is **false success**: a system reports terminal success without proof of the authoritative postcondition at the mutation boundary. The same shape is now visible across unrelated Hermes surfaces: - **ACP — #89948, adjacent #72439:** the conversation loop already knows a provider turn failed (`completed: false`, `failed: true`, `error: ...`), but `acp_adapter.server::prompt()` drops that verdict, emits the error summary as ordinary assistant text, and returns `stopReason: end_turn`. Protocol termination is laundered into successful model completion. - **Quick Entry — #89920 / #85590:** the original fire-and-forget path could clear/hide the draft before authoritative session creation and prompt delivery were acknowledged. #89920 is moving this surface toward an explicit ack contract; it is an implementation node for this architecture, not evidence that the class is closed elsewhere. - **Updater / deployment — #88251, #86443, #83846, #79678, architecture #88683:** source/version movement can be reported as a successful update while the packaged Desktop executable is stale, missing, rebuilt from stale source, or destroyed before replacement succeeds. Source correctness is not shipped-artifact correctness. - **Desktop preview activation — #89272:** `open_preview` can return `{success:true}` when an event is emitted even though renderer normalization/activation is asynchronous and may fail or be clobbered. Producer emission is not route/tab publication. - **Webhook fan-out — #85523:** aggregate success can conceal per-target failure. One successful target does not prove the fan-out completed; every target must be accounted for with an honest result. There are additional instances of the same contract failure already tracked elsewhere, including result/fallback races, recovery markers, and delivery claims. They should interlock here when their failure is specifically “terminal success projected before the owning boundary proved the promised effect.” This issue is the shared architecture node. Linked incident issues and PRs remain the implementation/provenance nodes and retain their original reporters, evidence, and component ownership. --- ## The defect: completion laundering The deeper failure is **completion laundering**: a weaker lifecycle fact crosses a boundary and is reinterpreted as a stronger one. Examples: ```text request emitted → “opened” request accepted → “created” promise resolved → “published” source updated → “application updated” one target delivered → “fan-out succeeded” turn terminated → “model answered successfully” marker written → “recovery completed” ``` The left-hand events are often real and useful. The bug is treating them as proof of the right-hand claims. The general anti-pattern is: ```text caller intent ↓ intermediate operation ↓ weak success signal ───────────────┐ ↓ │ promoted async / remote / durable mutation │ without proof ↓ │ authoritative postcondition │ ↓ │ observable completion ◀─────────────┘ ``` The system becomes especially dangerous when the intermediate layer has enough information to sound authoritative: a normal assistant message, `end_turn`, `{success:true}`, exit 0, a resolved promise, “Already up to date,” or a green aggregate response. --- ## Design principle > **Completion requires a typed verdict and proof at the mutation boundary. A payload, return value, resolved promise, emitted event, progress message, source transition, or partial target success is not sufficient.** The component that owns the authoritative mutation must also own the evidence that allows the operation to advance to terminal success. A caller may observe earlier phases, but those phases must remain typed as earlier phases. --- ## Canonical lifecycle Not every surface needs every phase, but asynchronous/mutating operations should distinguish the semantic equivalents of: ```text attempted → accepted → started → committed → published / delivered / observable → verified / reconciled ``` Failure can occur between any two phases. A useful shared vocabulary is: ```ts type CompletionState = | 'accepted' // request admitted; effect not proven | 'started' // execution began | 'committed' // authoritative local mutation committed | 'delivered' // external consumer/provider accepted the effect | 'verified' // declared postcondition observed | 'partial' // aggregate operation has mixed terminal outcomes | 'failed' // definite failure | 'ambiguous' // effect cannot be proved present or absent | 'stale' // verdict belongs to a superseded generation ``` This is a semantic contract, not a requirement that Python, TypeScript, Rust, adapters, and provider SDKs share one physical type. --- ## Completion must be bound to identity and generation A verdict without identity is not enough. Async work can finish late, retries can overlap, routes can switch, sessions can be replaced, and fan-out targets can diverge. The completion proof therefore needs to bind to the exact operation and the exact mutation it claims to certify. Conceptually: ```ts type Completion<T> = { operationId: string generation: string | number requestedIdentity?: unknown authoritativeIdentity?: unknown state: CompletionState authority: string observedGeneration?: string | number result?: T receipts?: unknown[] failures?: unknown[] proof?: { kind: string value: unknown } error?: { code: string message: string retryable?: boolean } } ``` The representation can vary. The invariant cannot. A delayed completion for generation N must not acknowledge, clear, hide, replace, finalize, or release generation N+1. --- ## `ambiguous` is a first-class terminal verdict A timeout is not necessarily a failure. If Hermes dispatched a mutation and then lost the acknowledgement, there are at least three possibilities: 1. the mutation definitely did not occur; 2. the mutation definitely occurred; 3. the mutation may have occurred, but Hermes cannot prove either outcome. Case 3 is **ambiguous**, not success and not failure. This distinction matters because blindly retrying an ambiguous mutation can create duplicate sessions, duplicate messages, duplicate webhooks, duplicate external side effects, or destructive double execution. Therefore: - timeout/lost acknowledgement must not be normalized to success; - timeout/lost acknowledgement must not automatically be normalized to safe retry; - retries across ambiguous boundaries require stable operation identity/idempotency or an authoritative read-back/reconciliation step. This is directly relevant to Quick Entry correlation and any remote/provider mutation path. --- ## Aggregate operations require total accounting Fan-out exposes another common laundering path: one child result becomes the parent verdict. For N targets, aggregate success requires an accounted-for terminal result for all N targets. ```text 3 succeeded + 1 failed = partial 3 succeeded + 1 unknown = partial/ambiguous 4 succeeded = success ``` A warning attached to a success response does not make the result honest if callers branch on the success bit. For #85523 specifically, fan-out results must preserve per-target identity and outcome. No target may disappear behind a truthy aggregate. --- ## Incident-specific authoritative postconditions | Surface | Weak signal currently/previously mistaken for completion | Authoritative postcondition | |---|---|---| | ACP (#89948) | assistant text emitted + `end_turn` | Provider turn verdict is propagated; a failed provider turn remains typed failed/error to the ACP client and cannot be recorded as an ordinary successful answer. | | ACP model selection (#72439) | `session/set_model` returns success | Requested/effective model is valid for the selected provider, or the request returns a typed rejection before poisoning the persisted session. | | Quick Entry (#89920 / #85590) | submit emitted / renderer accepted work | Exact correlated submission is acknowledged after the requested session is authoritatively created and the prompt is bound to that session; only that acknowledgement may clear/hide the matching draft. | | Desktop preview (#89272) | tool event emitted / promise resolved | Renderer acknowledges the requested preview target/generation is actually published according to the active-surface policy; readiness may be a separate later phase. | | Desktop update (#88251 / #86443 / #83846 / #79678) | Git/source/version step succeeded or process exited 0 | Required packaged executable exists at the target generation, passes the declared probe, and the last known-good artifact is not destroyed before replacement verification. Managed runtime generation must be handled by #88683's deployment transaction. | | Webhook fan-out (#85523) | at least one target succeeded / aggregate truthy result | Every intended target has an explicit terminal result; only all-success is success, mixed results are `partial`, and unknown remote outcomes remain explicit. | --- ## Invariants ### 1. Admission is not completion Emitting an event, queueing work, accepting input, spawning a subprocess, resolving a route, or starting a provider call may return `accepted` or `started`. It cannot return the terminal state promised to the caller unless that is genuinely the caller's contract. ### 2. Success requires proof owned by the mutation boundary The layer that can know whether the effect happened must return the receipt/proof used to advance the operation. Upstream layers must not reconstruct completion from circumstantial state. ### 3. Verdicts are monotonic in meaning A downstream compatibility layer may translate representation, but it may not silently strengthen: ```text accepted → committed committed → delivered partial → success failed → success ambiguous → success ``` Nor may it discard a failure/result field and retain only a generic terminal marker. ### 4. Operation generation is mandatory where stale completion is possible Late completion from an older operation is a deterministic no-op against successor state. This applies to draft clearing, route publication, session activation, destructive replacement, retry bookkeeping, and any async state machine where multiple generations can overlap. ### 5. Result-bearing completion beats generic fallback completion A generic “done” hook cannot race with and overwrite/pre-empt a richer result for the same operation. Fallbacks must preserve the strongest authoritative verdict, not win by timing. ### 6. Aggregate success requires total accounting Every declared child operation must appear in the parent result. Missing children are not success. ### 7. Destructive replacement is stage → verify → switch → clean The previous working artifact/state remains recoverable until the candidate is verified. No updater/recovery path may destroy the last known-good state and then report success because an earlier source step completed. ### 8. Markers record achieved postconditions, not intentions A “settled,” version, recovery, migration, or completion marker is written only after the state it represents is verified. ### 9. Ambiguity survives the boundary If the owner cannot prove present or absent, the caller receives `ambiguous` (or equivalent). It must not receive a fabricated certainty. ### 10. User-visible success cannot outrun machine-verifiable success UI clearing, green banners, “Update complete,” normal assistant rendering, route transitions, and success HTTP responses are consumers of the typed verdict. They cannot be independent authorities. --- ## Relationship to qualified identity This contract is the temporal/outcome counterpart to Hermes' qualified-identity work. The two rules are structurally parallel: > **Identity:** once identity becomes more specific, no downstream layer may make it less specific and later infer the missing dimensions. > **Completion:** once outcome evidence becomes more specific, no downstream layer may discard it and later infer success from a weaker lifecycle signal. A correct mutation proof therefore binds both: ```text WHO / WHAT connection + profile + provider + route + resource/session/target AND WHAT HAPPENED operation + generation + verdict + receipt/postcondition ``` Preserving identity without completion evidence still permits coherent false success against the correct resource. Preserving completion without qualified identity permits a valid receipt to be attached to the wrong resource. Both dimensions have to survive end-to-end. --- ## Required adversarial tests Each adopting surface should test the applicable failure modes, not merely steady-state success: - delayed generation-N acknowledgement after generation N+1 starts; - timeout after the mutation may already have committed; - retry after ambiguous completion; - duplicate acknowledgement; - consumer/event handler absent after producer admission; - promise resolves but publication/read-back fails; - provider returns a definite error with a normal-looking payload; - fallback completion races result-bearing completion; - one fan-out target fails while others succeed; - one fan-out target never returns while others succeed; - per-target result serialization drops a failure; - candidate artifact build fails after source update; - candidate artifact build fails after cleanup begins; - process exits 0 but required artifact/postcondition is absent; - crash/restart between intent, commit, verification, and marker write; - stale completion attempts to clear newer UI/user state; - compatibility facade drops `failed`, `partial`, `ambiguous`, generation, target identity, or proof. The important test shape is not “did this function return?” It is “can any weaker intermediate event still produce terminal success while the authoritative postcondition is false?” --- ## Acceptance criteria This architecture issue is complete when: 1. Hermes has a documented shared completion vocabulary covering at least success, failure, partial, ambiguous, and stale/superseded outcomes. 2. Async mutation boundaries carry operation identity/generation where stale acknowledgement is possible. 3. The linked ACP path cannot convert a known provider failure into ordinary assistant text plus an unqualified successful turn. 4. Quick Entry clears/hides only on the acknowledgement for the exact requested submission/session generation; timeout ambiguity cannot erase the draft or blindly duplicate the mutation. 5. Desktop preview/tool activation distinguishes event admission from renderer publication and returns an authoritative acknowledgement for the requested target/generation. 6. Updater/deployment success is gated on required packaged/runtime postconditions, not source movement or exit status alone; #88683 remains the broader deployment transaction owner. 7. Webhook fan-out exposes honest per-target outcomes and returns `partial`/equivalent for mixed results rather than aggregate success. 8. Compatibility/facade layers preserve typed verdict, identity, generation, and proof instead of collapsing them to booleans, normal payloads, or generic terminal markers. 9. Stale completions are deterministic no-ops against successor state. 10. Failure-injection tests prove that no linked surface can manufacture terminal success from an earlier lifecycle phase. --- ## Interlocks / topology ### Direct implementation nodes - #89948 — ACP drops `failed/error` and reports failed provider turns as normal answers. - #89920 — Quick Entry acknowledgement + atomic new-session submission; concrete repair of one false-success path from #85590. - #89272 — Desktop preview active-tab desync; includes the `open_preview` fire-and-forget success boundary. - #85523 — webhook Task 10; requires honest per-target fan-out outcomes. ### Deployment/update class - #88683 — authoritative deployment plan + transactional activation; broader owner for installation/update/bootstrap topology. - #88251 — source can advance while packaged Desktop remains stale. - #86443 — destructive Desktop rebuild/update ordering can remove the last working artifact and still project success. - #83846 — ZIP fallback can remove packaged Desktop while later updates report “Already up to date.” - #79678 — updater can successfully pull and then restore stale detached HEAD while printing success. ### Adjacent ACP contract - #72439 — `session/set_model` accepts an invalid model and the next provider failure is surfaced as a silent/normal `end_turn`; complements #89948 by moving rejection to the mutation that introduced the invalid state. ### Existing architecture relationship This issue does **not** replace the narrow incident fixes or #88683. It supplies the shared completion invariant they should compose with. When another incident is found, interlock it here only if its core failure is: ```text weaker lifecycle fact ↓ projected as terminal success ↓ without authoritative mutation proof ``` That keeps this issue a real defect-class node rather than a generic reliability tracker.

signals.title: architecture(desktop): make route identity immutable, generation-bound, and resource-owned across multi-gateway Desktop
signals.text: ## Summary Desktop now has real multi-gateway routing, but the architecture still treats route identity as reconstructible metadata rather than an immutable authority proof. #89719 successfully shipped registered-gateway switching and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation across REST, WebSocket, sessions, messaging, cron, projects, settings, and status state. Background gateways retain sockets and continue work. That is the correct product direction. However, one review finding crossed into `main`: `resolvedConnectionId()` can take a descriptor that already corresponds to an exact registry route and reconstruct a weaker identity from URL or `user@host`, selecting the first match. Legal duplicate registrations can therefore alias: - identical URLs with different auth mode, headers, credentials, Cloud organization, or account; - identical SSH user/host pairs with different port, key path, remote Hermes path, or remote profile. Because the rest of the new source-aware machinery then follows that reconstructed ID consistently, the result is a particularly convincing split-brain: the system can be internally coherent under the wrong source identity. That concrete defect should be fixed, but it exposes a deeper class that needs an architectural contract rather than another matcher patch. ## Core design principle > Once identity becomes more specific, no downstream layer may make it less specific and later infer the missing dimensions from foreground, endpoint, transport, or mutable registry state. Exact route identity must be **sticky, monotonic, generation-bound, and resource-owned**. ## Current evidence ### 1. Exact route provenance already exists before transport details are lost The existing `desktop-remote-route` planner resolves registry provenance before URL normalization, OAuth, SSH tunnelling, or other transport steps discard distinguishing information. Its identity matcher includes the dimensions that actually distinguish legal registrations: - auth mode; - headers; - token envelope; - Cloud organization; - SSH host/user/port; - key path; - remote Hermes path; - remote profile. For non-primary matches it accepts only a unique result. This is the right place in the pipeline to freeze route ownership. ### 2. `resolvedConnectionId()` weakens that proof after the fact The compatibility helper added by #89719 reconstructs identity from: - normalized `baseUrl` for remote/Cloud; - normalized `user@host` for SSH. It uses the first registry match and its descriptor type does not make an already-resolved `connectionId` authoritative. This can overwrite the exact identity already established by the route planner. ### 3. Source scoping is broad, but ownership is still ambient in many consumers `hermesApi()` injects the renderer's currently active source into requests. That works for foreground-global actions, but existing resources such as sessions, cron jobs, projects, approvals, OAuth flows, artifacts, and files should execute against their **owning route**, not whatever route happens to be foreground when an asynchronous callback finally runs. This becomes load-bearing now that background gateways remain live across foreground switches. ### 4. Some namespaces are source-aware at transport boundaries but still bare internally Gateway event dispatch now compares composite source/profile scope, which is correct. But many downstream stores and transient maps still key by bare runtime/session IDs, with source provenance kept separately or inferred from the active route. Copied/restored Hermes homes can reproduce IDs exactly. Multiple registered gateways make those duplicate namespaces concurrent. ### 5. Source switching still relies on manual global-state invalidation `wipeSessionListsForGatewaySwitch()` explicitly clears sessions, cron, messaging, unread paint, transcript tails, artifacts, and other gateway-bound state. This works only as long as every new source-owned store is remembered in the wipe list. That is an omission-prone correctness mechanism. Multi-gateway state should be partitioned by route identity so switching changes the visible partition instead of destructively reusing one global namespace. ## The deeper class issues ### A. Identity proof is not monotonic A registered route and an unqualified legacy descriptor should not share one loose shape. Suggested direction: ```ts type ResolvedRoute = | { identity: { kind: 'registered' connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } | { identity: { kind: 'legacy-unregistered' provenance: 'environment' | 'profile-v1' | 'settings-v1' } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } ``` Only the legacy-unregistered branch may enter compatibility inference. A registered descriptor must never have its identity overwritten by a weaker downstream guess. ### B. Registration identity, physical backend identity, principal, and locator are conflated Desktop needs explicit equivalence relations for concepts that are currently easy to treat as interchangeable: - **registration identity** — saved `connectionId`; - **registration generation** — which endpoint/credential envelope that ID currently denotes; - **physical runtime identity** — backend installation / `installId`; - **authorization principal** — account, Cloud org, credential set, permission envelope; - **locator** — URL, SSH host, tunnel endpoint. These answer different questions. Two registrations may share a locator but represent different principals. Two locators may reach one physical installation. A registry ID can be edited in place to point at a different runtime. Physical sameness does not prove authorization equivalence. Callers should explicitly choose the relation they require instead of using a generic "same connection" test. ### C. The route algebra overloads omission, `local`, `primary`, and legacy fallback These are semantically distinct: - omitted / null connection selector; - explicit `local`; - registry `primary`; - `lastUsed`; - unknown or removed ID; - legacy profile-routed fallback. V2 routing should represent this structurally rather than through magic-string normalization. Suggested direction: ```ts type ConnectionSelector = | { kind: 'registered'; id: ConnectionId } // including `local` | { kind: 'legacy-primary' } ``` `primary` and `lastUsed` should resolve user intent into a concrete registered route **before** an operation begins. They should not be consulted later as fallback authority for an already-started operation. ### D. Gateway activation is coordinated but not one transaction A foreground switch currently spans independently changing facts: - registry entry and credential envelope; - resolved descriptor; - WebSocket URL; - opened socket; - active gateway pointer; - active profile pointer; - renderer connection descriptor; - ambient REST connection/profile; - cache invalidations; - `lastUsed`; - new-chat ownership. Descriptor resolution and socket activation should not be independent proofs. The activation path that actually prepares the socket should return the exact descriptor and identity used to establish it. The outcome should be typed and explicit: ```ts type ActivationReceipt = | { status: 'activated' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number connection: HermesConnection socketInstanceId: string } | { status: 'already-active' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number } | { status: 'superseded' | 'removed' | 'offline' | 'ambiguous' | 'cancelled' requested: RouteIntent current: RouteKey } ``` Only an exact successful receipt may authorize success side effects. This directly interlocks with #89586 / #89609: a declined activation must not resolve indistinguishably from a successful one, especially for same-source profile switches where comparing only `connectionId` proves nothing. ### E. A connection ID identifies a mutable slot, not an immutable route A registry entry can be materially edited while retaining the same ID. For example, `homelab` can change from endpoint/credential A to endpoint/credential B while stale callbacks, sockets, caches, and resources still carry only `homelab`. Material edits already trigger backend/socket recycling, which is necessary but not sufficient as the architecture grows. Introduce a monotonically increasing registration generation: ```ts type RouteKey = { connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number profile: ProfileKey } ``` Every descriptor, socket, request, response, event, cache entry, persisted resource handle, and activation receipt should carry the generation. Results from an obsolete generation may finish but must not commit into the new generation's state. This closes ABA-style edit/remove/re-add races and makes descriptor/socket agreement provable. ### F. Ambient active-route state must not authorize mutations on existing resources Foreground-global actions can use the current route. Existing resources should carry their owner. Instead of: ```ts archiveSession(sessionId) ``` prefer: ```ts archiveSession({ owner: session.route, sessionId: session.id }) ``` The same principle applies to: - session mutations and hydration; - cron jobs and runs; - projects and repo/worktree operations; - approvals and input requests; - OAuth flows; - artifacts; - filesystem and Git operations; - background/tile/window actions. This directly interlocks with #89916: filesystem and Git facades need the same route identity as the resource/session that owns them, not merely the current foreground gateway. ### G. Resource namespaces must be source-qualified, not just transport-qualified The canonical resource identity should include route ownership: ```ts type ResourceKey = { route: RouteKey resourceId: string } ``` At minimum, audit and qualify: - runtime session IDs; - stored session IDs and lineage aliases; - unscoped stream pins; - approvals and input requests; - provider-wait / compaction / drafting state; - transcript tails; - unread/read watermarks; - pin mirrors; - cron job and run IDs; - project IDs and project scope; - artifacts; - OAuth flow/session IDs; - query and capability cache keys; - window/HUD/quick-entry session references. Unscoped events should be pinned per socket or `RouteKey`, never through one renderer-global ref shared by multiple retained gateways. ### H. Manual cache wiping should stop being a correctness boundary Gateway-owned state should be partitioned by route identity. Foreground switching should select another partition rather than globally clearing one namespace and hoping every source-owned store was included. Generation revocation can explicitly retire obsolete partitions after connection edits/removals, but ordinary switching should not require destructive global wipes. This also aligns state lifetime with the already-shipped behavior where background gateway sockets remain alive and continue work. ### I. Compatibility needs a versioned protocol and retirement path Absence of `connectionId` can currently mean too many things: - older Electron main; - environment-provided unregistered route; - genuinely local legacy route; - ambiguous registry match; - accidentally dropped exact identity; - failed lookup. Optional fields are not a sufficient compatibility protocol. Prefer an explicit versioned IPC contract: ```ts type ConnectionProtocol = | { version: 1; route: LegacyRouteDescriptor } | { version: 2; route: RegisteredRouteDescriptor } ``` A v2 registry-scoped call must produce a v2 registered route. Legacy compatibility should remain explicitly unregistered unless a unique, full-fidelity pre-dial match proves ownership. Compatibility paths should also expose diagnostics/telemetry so they can be retired rather than becoming permanent alternate authority models. ### J. Multi-window and registry-write concurrency need explicit semantics Desktop supports multiple full renderer windows while `lastUsed` and registry entries are global persisted state. Define and test: - whether `lastUsed` is installation-global, window-specific, or primary-window-owned; - what happens when one window removes/edits a connection another window is activating; - how concurrent registry mutations are serialized; - whether writes use a registry revision / compare-and-swap contract. A monotonically increasing registry revision should make stale write rejection explicit. ## Required invariants The architecture should eventually be able to state and mechanically test all of these: 1. Once exact registered identity exists, no downstream layer can replace it with inferred identity. 2. Registry ordering cannot affect route resolution. 3. Zero or multiple compatibility matches fail explicitly. 4. Socket route, descriptor route, REST route, UI route, and activation receipt agree on one `RouteKey`. 5. A same-source profile activation decline produces no success side effects. 6. Edit/remove/re-add during dial cannot publish an obsolete generation. 7. Old-generation responses/events cannot commit after generation replacement. 8. Identical resource IDs on two gateways remain independent. 9. Unscoped events on simultaneous retained sockets cannot cross-pin. 10. Explicit `local` never aliases omitted legacy-primary routing. 11. One stalled activation cannot permanently wedge later user intent. 12. Multi-window activation and registry edits produce a serializable result. ## Diagnostics / observability Every routed operation should be traceable without logging secrets. Include a correlation tuple such as: ```text connectionId connectionGeneration profile activationEpoch socketInstanceId requestId resourceId ``` A split-brain should be diagnosable from one trace rather than inferred from contradictory UI symptoms. ## Implementation sequence ### Phase 1 — immediate shipped defect - Treat an existing descriptor `connectionId` as authoritative. - Never overwrite it through post-dial inference. - Restrict compatibility inference to genuinely unqualified legacy descriptors. - Reuse the full-fidelity pre-dial identity contract from #88922 / #88697. - Fail closed on zero or multiple matches. - Add duplicate URL/auth/org/header and SSH port/key/path/profile witnesses. ### Phase 2 — canonical route identity - Introduce structured `RouteKey` with connection generation. - Distinguish registered routes from legacy-unregistered routes at the type boundary. - Make explicit `local` a real registered identity, never omission. ### Phase 3 — activation transaction - Return a typed activation receipt from the prepare/dial/publish path. - Return the exact descriptor used by the activated socket. - Consume activation verdicts at all callers before any success side effects. - Bound activation leases / unresolved IPC so one operation cannot wedge the switch coordinator indefinitely. ### Phase 4 — resource ownership - Add `RouteKey` ownership to sessions, cron, projects, OAuth flows, artifacts, FS/Git resources, and other durable/background objects. - Remove ambient foreground routing from mutations against existing resources. ### Phase 5 — route-partitioned state - Source-qualify cache/store keys. - Replace broad switch-time wipe correctness with route-owned partitions and generation revocation. ### Phase 6 — compatibility and concurrency hardening - Version the Desktop IPC routing contract. - Add compatibility diagnostics and retirement criteria. - Add registry revisioning / serialized write semantics. - Define multi-window ownership of `lastUsed` and route mutations. ## Acceptance / adversarial matrix The closing test matrix should include at least: - two URL registrations with the same normalized URL but different auth mode; - same URL with different token/header envelopes; - same Cloud URL under different org/account identity; - two SSH registrations with same user/host but different port; - different key path; - different remote Hermes path; - different remote profile; - exact descriptor `connectionId` survives all of the above; - ambiguous legacy descriptor returns no registered identity; - `(homelab, default)` -> `(homelab, research)` decline leaves route/caches/preferences unchanged; - edit connection generation while activation is in flight; - remove and recreate a connection ID while old work is still completing; - two gateways with identical stored/runtime session IDs; - copied Hermes home with identical project/job/session IDs on two active sources; - simultaneous unscoped stream events from two retained sockets; - explicit local operations while registry primary is remote; - two Desktop windows switching different sources and mutating registry state concurrently. ## Interlocks / provenance - #89719 — shipped registered-gateway switcher and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation; this issue is the architectural follow-through from the merged residual. - #88325 / @dokterdok — substantive source of #89719's fifteen-commit salvage; provenance remains preserved. - #88307 — product request implemented by #89719. - #88922 / #88697 — exact pre-dial route identity architecture that must remain authoritative rather than being weakened post-dial. - #89586 / #89609 — activation-verdict work: completion must prove publication, not merely promise resolution. - #89483 — adjacent atomic-publication work that exposed the need to distinguish prepared, activated, superseded, and declined states. - #89622 — lifecycle race witness around activation leases / target disposal. - #88095 — complementary foreground session/profile ownership work. - #89916 — resource facade ownership: FS/Git must follow the owning route, not ambient foreground state. ## Non-goals This is not a request to replace all compatibility code immediately or to break single-source Desktop behavior. The goal is to establish one canonical identity/ownership model so compatibility code is explicitly fenced and cannot weaken exact v2 identity. It is also not sufficient to solve this by expanding `resolvedConnectionId()` with more matcher fields. That repairs the current witness but leaves the defect class open anywhere identity can later be erased and reconstructed. ## Definition of done This issue is complete when Desktop can prove, by type contract and adversarial tests, that: - exact route identity never becomes less specific downstream; - mutable registrations are generation-bound; - successful activation returns an authoritative receipt; - every durable/background resource carries its owning route; - source-qualified resources cannot alias across gateways; - foreground switching does not determine ownership of already-existing resources; - compatibility inference is explicit, ambiguity-safe, observable, and retireable; - multi-window and registry mutation semantics are serializable and documented. The target architecture should make the current #89719 split-brain impossible to represent, not merely unlikely to reproduce.

signals.title: [Architecture] GitHub automation has split authority: metadata writes succeed while repository-object writes fail
signals.text: ## Summary Our GitHub automation currently exposes a dangerous **split-authority state**: issue/PR metadata mutations succeed, while repository-object mutations fail with `403 Resource not accessible by integration`. This is bigger than one blocked patch or one connector session. It creates a system where an agent can successfully review, comment, retitle, reopen, relabel, and otherwise advance the *control-plane representation* of work while being unable to mutate the *source-of-truth repository objects* required to actually complete that work. The failure mode is especially deceptive because the GitHub App itself advertises the relevant permissions (`contents: write`, `pull_requests: write`, `actions: write`, `workflows: write`), so capability discovery says the operation exists and is writable. The missing dimension is **installation/repository scope**. Observed 2026-08-19 while closing Hermes obligations across #85523, #90048, #88764, #88551, and related PRs. ## Observed authority matrix ### Working The same connected GitHub surface can successfully mutate repository metadata: - create/update issue comments; - submit PR reviews; - update PR title/body; - close/reopen PRs; - update issues and topology. Those writes are live on `NousResearch/hermes-agent`. ### Failing Repository-object and Actions mutations return: ```text 403 Resource not accessible by integration ``` Verified against both `NousResearch/hermes-agent` and `andrexibiza/hermes-agent` where applicable: - Contents create; - Contents update of an existing file using its live blob SHA; - Contents delete of an existing file using its live blob SHA; - branch/ref creation and ref update; - Git Data blob/tree/commit publication paths; - PR creation from a new branch; - Actions rerun / failed-job rerun. The failures are not explained by a missing API wrapper: the Contents, Git Data, branch, PR, and Actions operations are all exposed. ## Installation evidence The connected GitHub App reports permissions including: ```text contents: write pull_requests: write issues: write actions: write workflows: write checks: read statuses: read ``` But installation discovery reports: ```text installations: [] installed accounts: [] installed repository search for hermes-agent: 0 repositories ``` That explains the otherwise contradictory behavior: the connector has a metadata-capable authority path, but there is no repository-installed GitHub App principal backing source/ref/Actions mutations. ## Why this is an architecture problem ### 1. Capability ≠ authorization ≠ installation scope Today these states are easy to conflate: ```text operation exists ≠ app permission includes operation ≠ app is installed on account/org ≠ repository is selected for installation ≠ current principal may mutate this repository object ``` Any agent harness that collapses those layers will produce false capability conclusions in both directions: - **false negative:** “Contents writes are unavailable” when the operation exists but authorization is incomplete; - **false positive:** “I can commit this repair” because the schema says `contents: write`, despite no installed repository principal. ### 2. Metadata success can masquerade as task progress An agent can leave the repository looking increasingly complete: ```text issue updated PR body corrected review posted CI interpretation recorded tracker topology reconciled ``` while the implementation itself remains uncommitted. For autonomous engineering, that is a serious completion-integrity hazard. A packet, issue comment, PR body, or review receipt is not equivalent to a branch/commit/merge receipt. ### 3. The failure arrives too late The current architecture discovers the missing repository principal only when a mutation is attempted. By then an agent may already have: - prepared a patch; - promised a rebase; - classified a task as executable; - updated tracker state; - spent substantial review/implementation effort. Installation scope should be discoverable as a first-class preflight capability. ### 4. Different GitHub object classes can have different authority paths The observed system is not simply “GitHub connected” or “GitHub disconnected.” It is closer to: ```text issue/PR conversation authority: writable repository content/ref authority: unavailable Actions control authority: unavailable public repository read authority: available ``` That needs to be represented explicitly. A single boolean connection state cannot model it. ## Required architecture ### A. First-class effective-capability report Before repository mutation, expose the effective authority tuple: ```text account / organization repository installation id repository selected by installation: yes/no operation class app-declared permission installation-granted permission object-level effective verdict ``` Example: ```json { "repository": "andrexibiza/hermes-agent", "installation": null, "operation": "contents.write", "declared_permission": "write", "effective": false, "reason": "app_not_installed_for_repository" } ``` Do not reduce this to generic `connected: true`. ### B. Distinguish operation classes At minimum model independently: - repository metadata/read; - issues/comments; - pull-request metadata/reviews; - Contents; - Git Data / refs; - PR creation; - Actions control; - workflow mutation; - checks/statuses. ### C. Typed authorization failures Translate GitHub’s generic 403 into the strongest locally provable reason: ```text app_not_installed repository_not_selected permission_not_granted branch_protection_denied organization_policy_denied resource_not_accessible_unknown ``` Preserve the raw GitHub status/message as evidence, but do not make every 403 look identical to the agent. ### D. Mutation preflight For engineering workflows, preflight the actual object class before claiming executability. Examples: ```text "rebase this PR" → verify ref/commit write authority on the head repository "implement this issue" → verify branch + Contents/Git Data + PR creation authority "rerun CI" → verify Actions write authority ``` A successful comment write is not evidence for any of those. ### E. Completion receipts must be object-class specific Completion should require receipts from the layer that owns the requested result: ```text code task → commit SHA + branch/PR/source diff rebase → new head SHA based on required base CI repair → exact-head workflow result review → posted review URL/id issue topology → live issue mutation ``` Metadata-only receipts cannot satisfy code-publication obligations. ### F. Recovery path should be actionable When the only missing prerequisite is installation scope, return the exact boundary: ```text GitHub App is connected but is not installed for andrexibiza/hermes-agent. Install/select that repository for the app before Contents/ref/Actions writes can succeed. ``` Do not tell the user merely to “check permissions,” and do not claim the API itself is unavailable. ## Required regression matrix 1. App schema exposes `contents: write`, no installation exists → preflight says `app_not_installed`, no mutation attempted. 2. Installation exists but repository is not selected → `repository_not_selected`. 3. Repository selected with read-only Contents → `permission_not_granted`. 4. Contents succeeds but Actions permission is absent → code publication allowed, CI rerun denied independently. 5. Issue comments writable while Contents unavailable → authority matrix represents both facts simultaneously. 6. Fork writable but upstream not writable → implementation can publish to fork and open cross-repo PR without assuming upstream source authority. 7. Upstream writable but fork not installed → do not automatically target the fork because the PR head happens to live there. 8. Branch protection rejects a write despite installation + permission → distinguish policy rejection from installation failure. 9. A generic GitHub 403 with insufficient evidence remains `resource_not_accessible_unknown`; never invent the cause. 10. Task-completion logic refuses to mark a code obligation complete from comments/reviews alone. ## Hermes incidents exposing the class This surfaced while processing several otherwise unrelated obligations: - #85523 — implementation patch exists, but code publication cannot occur through the current repository-object authority; - #90048 — exact current-main repair is prepared and locally verified, but no branch/PR can be published; - #88764 — semantic rebase contract is known, but refs cannot be rewritten; - #88551 / #88740 / #88758 — composed repair is specified, but no proof-preserving rebase can be published; - CI rerun attempts returned the same integration-level 403 even though issue/PR metadata remained writable. The common root cause is not any of those codebases. It is the authority model between the agent harness, GitHub App installation scope, and repository object classes. ## Design invariant > **Never infer repository mutation authority from tool presence, declared app permissions, successful metadata writes, or repository readability. Prove effective authorization for the exact object class and repository that owns the requested outcome.** This is the GitHub equivalent of the broader Hermes identity rule: do not discard exact authority information and reconstruct it later from weaker proxies. ## Acceptance criteria - Effective GitHub capabilities are queryable per repository and operation class before mutation. - Installation/account/repository-selection state is represented separately from declared app permissions. - Generic 403s are classified when evidence permits and remain explicitly unknown otherwise. - Engineering workflows preflight the mutation surface they actually require. - Completion logic requires source-of-truth receipts from the owning object class. - Split-authority states are visible and test-covered. - The UI/agent response gives an exact recovery action when repository installation/selection is the missing boundary. - No regression where comment/review success is treated as evidence of Contents/ref/Actions authority. ## Interlocks - #85523 — code-publication blocker that exposed the distinction repeatedly. - #90048 — prepared repair blocked at branch/commit publication. - #88764 — rebase blocked despite complete semantic rebase contract. - #88551 / #88740 / #88758 — proof-preserving compression repair requiring real repository-object mutation. This issue is intentionally about the **authority architecture**, not those individual implementation obligations.

signals.title: Gateway self-heal wedges after Telegram polling network outage — reconnect watcher never takes over
signals.text: # Gateway self-heal wedges after Telegram polling network outage (2026-08-20) **Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20)** | Linux (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0.0-28) | Python 3.12.3 Messaging: telegram (polling mode, direct connection, DoH-discovered fallback IP) + weixin Deployment: `systemd --user` service `hermes-gateway.service` (Restart=always) ## Summary After a Telegram long-polling network outage, the gateway's retryable-fatal error path **wedges the main loop**. The adapter correctly marks the platform retryable-fatal after 10 failed reconnect attempts, but the supervisor handler (`_handle_adapter_fatal_error`) logs the ERROR line and then **never proceeds** — the expected `queued for background reconnection` / `gateway staying alive, watcher will retry` log lines never appear, and the background reconnect watcher never takes over. Telegram stayed disconnected for **4h17m** until a manual process re-start. The cron scheduler (separate asyncio task) kept running normally the whole time; only the messaging main loop was wedged. ## Timeline (all times CST, UTC+8) | Time | Event | |---|---| | ~03:50 | Telegram long-poll connection reset (empty error, CLOSE-WAIT socket seen at 03:50:21) — typical network-path reset on direct connection | | 03:50:01 -> 04:02:31 | 10 exponential-backoff retries (5s->60s cap), all failed, error text empty | | 04:02:31,296 | adapter: `Telegram polling could not reconnect after 10 network error retries.` (logs "Restarting gateway.") | | 04:02:31,302 | gateway.run: `Fatal telegram adapter error (telegram_network_error): ...` | | 04:02:31 -> 08:07 | **COMPLETE LOG SILENCE** in both `gateway.log` and journald — no housekeeping, no reconnect attempts, no watcher activity. Cron jobs (agent.log) ran every 2 min uninterrupted. | | 07:00:45 | a cron job's `send_message` to Telegram **succeeded** (only a MarkdownV2 parse warning) -> network was back by 07:00, but the polling connection was never re-established (send-only, no receive) | | 08:07 | manual `systemctl --user restart hermes-gateway` -> Telegram connected in 2s, everything recovered | ## Evidence (key log lines) ``` 2026-08-20 03:50:01,269 WARNING ...: [Telegram] Telegram polling degraded (heartbeat probe); gateway stays alive and will retry. Error: 2026-08-20 03:50:21,272 WARNING ...: [Telegram] updater.stop() timed out during network-error reconnect (likely CLOSE-WAIT socket); forcing drain and restart without clean stop 2026-08-20 04:02:31,296 ERROR ...: [Telegram] Telegram polling could not reconnect after 10 network error retries. Restarting gateway. Last error: 2026-08-20 04:02:31,302 ERROR gateway.run: Fatal telegram adapter error (telegram_network_error): Telegram polling could not reconnect after 10 network error retries. Restarting gateway. ``` After the last ERROR line: nothing for 4h17m. PID stayed constant (207480); process alive, event loop alive (cron ran), but the gateway main loop produced no logging and performed no recovery. ## Root-cause analysis Code path: `plugins/platforms/telegram/adapter.py:2360` (`_polling_network_error_count > MAX_NETWORK_RETRIES` -> `_set_fatal_error(..., retryable=True)` + `_notify_fatal_error()`) -> `gateway/run.py:4325` `_handle_adapter_fatal_error()`. Expected sequence in `_handle_adapter_fatal_error`: 1. log ERROR (happened) 2. `_update_platform_runtime_status(...)` (unknown — no subsequent logs) 3. `await self._safe_adapter_disconnect(...)` (bounded by `_adapter_disconnect_timeout_secs`, ~210s default) 4. queue platform into `_failed_platforms` + log `queued for background reconnection` 5. log `gateway staying alive, watcher will retry in background` Observed: only step 1 produced output. Steps 2-5's log lines are absent from both `gateway.log` and journald for 4h17m. The reconnect watcher therefore never ran. `_safe_adapter_disconnect` is timeout-bounded, so the wedge is likely either in `_update_platform_runtime_status` (status file write path) or in an await that swallows CancelledError despite the `_await_adapter_cleanup_with_timeout` mitigation (e.g. `adapter.disconnect()` never yielding past the watchdog's cancel, with `consume_detached_task_result` keeping no visible trace). Notably, `errors.log` shows `updater.stop() timed out` (CLOSE-WAIT) earlier in the same outage, suggesting the python-telegram-bot teardown path was already wedged before the fatal handler ran. ## Impact - Telegram channel down ~4h17m (03:50 -> 08:07), only recoverable by manual process re-start. - All other gateway functions (cron scheduler, weixin send path, agent runs) unaffected. - This is the second failure mode of the same outage: the "keep gateway alive, reconnect in background" design (introduced to avoid re-start loops) failed to actually reconnect. ## Suggested investigation 1. Reproduce: simulate 10 consecutive Telegram network errors with a wedged socket and observe whether `_handle_adapter_fatal_error` reaches step 4. 2. Audit awaits between the ERROR log and the `_failed_platforms` enqueue for unbounded or cancellation-swallowing paths (especially `adapter.disconnect()` and the runtime status write). 3. Consider adding a watchdog on the platform-state file (`gateway_state.json`): if `telegram.state` stays non-connected for N minutes, force a hard re-start. ## Local mitigation (user side) A cron watchdog (`~/.hermes/scripts/gateway_watchdog.py`, every 5 min) now re-starts the gateway if `gateway_state.json` shows fatal/retrying/disconnected, or if `connected` has not refreshed in 15 min — with a 10-min re-start cooldown to avoid re-start storms. --- Reported by kevonlee (xwfl15632) · Hermes Agent v0.19.0 · 2026-08-20

signals.title: Windows: Desktop update hand-off hangs forever when gateway stays resident (windows.ps1 waits on ReadToEndAsync that never sees EOF)
signals.text: Summary Updating Hermes from the Desktop app on Windows can hang indefinitely at the "Updating Hermes" screen when a WeChat/Feishu gateway is configured to stay resident. The update pipeline itself completes (git pull, deps, rebuild), but the background hand-off script never finishes, so the result file is never written, the .hermes-update-in-progress marker is never cleared, and the Desktop stays on "Updating Hermes" until manually recovered. Environment - Hermes Agent 40.10.2, upstream main ad889540f - Windows 11, git install, Desktop app (Electron) - Weixin platform configured; gateway kept resident (this is the trigger) Root cause scripts/desktop-update/windows.ps1 — Invoke-HermesStep starts the updater with RedirectStandardOutput/RedirectStandardError and waits via: $outTask = $proc.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync() $errTask = $proc.StandardError.ReadToEndAsync() ... $proc.WaitForExit() ... $outTask.Result # never returns The updater is invoked as hermes update --yes --gateway --force --branch main. On the last step the updater spawns the resident gateway (gateway run --replace). The gateway inherits the updater's stdout/stderr pipe handles, so the pipe never reaches EOF, ReadToEndAsync never completes, and the hand-off script blocks forever on .Result. The hand-off then never writes .hermes-update-result.json, never removes .hermes-update-in-progress, and never relaunches the Desktop. Confirmed by inspecting scripts/desktop-update/windows.ps1 in main at ad889540f. Log evidence - logs/desktop-update-handoff.log stops after the step banner with no exit code line, while the updater itself had already completed (Hermes.exe rebuilt, desktop-build-stamp updated). - Killing the gateway immediately unblocks the script; the script then finishes the hand-off cleanly. - After manual recovery, logs/desktop.log shows detached update finished OK (branch main) and the gateway reconnects ([Weixin] Connected). Suggested fixes 1. Detach the gateway so it does not inherit the updater's pipes. Launch it with CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP/a separate job object, or otherwise close/repoint the inherited stdout/stderr handles so the parent pipe can reach EOF (e.g. redirect to NUL before spawning the resident child). 2. Don't block the hand-off on the updater's live descendant. In windows.ps1, avoid $proc.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync().Result as an EOF wait; use an explicit timeout plus WaitForExit, or spawn the updater with a detached console. 3. Stale-marker watchdog. If the hand-off script or updater makes no progress for > N minutes, write a failed result and clear .hermes-update-in-progress, so the Desktop never shows a dead-end "Updating Hermes" screen. Related Similar symptom family but different root cause: #87772 (stale marker after hung cua-driver installer). #90205 fixed a different hand-off hang (stdin treated as tty → "Restore local changes?" prompt) and is already in main; it does not address this pipe-EOF deadlock.
