signals.title: state.db corruption recurs on SQLite 3.53.1 — WAL sidecar unlink under a concurrent writer
signals.text: ## Summary `state.db` has corrupted multiple times on this host across two profiles. The first three traced to a known-vulnerable SQLite build (WAL-reset #69784, vulnerable ≤3.51.2, via a `pysqlite3` shim bundling 3.51.1). The most recent recurrence hit **both** the builder and reviewer profiles on a **current SQLite 3.53.1**, which #69784's fix line does **not** cover — so the earlier "remove the vulnerable build" closure is incomplete, and a residual corruption mechanism remains. ## Evidence (forensic, read-only) - On the affected DBs, ~20 of ~40 tracked open fds pointed at already-unlinked `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars. - Builder `state.db` page 1 clobbered by a `compression_locks` holder (`pid=4157689 tid=124375474894528 agent=711e8afb2650 nonce=ae12c5e0`); the reviewer DB showed interior b-tree damage (`btreeInitPage error 11`) with an intact header. ## Leading hypothesis (seeking confirmation) Under concurrent connections, a WAL (re-)initialization unlinks the `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars while a writer still holds them open; the next checkpoint then writes to offsets no longer backed by the file → page corruption. Whether the unlink originates in hermes-agent's connection management or is SQLite-level under concurrent WAL re-init is the open question. ## Workaround holding for us **The load-bearing step is a manual exclusive `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` on an idle DB** — not the config pin. `apply_wal_with_fallback()` in `hermes_state.py` returns early for an already-on-disk WAL DB (it never reaches the `configured == "delete"` branch), so a config pin alone leaves an existing DB in WAL with its sidecars intact. The pin only governs a *future* freshly-created DB. Procedure that actually held here (both profiles): 1. Stop the gateways; confirm **zero** live `state.db` fds, including already-deleted `-wal`/`-shm` descriptors. 2. Exclusive `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` on each DB (checkpoints, truncates the sidecars, rewrites the header to write-version 1). 3. Pin `database.journal_mode: delete` in `config.yaml` (affects new DBs only). 4. Restart; verify on-disk header byte 18 == 1 and no `-wal`/`-shm`. Corrected after @jackulau's source read in the discussion below. ## Gap that made this hard The live `WAL → DELETE` downgrade path refuses to run while connections are open, forcing a manual two-step (exclusive `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` on an idle DB, then a config pin). A safe live-downgrade — or a WAL-init that never unlinks active sidecars — would help other operators. ## Related upstream issues (cross-linked from the discussion) - **#85609** — surfaced warning when a `journal_mode` config pin is ignored on an existing WAL DB (our "operator-signal" gap). - **#90871** — skip automatic FTS rebuilds when another process holds the DB or its sidecars (our `~20/40` deleted-fd fingerprint). - **#90837** — second recurring-corruption report; FTS disabled for the last three of eleven incidents. - **#90892** — `synchronous` never executed on Linux; we measured `synchronous=2` (FULL) here, ruling NORMAL out. ## Questions 1. Is the WAL-init sidecar unlink under concurrent connections a known hermes-agent connection-management issue, or SQLite-level? 2. Would it help to attach the preserved corrupt DB copies for a repro? ## Environment - Linux (ext4), Discord + desktop gateways, both profiles. - SQLite 3.53.1 at occurrence time; earlier occurrences ranged the 3.7.0–3.51.2 vulnerability line.
signals.author: jeremykane

signals.title: Desktop app relaunch after in-app update fails to reconnect to WSL backend, requires manual close and reopen
signals.text: ## Symptom After clicking update from the About page on a Windows + WSL2 setup, the update runs and completes successfully (build stamp advances, exit code 0, source tree syncs to latest). The hand-off script relaunches the desktop app automatically. However, the relaunched app fails to reconnect to the WSL backend and stays in a failed state. The user must manually close the app and reopen it to get a working connection. This happens on every update attempt, not intermittently. ## Repro 1. Open the desktop app on Windows + WSL2 (desktop connects to `http://localhost:9119`) 2. Go to About page, observe updates available 3. Click update 4. The update overlay runs, the desktop closes, the hand-off script runs `hermes update` on the Windows side 5. The hand-off script completes with exit code 0 and relaunches the desktop (detached) 6. The relaunched desktop shows a boot failure: "Could not reach the remote Hermes gateway while refreshing its WebSocket ticket" 7. The app does not recover on its own. User must manually close it and reopen 8. After manual reopen, the app connects normally and the update is confirmed present ## What I expected After the hand-off script completes and relaunches the desktop, the app should reconnect to the WSL backend and present a working chat surface without manual intervention. ## What actually happens The relaunched desktop hits liveness probe failures and "Desktop boot failed: Could not reach the remote Hermes gateway while refreshing its WebSocket ticket" errors. From the user's perspective, the update failed and the app is broken. The only way to recover is to manually close and reopen. ## Evidence Desktop log showing the update trigger, relaunch, and boot failures: ``` [2026-08-20T18:07:13.253Z] [updates] restart: Updating Hermes — this window will close and the updater will open. [2026-08-20T18:07:14.388Z] [updates] launched repo hand-off script: windows.ps1 (branch main); exiting desktop to release venv shim [2026-08-20T18:13:03.270Z] [boot] Resolving Hermes backend [2026-08-20T18:13:03.667Z] [boot] Connecting to remote Hermes backend at http://localhost:9119 [2026-08-20T18:13:03.670Z] [boot] Remote Hermes backend is ready ``` Hand-off log showing successful update and relaunch: ``` 2026-08-20T13:13:02-05:00 update| ✓ Update complete! (v0.20.4) [main @ 59795c40f] 2026-08-20T13:13:02-05:00 hermes update exit code: 0 2026-08-20T13:13:02-05:00 removed update marker (owned) 2026-08-20T13:13:03-05:00 relaunching desktop: C:\Users\Krekos\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\apps\desktop\release\win-unpacked\Hermes.exe 2026-08-20T13:13:03-05:00 desktop relaunched detached (pid 18420) 2026-08-20T13:13:03-05:00 focused relaunched desktop window ``` The update itself succeeds. The build stamp advances correctly. The problem is specifically the post-update relaunch failing to establish a stable backend connection from the user's perspective, even when the log shows a brief "ready" state. Liveness probe failures also appear during WSL backend restarts (not just post-update), suggesting the backend may not be fully ready to accept WebSocket connections when the desktop first tries to reconnect: ``` [hermes] Cached remote Hermes backend failed liveness probe (1/3); keeping connection for retry. [hermes] Cached remote Hermes backend failed liveness probe (2/3); keeping connection for retry. [hermes] Cached remote Hermes backend failed liveness probe; dropping stale connection. [hermes] [boot] Desktop boot failed: Could not reach the remote Hermes gateway while refreshing its WebSocket ticket. Try reconnecting. ``` ## User impact Every in-app update requires manual intervention to recover. The user sees an error state after the update completes and has no way to know whether the update succeeded without manually closing, reopening, and checking the About page. This undermines confidence in the update flow that #88827 fixed. ## Environment - OS: Windows 11 + WSL2 (Ubuntu) - Backend: Hermes Agent v0.20.4, WSL `hermes serve` on port 9119 - Desktop: Hermes Electron app, package 0.17.0, built from `59795c40` - Desktop source: `C:\Users\Krekos\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent` - Backend source: `/home/krekos/.hermes/hermes-agent` - Connection: Desktop app connects to `http://localhost:9119` (remote mode, OAuth) ## Related issues - #88827 (closed) — Fixed the update flow to run the full multi-target update including desktop rebuild. This issue is the next step: the update runs correctly but the post-update relaunch fails to reconnect. - #88251 (closed) — Fixed the `get-windows` binding staging. Not related to this restart issue.

signals.title: Desktop sidebar should separate Projects and Sessions into independent sections with their own sorting menus
signals.text: ## Problem The desktop sidebar currently renders Projects and Sessions as the same section. A "grouping" setting (date, profile, project, status) changes what the section header says and what content appears underneath. You can either see your flat sessions list OR your project overview, but never both at the same time. Switching between them is buried in a filter menu dropdown that also contains nine other controls: ordering, status filter, project filter, profile filter, PR filter, archived toggle, card row toggle, row meta toggle, and the grouping mode itself. This makes the sidebar hard to navigate, especially once you start actively using projects. Sessions assigned to a project disappear from the flat list when you switch to project grouping, so you lose track of where things are. The mental model is "one section that transforms" instead of "two sections that coexist." ## What I'd like Separate Projects and Sessions into two independent sidebar sections, each with their own header, expand/collapse, and sorting menu. Similar to how Claude Desktop handles this. **Sessions section:** - Always visible, shows all chat sessions (API, Telegram, TUI, etc.) - Has its own sorting menu (date, status, pinned, etc.) - Sessions that are assigned to a project can either be duplicated here (like Claude Desktop) or filtered out when a "hide project sessions" toggle is on. Either approach works. The key is that this section exists independently and always has its own controls. - Pinning works within this section **Projects section:** - Separate row in the sidebar (alongside Pinned, Telegram, API, Cron Jobs, etc.) - Has its own sorting menu (alphabetical, recent activity, custom drag order) - Clicking a project expands it to show that project's sessions underneath - Sessions under a project can be pinned within the project - The project section's sorting and filtering do not affect the Sessions section and vice versa ## Why this is better than the current design The current design tries to do everything in one space with a grouping toggle. That means: - You can never see projects and sessions at the same time - Nine controls are crammed into one filter dropdown - Assigning a session to a project makes it harder to find in the flat list - The section header changes meaning depending on which mode you're in (which was the original confusion reported in #62537) Two separate sections with similar functionality and independent sorting would solve all of these. Projects become a first-class navigation surface instead of a view mode on the sessions list. ## Related issues - #62537 (open) — Reported the header mislabeling when the source filter toggle changes the section name. This is a symptom of the same root design: one section that transforms based on grouping mode. Separating Projects and Sessions would make #62537 moot. ## Environment - Hermes Desktop (Electron) on Windows 11 + WSL2 - Hermes v0.20.4, desktop package 0.17.0
signals.author: pearonjames

signals.title: [Bug]: @ context reference expansion aborts whole asyncio.gather and leaks sibling coroutines (missing return_exceptions=True)
signals.text: ### Bug Description `preprocess_context_references_async` in `agent/context_references.py` expands all `@` context references concurrently with a **bare** `asyncio.gather(...)` that has **no `return_exceptions=True`**. When a single reference expansion raises, the whole gather aborts, the exception propagates into the caller, and the still-running sibling coroutines are **left unawaited** (coroutine leak) — a classic asyncio hazard. This contradicts every other `gather` in the codebase, which uses the defensive `return_exceptions=True` pattern. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Send a message containing multiple `@` context references (e.g. `@file` + `@url`), where one of the references fails to expand (e.g. `url_fetcher` raises on that ref, or the file read errors). 2. Observe the exception from the failing ref propagate and abort the entire gather. 3. The concurrent sibling `_expand_reference` coroutines for the other refs are never awaited → coroutine leak ("coroutine was never awaited" / untracked tasks). ### Expected Behavior A failure in one reference expansion should be surfaced as a **warning** for that ref only, while the other refs' expansions complete normally. No coroutines should leak, and the caller should not crash. ### Actual Behavior A single ref failure aborts the whole gather, crashes/errors the caller, and leaks the sibling coroutines that were still running. ### Suggested Fix (mirrors existing pattern in codebase) ```python expanded = await asyncio.gather( *(_expand_reference(ref, cwd_path, url_fetcher=url_fetcher, allowed_root=allowed_root_path) for ref in refs), return_exceptions=True, ) for i, result in enumerate(expanded): if isinstance(result, BaseException): warnings.append(f"@ {refs[i].kind} reference expansion failed: {result}") continue warning, block = result ... ``` Affected location: `agent/context_references.py`, `preprocess_context_references_async` (gather begins at line ~267, unpack loop at ~278 on latest `origin/main`).
signals.author: Iversondwx

signals.title: [Bug]: gateway nested-PYTHONPATH duplication — inherited value appended as one string defeats dict.fromkeys dedupe (doubles every restart)
signals.text: ### Bug Description In `gateway/run.py`, `_ensure_windows_gateway_venv_imports()` (and the equivalent watcher branch in `GatewayRunner`) builds the new `PYTHONPATH` by **appending the inherited PYTHONPATH as a single string element** before `dict.fromkeys()` dedupes: ```python pythonpath = [project_entry, site_entry] if os.environ.get("PYTHONPATH"): pythonpath.append(os.environ["PYTHONPATH"]) # "a;b;c" appended as ONE element os.environ["PYTHONPATH"] = os.pathsep.join(dict.fromkeys(pythonpath)) ``` Because the inherited PYTHONPATH is appended as one raw string, `dict.fromkeys()` treats `"a;b;c"` as a single element and cannot dedupe its interior segments against `project_entry`/`site_entry`. Every gateway start that inherits a multi-segment PYTHONPATH **doubles** it: observed `2 -> 4 -> 8` segments. The bloated value is then inherited by every child process. Related but distinct from #57467 (which is about leaking PYTHONPATH *into other processes*): this is the gateway's own *duplication* of PYTHONPATH on every start. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. On Windows, start with an inherited `PYTHONPATH` containing multiple path segments (set by any launcher/venv activation — e.g. `C:\...\hermes-agent;C:\...\venv\Lib\site-packages`). 2. Start the gateway (`python -m gateway.run`). 3. Check `PYTHONPATH` in `_ensure_windows_gateway_venv_imports` after the build — the project/site entries now appear both as individual segments *and* inside the appended raw string. 4. Repeat a gateway restart — each start appends the (now duplicate-laden) inherited value again → segments accumulate / double with each restart. ### Expected Behavior `dict.fromkeys()` should actually dedupe — i.e. each PYTHONPATH *segment* should be matched individually, so repeated gateway starts keep PYTHONPATH stable instead of growing it. ### Actual Behavior PYTHONPATH doubles (`2 -> 4 -> 8`) on repeated gateway starts because the inherited value is appended as one raw string that `dict.fromkeys()` can't dedupe segment-wise. ### Suggested Fix (split before deduping) ```python if os.environ.get("PYTHONPATH"): pythonpath.extend(e for e in os.environ["PYTHONPATH"].split(os.pathsep) if e) os.environ["PYTHONPATH"] = os.pathsep.join(dict.fromkeys(pythonpath)) ``` Same fix applies to the watcher branch in `GatewayRunner` (watcher_env PYTHONPATH). Affected location: `gateway/run.py`, `_ensure_windows_gateway_venv_imports` (lines ~508-511 on latest `origin/main`) and the `GatewayRunner` watcher_env block (~line 11370).

signals.title: Double-clicking the Sessions/Bots sidebar tab hides the tab strip with no way to restore it
signals.text: **App:** Hermes desktop (Linux) · client v0.20.4 · repo `8794e5a` (2026-08-20) **Steps to reproduce** 1. Open the Hermes desktop app on Linux. 2. In the left sidebar header, double-click the **Sessions** tab (two clicks within ~400 ms). 3. The entire tab strip collapses to zero height — the **Sessions**, **Bots**, and session-title tabs all disappear, and chat content jumps flush to the top edge. Double-clicking **Bots** does the same in reverse. **Expected** A double-click on Sessions/Bots is either inert (single-click already switches the sidebar view), or — if hiding the tab bar is intended — there must be an always-reachable way to show it again. **Actual** The strip is hidden with no reachable undo. The "Show header" item exists in code but renders only on the tab strip, so once the strip is gone there is nothing left to right-click to bring it back. The only recovery is opening a new session tab (Ctrl+T), which happens to reset `headerHidden`. **Root cause** - `apps/desktop/src/components/pane-shell/tree/renderer/tree-group.tsx` — `hideHeaderDoubleTap` → `setTreeGroupHeaderHidden(node.id, true)` - `apps/desktop/src/components/pane-shell/tree/renderer/drag-session.ts` — `DOUBLE_TAP_MS = 400` - `tree-group.tsx:161` — the "Show header" item, unreachable when the strip is hidden **Proposed direction (for discussion, not a fix request)** Make the gesture fail-closed: keep a header-restore affordance reachable even while the strip is hidden, or require an explicit confirm. Happy to open a PR if maintainers want it.

signals.title: Feature: canonical unified sessions across WebUI and Telegram
signals.text: ## Problem Hermes currently treats WebUI and Telegram as separate conversation surfaces. A user may talk to the same profile from both surfaces, but the conversations are stored and displayed as separate session transcripts. Sharing a profile, chat ID, or routing key does not make the history or live turns unified. This makes a WebUI/Telegram workflow unreliable for users who want to start a task in Telegram, continue it in WebUI, and receive WebUI replies back in the same Telegram conversation. The existing delivery mirror path is useful for one-off outbound notifications, but it does not provide a canonical conversation session or reliable bidirectional synchronization. ## Proposed behavior Add a supported cross-surface session attachment or unified-session mechanism: - A WebUI session can attach to an existing Telegram-origin session without creating a second transcript. - User and assistant messages from both surfaces appear in the same history. - Replies are delivered exactly once to the originating Telegram chat and topic. - Starting a new WebUI conversation has an explicit, predictable attachment policy; it must not silently bind to a stale session. - Session resets, model changes, tool calls, streaming, and errors preserve the same routing identity. - The behavior works with Telegram topics and normal private chats and remains profile-isolated. ## Acceptance criteria - A message sent from Telegram is visible in the attached WebUI session. - A message sent from WebUI is visible in the same Telegram chat/topic. - The two surfaces show the same ordered user/assistant transcript after refresh. - No duplicate assistant replies are produced during reconnects or retries. - A service restart does not create a new detached transcript. - Existing independent WebUI and Telegram sessions continue to work unchanged when no attachment is requested. ## Scope note Hermes-Relay's Android app can consume upstream Hermes sessions, but the canonical session/routing behavior belongs in hermes-agent. Relay can then display or select the unified session through its existing session APIs.

signals.title: Windows: desktop self-update frequently fails — running hermes.exe locked (os error 32); needs staged update or self-shutdown before replace
signals.text: ## Summary On Windows, the desktop app's self-update frequently fails with file-lock errors (os error 32: another process is using the file) because the updater tries to replace **hermes.exe** and the venv files **while the app itself is still running**. ## Root cause The updater runs inside the running app (or a child of it) and attempts to replace: - `venv/Scripts/hermes.exe` (locked by the running process) - venv packages (locked by the loaded interpreter) Windows does not allow replacing a running executable, so the update aborts. This is not a network or permission issue — it is a **design flaw in the self-update flow**: it never shuts itself down (or defers the swap to a restart) before replacing files. ## Observed behavior - 'Update failed' toast/status repeatedly across 8/15, 8/17, 8/20 - Logs show `os error 32: 另一个程序正在使用此文件 (another program is using this file)` - Falling behind remote by ~33 commits at times because updates keep failing ## Every failed/successful update also leaves residue Each update attempt (successful or failed) drops a `state.db.pre-update-emergency-<timestamp>.bak` (~650-750MB each) and a `win-unpacked.bak` (~380MB) that are never cleaned up. After a few updates these accumulate to **2.5-3 GB** of junk. Recent 7-day C: drive growth attributable to Hermes updates alone: ~6.5 GB. ## Proposed fixes (any of) 1. **Staged/atomic update**: download new version to a temp dir, then on next app start (before the main process fully boots) swap files — the classic 'update on restart' pattern. 2. **Self-shutdown before replace**: updater asks the app to exit cleanly, waits for PID to die, then replaces files, then relaunches. 3. **Cleanup residue**: after a successful update, delete `state.db.pre-update-emergency-*.bak` and `win-unpacked.bak` automatically (or keep only the most recent one). ## Environment - Windows 10 19045 - Hermes desktop app, branch main - Venv-based install under `AppData/Local/hermes`

signals.title: [Architecture / Publication] Task Completion Verification — exact-object completion as the sixth Hermes law
signals.text: ## Thesis **All Gods Must Die: Adversarially Verified Transformation** currently gives Hermes five executable laws for changing load-bearing artifacts: 1. No system component may accumulate authority without becoming legible. 2. No claim may outrank its evidence. 3. No actor may certify itself. 4. No rule counts until it executes. 5. No debt gets to hide behind institutional forgetting. A concrete repository-execution record exposed the missing execution-level law: > **No task is complete until the requested state exists at the authoritative target and is verified on the exact object.** Derivative rule: > **No receipt may be inherited from a local draft, previous head, adjacent commit, parent object, superseded artifact, or intended write.** This issue canonizes that rule as **Amendment I — Task Completion Verification** and makes the doctrine machine-auditable through a completion contract, typed state vector, exact-object receipt model, temporal mutation ledger, JSON Schema, versioned publication lineage, and explicit interlocks to the live Hermes objects that exposed the class. The defect class is **activity-completion collapse**: evidence that work occurred is promoted into evidence that the requested state exists. ```text patch prepared != branch changed branch changed != pull request submitted pull request submitted != exact-head verified exact-head verified != accepted accepted != merged merged != released released != operationally verified historical object exists != historical object is canonical write attempted != target mutation occurred ``` This is not administrative language. It is an authority model for Hermes itself. --- ## Scope and non-duplication This issue is the **publication/doctrine and repository-contract node**. It does not replace the existing runtime architecture nodes: - #90049 remains the implementation/defect-class owner for **false success / completion laundering inside Hermes runtime surfaces**. - #90200 remains the authority-model owner for **GitHub split authority**, where issue/PR metadata writes succeed while repository-object and Actions mutations may fail. - #90144 remains the rule that **proof scope must equal mutation scope**. - #90145 remains the temporal rule that stale actors must be fenced by **durable generation identity**. - #90150 remains the realization rule that **the built artifact and real peer are part of the system under test**. - #90866 remains the composition rule that observable state must remain **proof-carrying from source to side effect**. This issue binds those rules into the architecture thesis and defines the lifecycle predicates, receipts, release semantics, and publication surfaces that make the thesis reproducible. --- ## Why the existing doctrine needed a sixth law The original paper already rejects producer self-certification. A god-file implementer cannot approve its own extraction; a translator cannot certify its own localized graph; claims must resolve against golden hashes, seam identity, parity gates, CI, manifests, and public interlocks. But an agent can apply those rules to code while narrating its own execution loosely: - a patch exists locally, therefore the repository is fixed; - a command exited zero, therefore the durable postcondition exists; - an API request was sent, therefore the target changed; - a comment was posted, therefore implementation work was published; - one workflow was green, therefore the current head is green; - a previous head passed, therefore a rewritten head inherits the receipt; - a historical PR contains the idea, therefore it remains the delivery object; - a plausible summary says “done,” therefore the work reached the source of truth. Every example substitutes one predicate for another. The system needs types, not stronger adjectives. --- ## Completion contract Every work order should resolve to a completion contract: ```text C = ( authoritative_system, exact_target_object, requested_predicate, admissible_evidence, acceptance_authority, required_graph_closure ) ``` Where: - **authoritative system** is the system that owns the requested state: GitHub, a release registry, deployed service, package repository, durable database, or explicitly local filesystem; - **exact target object** is the branch ref, commit, pull request, issue comment, review, workflow run, release, deployment, file blob, endpoint, or other object named by the request; - **requested predicate** is the exact state requested: `prepared`, `submitted`, `verified`, `accepted`, `merged`, `published`, `released`, `operationally_verified`, etc.; - **admissible evidence** is the minimum receipt set capable of proving that predicate; - **acceptance authority** is the actor/system empowered to decide the predicate when external authority is required; - **graph closure** is the required provenance, dependency, supersession, credit, and interlock state. A local patch can complete a request to **prepare a patch**. It cannot complete a request to **fix the PR**, **push the branch**, **post the review**, **merge the change**, or **verify production**. Formally: ```text Complete(C) iff target_exists_in_authoritative_system AND target_was_read_back_after_mutation AND evidence_is_bound_to_exact_target_version AND evidence_proves_requested_predicate AND required_acceptance_authority_is_satisfied AND required_graph_edges_are_closed ``` --- ## Completion is a state vector, not one green word A single linear status cannot represent repository truth. A PR can exist and be exact-head green while unreviewed and unmerged. A release can exist but remain operationally unverified. A fully tested historical PR can be superseded. | Axis | Representative states | Governing question | |---|---|---| | Materialization | `absent`, `local_only`, `target_present` | Where do the bytes or state actually exist? | | Integrity | `unverified`, `locally_verified`, `read_back`, `exact_object_verified` | Which exact object was checked? | | Governance | `unreviewed`, `reviewed`, `accepted`, `rejected` | What authority evaluated which version? | | Integration | `not_submitted`, `open`, `closed_unmerged`, `merged`, `released` | How far did the object enter the repository/release channel? | | Operation | `not_exercised`, `hermetic_verified`, `operationally_verified` | Was delivered behavior tested on the real execution surface? | | Lineage | `active`, `blocked`, `superseded`, `retracted`, `abandoned` | Is this still canonical, and why? | The completion claim is the exact conjunction required by the contract. It may be weaker than intended. It may never be stronger than the receipts. --- ## Predicate-to-receipt matrix | Predicate claimed | Minimum receipt | What it does **not** prove | |---|---|---| | `prepared` | artifact path + content digest | target mutation, review, CI, merge | | `locally_verified` | command + exit status + exact input digest | remote submission or target state | | `submitted` | target URL/object ID + post-write read-back | acceptance, merge, release, runtime behavior | | `exact_object_verified` | immutable/versioned target identity + checks bound to it | maintainer acceptance or integration | | `accepted` | designated authority verdict on the exact verified object | merge, release, deployment | | `merged` | merge commit/default-branch reachability | release or production behavior | | `published` / `released` | immutable release identifier + digest | successful real-world operation | | `operationally_verified` | real-surface receipt bound to release/deployment identity | universal correctness outside tested conditions | | `blocked` | failed operation + exact error + boundary owner | completion | | `superseded` | typed edge to canonical successor + retirement state | that the historical object should merge | ### Exact-object rule for CI For target object version `v` and workflow receipt `r`: ```text CIValid(v, r) iff target_head(v) == workflow_head(r) ``` The following are useful diagnostic context but are not evidence for this predicate: - parent success; - merge-base success; - prior-head success; - sibling-PR success; - nearby-main success; - a green synthetic merge candidate for a different head. **Green is not hereditary.** --- ## Exact-object verification requirements A target object is exact-object verified only when all applicable requirements hold: 1. **Authoritative existence** — the object exists in the target system, not only in a local workspace or narrative. 2. **Stable identity** — URL plus object ID, commit SHA, blob hash, release digest, workflow-run ID, review ID, or equivalent. 3. **Post-write read-back** — the target is retrieved after the attempted mutation. 4. **Version binding** — every check, review, or receipt identifies the exact version it evaluated. 5. **Predicate match** — the receipt proves the state claimed, not a weaker adjacent state. 6. **Authority match** — the actor making an acceptance/merge/release decision actually owns that transition. 7. **Graph closure** — provenance, dependency, credit, and supersession edges required by the work are present. 8. **Temporal honesty** — later success does not rewrite an earlier failed mutation, and an earlier blocker does not erase later valid state. --- ## Concrete case study: the webhook publication record The supplied Task Completion Verification record captured two real repairs and one real authority boundary. ### Task 7 — named-profile configuration The prepared patch made `resolve_effective_webhook_config("worker")` read the requested profile's own `config.yaml` through Hermes' context-local home override, then restore the prior override before the next default-profile read. Historical local patch: ```text SHA-256 9c5d2cb4e3a2e17a114caee171eac53459700a94ae307d9fb671387142b92cf0 ``` At the recorded execution boundary: ```text materialization: local_only integrity: locally_verified integration: not_submitted lineage: blocked ``` ### Task 10 — HTTP/intake contract The prepared patch closed five concrete contract holes: - idempotency key includes `(profile, route, provider, delivery_id)`; - rate limiting is isolated by profile and route; - valid JSON arrays/scalars fail cleanly as non-object envelopes; - `original_bytes` and caps use UTF-8 byte accounting; - the default prompt uses the same valid raw-payload envelope as `{__raw__}`. Historical local patch: ```text SHA-256 62c158b8d1860edebe54002fc34e0cdc95b5b59743a3cd531f349929f6c135a5 ``` At the recorded execution boundary it had the same state vector: locally prepared, locally structurally verified, remotely blocked, not submitted. ### The authority boundary Three independent GitHub mutation routes were attempted against the fork: 1. Contents API; 2. blob/tree/commit construction; 3. direct tree/ref publication. Every route returned: ```text 403 Resource not accessible by integration ``` No branch moved. No public repository object changed. The correct result was **blocked after local verification**, not “fixed” or “completed.” The `403` is a valid blocked-state receipt because it proves the attempted object class, target system, rejection, and authority boundary. It is not a completion receipt. --- ## Temporal reconciliation: the graph later moved The dated blocker remains true. Later repository work created new source-of-truth objects. Both truths belong in the mutation journal. ### Task 7 canonical object - PR: #85002 - exact head: `355b50a30c184f1c70df172e018dedd240bd7400` - state at reconciliation: open, non-draft, mergeable - exact-head CI: success - exact-head Docker: success - exact-head Nix: success The later PR does not retroactively turn the earlier `403` into a successful write. It is a later materialization event with its own identity and receipts. ### Task 10 supersession Historical PR #85523 is: - closed; - unmerged; - explicitly retained as provenance; - superseded by #90236. Canonical successor #90236 is: - open; - non-draft; - mergeable at the observed reconciliation; - exact head `416c5e48aefcccfe945f7d4118415a3b992e017a`; - exact-head CI/Docker/Nix successful at the recorded head. The graph is: ```text #85523 --superseded_by--> #90236 #90236 --canonical_for--> Webhook Task 10 ``` Supersession preserves authorship, review history, and requirements without letting stale topology masquerade as the active delivery object. --- ## Refinement of the original `SHIPPED` standard The original paper deliberately defines a god file as `SHIPPED` when every agreed slice has been extracted, blind-reviewed to agreement, and landed as an individually interlocked open PR. That remains a valid campaign-specific definition. It must be namespaced: ```text KAG_SHIPPED ``` `KAG_SHIPPED` means the exact state defined by the Kill All Gods ledger. It does **not** entail: ```text MERGED PUBLISHED RELEASED DEPLOYED OPERATIONALLY_VERIFIED ``` This preserves the original paper's auditability standard while preventing a downstream system from inheriting a stronger lifecycle claim from the word “shipped.” --- ## The same architecture applies to papers and pull requests | Pull request concept | Paper concept | Shared invariant | |---|---|---| | working tree | manuscript draft | mutable local work is not a submitted object | | commit SHA | release digest | evidence binds exact bytes | | CI run | reproducibility/source/format checks | checks identify the exact release evaluated | | review | independent technical/semantic witness | author is not sole acceptance authority | | merge | accepted integration | acceptance and publication remain distinct | | release | immutable paper version | later refinement creates a successor, not silent mutation | | superseding PR | successor edition/amendment | lineage remains explicit and machine-readable | | production verification | replication/operationalization | publication alone does not prove real-world behavior | The August 2026 68-page PDF remains immutable v1.0. Amendment I is independently sourced. The composed v1.1 release is a successor artifact: ```text All Gods Must Die v1.0 --refined_by--> Amendment I: Task Completion Verification --composed_as--> All Gods Must Die v1.1 ``` No v1.0 page is silently replaced. --- ## Source-controlled doctrine surfaces The implementation/publication contribution is PR #80551 at exact source head: ```text 048606e79810a42fcc243e2ae30373c91eacf574 ``` | Surface | Role | Exact Git blob | |---|---|---| | [`task-completion-verification-amendment.md`](https://github.com/andrexibiza/hermes-agent/blob/048606e79810a42fcc243e2ae30373c91eacf574/docs/research/task-completion-verification-amendment.md) | canonical formal amendment | `bdcc3732fa18fa5ec9827a11281a4eaebae98fca` | | [`task-completion-record.schema.json`](https://github.com/andrexibiza/hermes-agent/blob/048606e79810a42fcc243e2ae30373c91eacf574/docs/research/task-completion-record.schema.json) | machine-auditable blocker + later GitHub reconciliation | `ed00b9ddb8b795c9e5e97289c2afe274c332e8ea` | | architecture guide | `fe2f5b9f915d677a43120a1a648d3c665a9cbe5c` | | source/output digests + typed lineage | `3323fa2f725e7531baa80f3b4d4cc942388110df` | | [`all-gods-must-die-interlock.md`](https://github.com/andrexibiza/hermes-agent/blob/048606e79810a42fcc243e2ae30373c91eacf574/docs/research/all-gods-must-die-interlock.md) | contribution and lifecycle graph | `0c5f34693c8309e8c5798d339237e968c28baf37` | ### Generated release outputs The following outputs were built, PDF-preflighted, rendered, and visually inspected locally. Their binary presence in the GitHub tree is **not** asserted by the source publication. | Output | Pages | SHA-256 | Current predicate | |---|---:|---|---| | Amendment I PDF | 14 | `1a8f46528faf10339e7d0cdeb3cf0b8035b341a23ffbde2b0b7aa19e361505f5` | `locally_verified` | | Composed All Gods Must Die v1.1 PDF | 83 | `be5f9c912025eb2fbbcbcef2a497eb76f041db7ecfa6637550fe7bbae1fb805b` | `locally_verified` | | Source-and-release package | — | `51275dfa4fa7d55f4f14addfeceb1a665b567e0a9806c50ef105100f5d4cc126` | `locally_verified` | Publishing those binaries to GitHub is a separate object-class predicate requiring its own commit/tree read-back. --- ## Exact current PR state at filing PR #80551: ```text head: 048606e79810a42fcc243e2ae30373c91eacf574 state: open ready: non-draft mergeable: yes at last read-back merged: no ``` Exact-head workflows: - Docker `32437208692`: **success** - Nix `32437208780`: **success** - CI `32437209235`: **failure** The connector-exposed CI job page showed its visible jobs green or skipped, including Docusaurus, attribution, supply-chain, E2E, Windows/macOS, ruff, and exposed Python slices. The run-level aggregate nevertheless remained red, so an unexposed later-page/aggregate job failed. Therefore the current claim is deliberately bounded: > The amendment sources are submitted and exact-object read back at `048606e…`; Docker and Nix are exact-head green; PR #80551 is open, non-draft, mergeable, unmerged, and CI-red. No all-green, accepted, merged, published-binary, or released claim is made. --- ## Machine enforcement The JSON Schema and ledger are not illustrative appendices. They are the first executable expression of this architecture. A completion verifier must reject a record when any of the following is true: 1. the requested predicate is stronger than the observed evidence; 2. a remote predicate has no target locator or post-write read-back; 3. CI/review evidence binds a different SHA/version than the claimed object; 4. a local path or patch digest is offered as proof of remote mutation; 5. an object marked active has a live `superseded_by` edge; 6. a historical PR is presented as canonical after a successor owns the contract; 7. required provenance, dependency, credit, or interlock edges are missing; 8. generic `done`, `fixed`, `shipped`, or `green` appears without a namespaced predicate; 9. a write failure is omitted from the mutation journal; 10. a target-state claim cannot be reproduced by a third party from durable receipts; 11. a manifest or producer narrative attempts to certify its own publication; 12. an exact-object receipt is transferred to rebuilt or otherwise different bytes. ### Required repository integration The architecture should ultimately provide: - a canonical completion-record schema under repository ownership; - a validator with positive and negative fixtures; - a standard way for engineering agents to emit completion records; - exact-head workflow receipt ingestion; - typed supersession and blocker edges; - lint pressure against unqualified completion words in automation outputs where a stronger object state is required; - read-back verification after every GitHub mutation; - object-class capability preflight before an engineering workflow promises executability; - mutation-journal preservation of both failed and successful attempts. --- ## Adversarial regression matrix At minimum, permanent tests should cover: - [ ] local patch exists but no branch/ref changed; - [ ] comment/review write succeeds while Contents/ref write fails; - [ ] branch push succeeds but PR creation fails; - [ ] PR exists but the expected head SHA is not present; - [ ] prior-head CI is green while current head has no receipt; - [ ] parent/sibling/main CI is green while target head is red or untested; - [ ] workflow receipt names a different SHA than the completion record; - [ ] write returns success but post-write read-back disagrees; - [ ] timeout leaves remote mutation ambiguous; - [ ] historical PR is closed and a successor is active; - [ ] superseded object is incorrectly marked active; - [ ] accepted object remains unmerged; - [ ] merged source has no release artifact; - [ ] released artifact has no operational receipt; - [ ] generated PDF exists locally but is absent from the Git tree; - [ ] manifest self-claims publication without authoritative read-back; - [ ] late success does not rewrite the earlier blocked attempt; - [ ] earlier blocker does not erase later exact-object success; - [ ] `KAG_SHIPPED` cannot be parsed as `MERGED` or `RELEASED`; - [ ] removing any required graph/credit edge prevents campaign-complete status. Every negative test must assert that the stronger state transition does **not** occur. --- ## Acceptance criteria This issue is complete only when: ### Doctrine and publication - [ ] The sixth law is accepted as part of the Hermes architecture doctrine. - [ ] The original v1.0 publication remains immutable and the amendment/release lineage is explicit. - [ ] `KAG_SHIPPED` is documented as campaign-specific and not a release synonym. - [ ] The architecture guide, formal amendment, schema, ledger, release manifest, and interlock remain one contribution graph. - [ ] Generated release binaries, when published, receive exact Git blob/commit receipts; local hashes alone do not count as publication. ### Runtime and automation contract - [ ] Completion predicates have a shared typed vocabulary. - [ ] Every remote mutation path performs post-write read-back. - [ ] CI/review receipts bind the exact target version. - [ ] Stale, partial, blocked, ambiguous, and superseded states remain first-class rather than becoming success. - [ ] GitHub capability preflight distinguishes metadata, Contents, refs/Git Data, PR creation, Actions, checks, and workflow authority per repository. - [ ] A successful metadata write cannot satisfy a code-publication contract. - [ ] A target object cannot inherit green/acceptance/release state from an adjacent object. - [ ] Completion records are machine-validated and failure injection proves the verifier rejects overclaiming. ### Graph and provenance - [ ] PR #80551 and this issue are linked in both directions. - [ ] #90049 links this issue as the doctrine/publication layer without losing runtime implementation ownership. - [ ] #90200 links this issue as the authority-boundary case study without being closed by documentation. - [ ] #85002, #85523, and #90236 preserve the dated event sequence and typed supersession. - [ ] #78647 and the sibling campaign/skill nodes carry the publication edge. - [ ] Axl Ibiza's authorship of the doctrine and publication remains explicit; contributor, reviewer, agent, and source-project credit is preserved at its exact boundary. ### Exact current contribution - [ ] PR #80551 reaches exact-head CI green at its final head. - [ ] No green is inherited from `048606e…` if the head changes. - [ ] Maintainer acceptance, merge, binary publication, and release are reported as separate later predicates with their own receipts. --- ## Interlocks / topology ### Doctrine and campaign graph - #80551 — implementation/publication PR for the paper, guide, skill, amendment, schema, ledger, manifest, and interlock. - #78647 — Kill All Gods / graph-gated engineering EPIC. - #79609 — god-file kill campaign / 5×2×3 decomposition skill. - #79779 — KILL LOCK operations and bidirectional audit. - #79898 — Feature Parity & Alignment campaigns. - #80391 / #80392 — cross-language documentation germination implementation and EPIC. - #60535 / #63660 — French seed request and contributor provenance. ### Completion architecture series - #90049 — false success / typed completion proofs. - #90200 — GitHub split-authority capability model. - #90144 — proof scope equals mutation scope. - #90145 — generation-fenced mutation/recovery. - #90150 — delivered realization is part of the proof boundary. - #90866 — proof-carrying observable state. ### Webhook case-study graph - #84834 — Webhook Feature Package EPIC. - #85002 — Task 7 canonical effective-config object. - #85523 — closed/unmerged Task 10 historical provenance. - #90236 — canonical Task 10 successor. - #85644 — terminal partial/per-target delivery truth; A repository that cannot preserve who produced, audited, corrected, or verified a defense cannot fully explain the provenance of its own safety system. --- ## Non-goals - Replacing #90049 or the concrete runtime fixes it interlocks. - Treating all work as incomplete until merge; the requested predicate controls the contract. - Redefining the original paper's campaign ledger retroactively without namespacing it. - Claiming that exact-head CI proves maintainer acceptance, release, deployment, or universal correctness. - Requiring one universal physical completion class across Python, TypeScript, GitHub, papers, and deployments. - Publishing the locally generated PDFs by assertion rather than creating and reading back exact Git objects. - Erasing historical failed attempts after a later success. - Letting historical provenance retain active implementation authority after typed supersession. signals.title: [Bug] Desktop right rail dead at boot: files pane hidden while toggle reads open, or tree stuck on loading skeleton forever
signals.text: ## Environment - **Hermes version**: v0.20.4 line, git install at current `main` (`76952ba54f`) - **OS**: Windows 11 Pro, x64 - **Surface**: Hermes Desktop (Electron app) - **Layout**: default three-column layout, files pane in the right rail ## Summary Two independent boot-time bugs can leave the right-hand file rail dead in different ways. Both reproduce deterministically on Windows with a restored session that has a project cwd; both currently require a manual workaround (layout preset switch + reset, or restarting until timing happens to win). 1. **Rail invisible, toggle reads open** — `$fileBrowserOpen` says OPEN while the rail renders nothing: the right side is collapsed, or the `files` pane is chrome-hidden (`paneStates.v1` records `"file-browser":{"open":true}` alongside `"files":{"open":false}`), or the pane is missing from the tree. Only a layout-preset switch plus reset fixes it. 2. **Rail shell visible, tree stuck on the loading skeleton forever** — the pane mounts, the project name header renders, but `[data-slot="tree-skeleton"]` never goes away and zero rows appear. ## Root cause 1 — visibility drift never re-syncs At bind time `bindPaneVisibility('files', ...)` calls `setTreePaneHidden('files', true)` because no workspace has arrived yet. When the cwd lands, `setTreePaneHidden(false)` only fronts the tab (`frontPaneInGroup`) — it does not un-collapse a collapsed side nor re-adopt a pane that left the tree. Boot-time dock-enforcement of plugin panes (Bot Mode) can also rewrite the persisted tree mid-boot, so the stored state and the toggle disagree in both directions. Nothing reconciles them afterwards; `resetLayoutTree` is the only path that replays `sideOpeners`. ## Root cause 2 — requestId guard eats an in-flight read, nothing retries Boot sequence observed via CDP console capture: ``` useProjectTree effect: cwd=<project> -> loadRoot(force) starts, requestId=2 <gatewayScope change / beforeConnectionSwitch> -> resetProjectTreeState(), requestId=3 readProjectDir resolves in 18ms with 22 entries commit REJECTED: requestId=2 != latest.requestId=3, latest.cwd="" ``` After the rejection the atom stays cleared (`cwd=''`, `loaded=false`, `rootLoading=false`) while the workspace is active. The load-retry effects key on `connectionKey`/`cwd`/workspace ticks — all already settled by then — so no retry ever fires and the skeleton shows forever. `loadRoot`'s own early-return guard (`current.rootLoading`) also blocks any incidental re-entry. ## Repro 1. Sign in with a session whose cwd points at a real local project. 2. Restart the desktop app. 3. On a slow-enough gateway handshake (or any run where the connection events land after the first root read starts), the right rail either doesn't appear, or appears with an eternal skeleton. 4. `localStorage['hermes.desktop.paneStates.v1']` shows the contradictory `"file-browser":{"open":true}` / `"files":{"open":false}` pair in case 1. Verified live over CDP (`--remote-debugging-port`): `treeitems: 0` with a present skeleton before the fix; manual `window.hermesDesktop.readDir(cwd)` resolves fine in the same session, proving the data layer was healthy and the state machine was the problem. ## Fix (branch pushed, PR incoming) Two small self-heals, each bounded and routed through existing recovery paths: - **controller.tsx**: subscribe to `computed([$hasWorkspace, $fileBrowserOpen])`; when it turns true, let adoption settle (`setTimeout 0`), then if the pane is missing from the tree / side collapsed / pane hidden, call `revealTreePane(FILES_PANE_ID)` — the same path a layout reset takes. An explicit ⌘J close writes the toggle false, so deliberate closes are not fought. - **use-project-tree.ts**: an effect keyed on `[cwd, state.cwd, state.rootLoading]` that forces exactly one reload whenever the tree atom is wiped while a cwd is present. Deliberate clears (profile switch, Home) also clear the session cwd, so the guard stays hands-off there. Related: #79518 (same family — reveal/adoption preserving stale hidden flags), #65173/#65376/#66059 (file-browser toggle state fights around boot).

signals.title: Desktop boot death-loop: ~/.hermes/.env override=True clobbers HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN injected by the desktop
signals.text: ## Summary The Hermes desktop app (Electron) fails to boot on a machine where `~/.hermes/.env` contains a `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN` line. The app gets stuck in an infinite boot loop: spawn backend → backend HTTP-ready → WebSocket handshake 403 → backend killed as "stale" → respawn → repeat. ## Root cause The desktop spawns `hermes serve` and passes a **fresh per-boot** session token to the child via the environment: - `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:10173` and `:10537` — `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN: token` (a freshly minted `crypto.randomBytes(32)` value). On the backend side, `hermes_cli.main` imports `load_hermes_dotenv()` at module-import time (`hermes_cli/main.py:706`). That function loads `~/.hermes/.env` with **`override=True`** (`hermes_cli/env_loader.py:500`): ```python if user_env.exists(): _load_dotenv_with_fallback(user_env, override=True) ``` So if `~/.hermes/.env` contains a `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN` line (stale, from any prior session — in the reported case a leftover `hermes-mobile-…` value), dotenv **overwrites** the fresh value the desktop injected into the child env. The server's in-memory `_SESSION_TOKEN` (resolved from env at `hermes_cli/web_server.py:498-502`) then differs from the token the desktop remembers (`spawnToken`). The desktop's boot sequence (`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:10648-10661`) resolves the served token (falls back to `spawnToken`), then probes `/api/ws?token=<token>`. Validation is `_ws_auth_reason` → `hmac.compare_digest(token, _SESSION_TOKEN)` (`hermes_cli/web_server.py:15922-15927`). Because the two tokens diverge, the handshake returns **HTTP 403**, the backend is classified as "stale" (`main.ts:10599` `Ignoring stale Hermes backend exit`), SIGTERM'd, and respawned forever. ## Reproduction 1. Put `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN=anything-stale` in `~/.hermes/.env`. 2. Launch the desktop app (or run `hermes serve` with `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN=fresh` in env). 3. Observe: `GET /api/ws?token=fresh` → 403, while `GET /api/ws?token=anything-stale` → 200. Confirmed locally on macOS arm64, source `9d86ac62b41d2b953aafc7d9c1e75711762f68e5`. ## Why it's a footgun / not just "user error" `_clear_known_keys_missing_from_dotenv` (`env_loader.py:114-145`) is deliberately narrow — it only scrubs a small `_PROFILE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS` allowlist. `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN` is a value a **parent process** (the desktop shell) explicitly injects into the child's environment; `.env` should not win over an explicit parent-process injection. Any `.env` carrying that key — which is easy to accumulate (mobile sessions, manually-exported shells, copied config) — will silently break the desktop boot with no obvious error to the user. ## Suggested fix (one of) - In `load_hermes_dotenv`, do **not** let `.env` override env vars that were already present and are in an explicit "injected by parent" allowlist (e.g. `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN`, or more generally any key a parent/spawner set). i.e. `override=False` for those keys, or skip them in the dotenv load. - Or: the desktop should write its token to a place the backend reads as authoritative (or not export the key to `.env` at all), so the two can't diverge. ## Workaround (already applied on the affected machine) Remove the stale `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN` line from `~/.hermes/.env`. The desktop regenerates the token every boot, so nothing else depends on the on-disk value. After removal the backend boots cleanly (`Hermes backend is ready`). Reported on behalf of a user; verified against source `9d86ac62b41d2b953aafc7d9c1e75711762f68e5`.

signals.title: fix(tools): resolve uv/uvx MCP commands under GUI-style PATHs (fixes #37589)
signals.text: ## What does this PR do? Fixes bare ``command: uv`` / ``command: uvx`` MCP server configs from Hermes Desktop on macOS. The Hermes Desktop app inherits a minimal LaunchAgent PATH (``/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin``) that doesn't include ``~/.local/bin`` (the uv user installer target), ``/opt/homebrew/bin`` (Apple Silicon Homebrew), or ``/usr/local/bin`` (Intel Homebrew / Linux from-source). A bare ``uvx`` MCP server therefore fails with ENOENT at ``execvp`` from Desktop even though it works fine from an interactive terminal — exactly the failure mode reported in #37589. ## Changes - ``tools/mcp_tool.py`` (``_resolve_stdio_command``) - Added ``uv`` and ``uvx`` to the bare-command candidate allowlist (was only ``npx``/``npm``/``node`` before). - Added ``$HERMES_HOME/bin/<cmd>`` as a candidate for managed uv/uvx (from #37660). Managed uv is preferred over ``~/.local/bin``, Homebrew, etc. so MCP servers use the same uv as the CLI update path. - Added a new ``/opt/homebrew/bin/<cmd>`` candidate for the Apple Silicon Homebrew case (``brew install uv``). The existing ``/usr/local/bin`` candidate continues to cover Intel Homebrew and Linux from-source builds. - Candidate ordering: Hermes-bundled Node → **managed uv** (``$HERMES_HOME/bin``) → ``~/.local/bin`` → ``/opt/homebrew/bin`` → ``/usr/local/bin``. - ``tests/tools/test_mcp_tool_issue_948.py`` - New test: ``test_resolve_stdio_command_finds_uvx_in_user_local_bin`` — covers the dominant install location for uv on Apple Silicon / Ubuntu. - New test: ``test_resolve_stdio_command_uvx_unchanged_when_already_on_path`` — ensures ``shutil.which`` still takes precedence (no double-resolve of a working bare command). - New test: ``test_resolve_stdio_command_skips_unknown_commands`` — negative test that catches the inverse regression of someone widening the allowlist so far that a bare ``command: my-tool`` gets rewritten to a coincidentally-named file at ``/opt/homebrew/bin/my-tool``. - New test: ``test_resolve_stdio_command_prefers_managed_uv`` — verifies that ``$HERMES_HOME/bin/uv`` wins over a stale ``~/.local/bin/uv`` (cross-reference with #37660). - The 4 existing ``npx`` tests continue to pass unchanged. ## How to test 1. ``~/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/tools/test_mcp_tool_issue_948.py -q --timeout=60`` — 9/9 pass. 2. ``~/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/tools/ -q --timeout=60 -k "mcp"`` — no regressions in the broader MCP test surface. ## Notes - The CLI / TUI paths were never affected (they inherit a full terminal PATH). This is a Desktop/launchd-only fix. - Sandbox / docker config can still pass an explicit ``env.PATH`` and the resolver will still honour it via ``_prepend_path``. The fallback is only consulted when the bare command isn't on the inherited PATH at all. - No change to behaviour for any command outside the ``npx/npm/node/uv/uvx`` allowlist — random bare commands like ``python`` or ``my-tool`` are left alone (the new negative test pins this). - The managed-uv candidate (``$HERMES_HOME/bin``) was added in coordination with #37660, which introduced managed uv at that location. Without it, MCP servers on Desktop would fall back to a stale ``~/.local/bin`` or brew-managed uv instead of the hermes-managed one. Closes #37589

signals.title: docs: canonize All Gods Must Die doctrine and exact-object completion amendment
signals.text: ## What this contribution is This PR canonizes **All Gods Must Die: Adversarially Verified Transformation** as a first-class Hermes publication, guide, reusable production skill, and versioned architecture doctrine. The original paper unifies god-file decomposition and multilingual documentation parity under one rule: > Make critical claims mechanically falsifiable, separate production from adjudication, and refuse hidden debt. Hermes is the system under study: a stateful, self-regulating cybernetic agent whose LLM layer supplies neural plasticity and whose deterministic skeleton — CI gates, cryptographic hashes, graph checks, seam identity, manifests, approval boundaries, memory/profile isolation, and adversarial witnesses — makes that plasticity answerable to structure. Hermes is explicitly framed as a **weapon for sovereignty, not war**: an instrument for preserving user agency over model choice, context, memory, tools, execution, provider routing, and technical records. Cyber defense is an internal function because Hermes lives inside the CLI, gateway, tool, memory, provider-egress, desktop-auth, documentation, and CI surfaces she defends. ## Amendment I — Task Completion Verification This PR now embeds a successor architecture refinement derived from the concrete `Task Completion Verification` execution record. The original five laws gain a sixth: > **No task is complete until the requested state exists at the authoritative target and is verified on the exact object.** Derivative rule: > **No receipt may be inherited from a local draft, previous head, adjacent commit, parent object, superseded artifact, or intended write.** This closes the **activity-completion collapse** failure class: a prepared patch is not a changed branch; a changed branch is not a pull request; a pull request is not approval; approval is not merge; merge is not release; release is not operational proof. Completion is represented as a typed state vector across: - materialization; - integrity; - governance; - integration; - operation; - lineage. The amendment preserves the original god-file campaign's `SHIPPED` definition as the namespaced predicate `KAG_SHIPPED`. It does **not** imply `MERGED`, `PUBLISHED`, `RELEASED`, or `OPERATIONALLY_VERIFIED`. The webhook case study preserves both time-bounded truths: - the supplied Task 7 and Task 10 patches were locally prepared and structurally verified, but three GitHub write routes failed with `403 Resource not accessible by integration`; no public state changed in that execution; - later repository reconciliation identifies #85002 as the current Task 7 object, #85523 as closed/unmerged historical Task 10 provenance, and #90236 as its canonical successor. The later target objects do not retroactively turn the earlier 403 into a successful write. The earlier blocker does not deny the later target state. Both events remain in the mutation journal. ## Publication surfaces ### Original v1.0 contribution - `website/docs/guides/all-gods-must-die.md` — long LLM-readable guide, registered in the Guides & Tutorials sidebar. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation.pdf` — immutable 68-page compiled publication. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation.tex` — reproducible LaTeX source. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation.bib` — merged bibliography. - `skills/research/long-document-production/SKILL.md` — reusable long-document production skill. - `website/scripts/generate-llms-txt.py` — curated `llms.txt` inclusion. ### Task Completion Verification source-controlled surfaces - `website/docs/guides/task-completion-verification.md` — exact-object completion architecture guide. - `docs/research/task-completion-verification-amendment.md` — canonical source-readable Amendment I. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation-v1.1.tex` — successor composition source preserving immutable v1.0 and appending Amendment I. - `docs/research/task-completion-record.schema.json` — machine-auditable completion-record contract. - `docs/research/task-completion-verification-ledger.json` — dated local-blocker and current GitHub reconciliation records. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-v1.1-release-manifest.json` — source digests, generated-output digests, typed lineage, and packaging-time truth. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-interlock.md` — contribution graph and lifecycle boundary. ### Generated release outputs The amendment PDF and composed v1.1 PDF were built, preflighted, rendered, and visually inspected locally. Their digests are recorded in the release manifest. **Their GitHub binary publication is not asserted by this PR source update.** - Amendment I: 14 pages; SHA-256 `1a8f46528faf10339e7d0cdeb3cf0b8035b341a23ffbde2b0b7aa19e361505f5`. - Composed v1.1: 83 pages; SHA-256 `be5f9c912025eb2fbbcbcef2a497eb76f041db7ecfa6637550fe7bbae1fb805b`. ## Hermes-agent security hardening evidence The paper documents the actual Hermes-agent security series: - `#77008` — Bitwarden encrypted-only disk cache and legacy plaintext migration/removal. - `#77012`, `#77020` — exact-value protection in status lines and logs. - `#77179`, `#77185`, `#77198` — applied-secret provenance and exact-value provider-egress masking. - `#77027`, `#77181`, `#77193` — child-process environment scrubbing, including renamed and arbitrary external secrets. - `#77528`, `#78033`, `#78036` — TUI compute host, LSP, plugin sidecar, and `shell.exec` scrub-bypass closure. - `#77527` — real Windows ACL protection through `icacls`, including the existing-file mode-preservation branch. - `#77039` — hermetic end-to-end no-exfiltration acceptance gate through the real secret-loading entrypoint. - `#77031` — credential-read scope audit whose correct result was no fabricated code change. - `#76958`, `#78901`–`#78904` — stale desktop session-token clobbering, provenance diagnostics, bounded retry, and real subprocess regression harness. - `#78806` — refusal to mutate git-managed state inside a real `.git` directory. ## Interlock and contribution graph **Current contribution:** `#80551`. **Part of #78647** — graph-gated engineering / large-file decomposition tracker. **Related sibling contributions:** - `#79609` — `godfile-kill-campaigns`, the 5×2×3 blind-witness decomposition skill. - `#79779` — `campaign-operations-kill-locks`, the bidirectional audit and KILL LOCK skill. - `#79898` — `feature-parity-alignment-campaigns`. - `#80391` — cross-language docs germination pipeline. - `#80392` — cross-language docs germination EPIC. - `#60535` / `#63660` — French documentation issue and seed provenance. - `#85002` — Task 7 case-study object. - `#85523` → `#90236` — Task 10 historical provenance and canonical successor. The interlock manifest defines the required edges: 1. PR → EPIC via an operative `Part of #78647` binding. 2. PR → sibling contributions via explicit `Related #N` lines. 3. EPIC → PR via the literal PR token posted on the EPIC thread. 4. Sibling surfaces → this contribution via literal PR tokens where relevant. 5. Skill → skillset through `related_skills` and the in-repo skill path. 6. Credit → artifact through authorship, provenance, contributor identity, and source ledgers. 7. Release → predecessor through explicit `derives_from` / `refines` lineage. 8. Historical object → canonical successor through typed supersession. Interlock is bidirectional or incomplete. Completion is exact-object bound or unproven. ## Attribution Axl Ibiza, MBA authored the doctrine, architecture, campaign design, source selection, editorial direction, and acceptance standard. signals.title: fix(desktop): prevent Windows installs from using stale system Node
signals.text: ## What does this PR do? On Windows, Desktop dependency installation can run npm with Hermes-managed Node while npm lifecycle children resolve an older system Node from PATH. Electron postinstall then fails with `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`, blocking Desktop builds and updates even though Hermes has already installed a compatible Node runtime. This change makes the dependency-install environment move all Hermes-managed Node directories to the front of PATH. It removes normalized duplicate entries first, including Windows case and trailing-separator variants, while preserving the order of unrelated PATH entries. ## Related Issue Closes #82309 ## Type of Change - [x] Bug fix - [x] Tests ## Changes Made - `hermes_constants.py` - normalize PATH entries with platform path semantics, remove managed-directory duplicates, and prepend canonical managed Node directories. - `tests/test_hermes_constants.py` - cover managed Node reordering and Windows duplicate normalization. - `tests/hermes_cli/test_gui_command.py` - cover Desktop install environments when managed Node is missing from PATH or appears after system Node. ## How to Test 1. On Windows, place a system Node directory first in PATH and existing Hermes-managed Node directories later. 2. Build the Desktop dependency environment and confirm the managed directories lead PATH, duplicate variants are removed, and bare `node` resolves to the managed runtime. 3. Run the focused regression tests: ```bash scripts/run_tests.sh tests/test_hermes_constants.py -k 'managed_node_dirs_move_ahead or windows_managed_node_path_collapses' scripts/run_tests.sh tests/hermes_cli/test_gui_command.py ``` Observed results: 2 focused PATH tests passed and all 13 Desktop GUI command tests passed. In the Windows real environment, bare `node` resolved to managed Node v22.23.1 after the change instead of the older system Node. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix - [x] I've run the repository test entry on the relevant tests and all selected tests pass - [x] I've added tests for this bug fix - [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows 10/11 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] Documentation update is not required for this internal PATH correction - [x] Config example update is not applicable because no config keys changed - [x] Contributor guide update is not applicable because no architecture or workflow changed - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact; POSIX comparison remains case-sensitive and uses POSIX path normalization - [x] Tool description and schema updates are not applicable ## Screenshots / Logs ```text Focused managed Node PATH tests: 2 passed Desktop GUI command tests: 13 passed Ruff: all checks passed Windows real-environment verification: managed Node v22.23.1 selected before system Node ```

signals.title: fix(desktop): surface actionable error when Nous Cloud agent returns 503 (#85335)
signals.text: ## Fix for #85335 ### Problem When Hermes Desktop connects to a Nous-managed cloud agent (e.g. `https://ares-3009.agents.nousresearch.com`) and that backend returns **HTTP 502/503/504**, the error surfaced as a generic "Hermes backend did not become ready" message with no guidance that the cloud server itself is down — and the app appeared stuck in a retry loop. The user cannot restart a Nous-managed cloud instance themselves and had no actionable recovery path. ### Fix (whole class, all failure boundaries) Classifies a Nous Cloud **502/503/504** server-side fault at **every** startup boundary, carries a structured signal to the renderer, and renders an actionable recovery screen. Not just the one site the report hit: - **`backend-health.ts`** — `isServerSideHttpError` (structured-first on `err.statusCode`, legacy `^NNN:` prefix as fallback, non-`Error` inputs rejected), `isNousCloudAgentUrl`, and a single `makeNousCloudBackendDownError` factory. Used in `waitForHermesReady` (readiness exhaustion). - **`main.ts`** — runs the Cloud classifier at the **OAuth WS-ticket mint boundary** (`mintGatewayWsTicket`) before the `gatewayTicketFailure` wrap, so a Cloud 503 from the ticket endpoint surfaces the actionable message instead of the generic reachability error. 401/403 still route to reauth. Also carries `isCloudBackendDown` / `statusCode` through `DesktopBootProgress` so the renderer can key on the structured result. - **`connection-config.ts`** — `gatewayTicketFailure` preserves the source error's integer `statusCode` (401/403 → reauth, unchanged). - **`global.d.ts`** — `DesktopBootProgress` gains `isCloudBackendDown?` / `statusCode?`. - **`boot-failure-overlay.tsx`** — the recovery screen now branches on `isCloudBackendDown`: cloud-specific title/description, local-only **Repair dropped**, and the actionable portal / Local-mode / Discord guidance. The electron factory's full message is still shown in the error box. - **i18n** — `cloudDownTitle/Description/Hint` keys (en + ar/ja/zh/zh-hant). The actionable message a user now sees: names the failing cloud host, reports the HTTP status, points to https://portal.nousresearch.com, offers switching to Local mode, and gives the Discord support link. ### Tests - `backend-health.test.ts` — 502/503/504 structured + legacy + non-Error rejection, cloud-wrap on readiness exhaustion, non-cloud 503 not wrapped, factory shape/cause/guards. - `connection-config.test.ts` — OAuth ticket-mint **503 → transport failure with `statusCode` preserved**; **401 → reauth (never Cloud-down)**; integer-only statusCode copy. - `boot-failure-overlay.test.tsx` — cloud-down recovery renders, Repair dropped, portal guidance shown (4/4 passing). - TypeScript: `tsc --noEmit` clean across the desktop project (0 errors). ### Verification - Renderer overlay suite: 4/4 passing. - Electron suites: present but the vitest runner hangs in this environment (documented limitation); verified via the same direct-execution path the author used. Fixes #85335 Related (same debugging session, separate class): #85333 (read_file dedup) via #85353.

signals.title: Freemaxxing: authenticated proven-free local failover router
signals.text: ## What Ships **Freemaxxing** as a first-class Hermes model-provider plugin with one stable route: ```text provider = freemaxxing model = freemaxxing ``` An authenticated loopback router owns concrete model selection, backend health, bounded failover, and credential refresh. Hermes core keeps the opaque provider/model identity. This is a clean one-commit restack on current `main`; the pre-hardening head is preserved at `archive/85631-pre-hardening-0502d095` and is no longer in this PR. ## Cost authority: proven free or excluded Freemaxxing does not treat “an API token exists” as proof that a route is free. | Tier | Backend | Admission rule | |---|---|---| | 0 | Nous Portal | Only the explicit free DeepSeek Flash allow-list is admitted | | 1 | OpenRouter | Only model IDs ending in `:free` are admitted | Hugging Face is deliberately removed from automatic routing. Routed HF inference can consume credits and become pay-as-you-go; unknown or ambiguous pricing therefore fails closed. There is no silent paid fallback. ## Profile isolation The current loopback router is explicitly single-profile-only. When `gateway.multiplex_profiles` is active, Freemaxxing rejects initialization before reading Nous, OpenRouter, or fallback credentials. A safe multiplex implementation needs a profile-addressed capability mapped to a per-profile pool. Until Hermes has that wire, native providers remain the correct route for multiplexed gateways. Tests exercise two distinct profile scopes and prove neither can inherit the process capability or establish shared pool authority. ## Local capability and lifecycle - Listener binds only to `127.0.0.1`. - Every operational endpoint requires a random per-process bearer. - Blank tokens and token-mode changes are rejected; an unauthenticated listener cannot be reused or upgraded in place. - `GET /v1/healthz` exposes only a minimal liveness marker. - Provider discovery opens the authenticated listener but does not resolve upstream secrets, catalogs, or pool state. - Upstream authority is constructed lazily after the first authenticated runtime request. - Static picker discovery returns only the opaque `freemaxxing` model and cannot establish runtime authority. ## Failure and resource authority - `429`: bounded `Retry-After` cooldown, then fail over. - `5xx`, timeout, reset, DNS, and pre-status connection failure: short cooldown, then fail over. - Model-not-found: skip without poisoning general backend health. - `401/403`: one serialized credential refresh where supported, then skip. - Other `4xx`: return a client error without replaying a malformed request. - HTTP 200 with truncated, oversized, non-UTF-8, malformed, or non-object JSON: classify as transient and fail over before committing a response. - Streaming: first-line preflight before downstream `200`; bounded SSE lines/events; failover only before commit. - Downstream client cancellation does not cool down a healthy upstream backend. - Bounds: request 1 MB, catalog 2 MB, non-streaming response 10 MB, SSE line 1 MB, SSE event 2 MB. - Credentialed upstream requests use Hermes’ redirect-safe `open_credentialed_url` path. ## Code shape The implementation is split by authority: - `policy.py` — free-route admission, shared limits, typed failures - `pool.py` — backend state, strict tiering, round-robin, catalog single-flight - `upstream.py` — bounded credentialed HTTP and response-integrity classification - `handler.py` — authenticated OpenAI-compatible request/stream surface - `server.py` — immutable loopback listener lifecycle - `proxy.py` / `router.py` — stable public composition surfaces - `__init__.py` — lazy provider registration and profile-scope gate No Hermes core files are changed. ## Verification ```bash python -m pytest -q \ tests/plugins/model_providers/test_freemaxxing_proxy.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_freemaxxing_routing.py ``` Focused result on the exact implementation assembled for this head: ```text 31 passed ``` The tests import only the canonical production package module and cover the generic runtime credential resolver, listener authentication, profile isolation, proven-free admission, failover, refresh serialization, response bounds/integrity, streaming pre-commit behavior, and downstream cancellation attribution. ## Scope hygiene The PR is one commit ahead of current `main`, zero commits behind, and contains only the Freemaxxing plugin, its documentation/manifest, and focused tests.

signals.title: fix(desktop): pin active-profile.json when creating a new profile
signals.text: ## Problem When a profile is created via the CLI (e.g. `hermes profile create mr_john --clone`), the desktop app's `active-profile.json` is never written. The file is only created when the user picks a profile in the desktop UI picker — CLI spawns bypass the UI entirely. Missing file → `primaryProfileKey()` falls back to `default` → the desktop silently launches the `default` backend instead of the new profile's backend. The new profile's tools and config are unreachable from the desktop surface — no error, no warning, just a quiet fail-open to `default`. This is a real footgun: a perfectly healthy CLI-spawned profile looks broken in the desktop because the backend is pinned to the wrong profile. ## Fix Call `_pin_active_profile()` at the very end of `create_profile()` — writes `{"profile": <name>}` to the desktop's `active-profile.json` (e.g. `%APPDATA%\Hermes\active-profile.json` on Windows). Uses the existing `desktop_userdata_dir()` helper from `gui_uninstall.py`, so the path resolution is already platform-correct. Best-effort and fully non-failing: if the desktop directory doesn't exist (headless installs) or is unwritable, the write is skipped silently. Profile creation always succeeds. ## Files - `hermes_cli/profiles.py` — new `_pin_active_profile()` helper (18 lines) + call site at the end of `create_profile()`. 24 insertions, 0 deletions. ## Testing - [x] `create_profile()` writes `active-profile.json` to the desktop userData dir - [x] Headless installs (no desktop dir) — no failure, profile created normally - [ ] Manual: CLI profile create → desktop relaunch → session lands on new profile with its tools visible
