signal.title: [Architecture / Publication] Task Completion Verification — exact-object completion as the sixth Hermes law
signal.text: ## Thesis **All Gods Must Die: Adversarially Verified Transformation** currently gives Hermes five executable laws for changing load-bearing artifacts: 1. No system component may accumulate authority without becoming legible. 2. No claim may outrank its evidence. 3. No actor may certify itself. 4. No rule counts until it executes. 5. No debt gets to hide behind institutional forgetting. A concrete repository-execution record exposed the missing execution-level law: > **No task is complete until the requested state exists at the authoritative target and is verified on the exact object.** Derivative rule: > **No receipt may be inherited from a local draft, previous head, adjacent commit, parent object, superseded artifact, or intended write.** This issue canonizes that rule as **Amendment I — Task Completion Verification** and makes the doctrine machine-auditable through a completion contract, typed state vector, exact-object receipt model, temporal mutation ledger, JSON Schema, versioned publication lineage, and explicit interlocks to the live Hermes objects that exposed the class. The defect class is **activity-completion collapse**: evidence that work occurred is promoted into evidence that the requested state exists. ```text patch prepared != branch changed branch changed != pull request submitted pull request submitted != exact-head verified exact-head verified != accepted accepted != merged merged != released released != operationally verified historical object exists != historical object is canonical write attempted != target mutation occurred ``` This is not administrative language. It is an authority model for Hermes itself. --- ## Scope and non-duplication This issue is the **publication/doctrine and repository-contract node**. It does not replace the existing runtime architecture nodes: - #90049 remains the implementation/defect-class owner for **false success / completion laundering inside Hermes runtime surfaces**. - #90200 remains the authority-model owner for **GitHub split authority**, where issue/PR metadata writes succeed while repository-object and Actions mutations may fail. - #90144 remains the rule that **proof scope must equal mutation scope**. - #90145 remains the temporal rule that stale actors must be fenced by **durable generation identity**. - #90150 remains the realization rule that **the built artifact and real peer are part of the system under test**. - #90866 remains the composition rule that observable state must remain **proof-carrying from source to side effect**. This issue binds those rules into the architecture thesis and defines the lifecycle predicates, receipts, release semantics, and publication surfaces that make the thesis reproducible. --- ## Why the existing doctrine needed a sixth law The original paper already rejects producer self-certification. A god-file implementer cannot approve its own extraction; a translator cannot certify its own localized graph; claims must resolve against golden hashes, seam identity, parity gates, CI, manifests, and public interlocks. But an agent can apply those rules to code while narrating its own execution loosely: - a patch exists locally, therefore the repository is fixed; - a command exited zero, therefore the durable postcondition exists; - an API request was sent, therefore the target changed; - a comment was posted, therefore implementation work was published; - one workflow was green, therefore the current head is green; - a previous head passed, therefore a rewritten head inherits the receipt; - a historical PR contains the idea, therefore it remains the delivery object; - a plausible summary says “done,” therefore the work reached the source of truth. Every example substitutes one predicate for another. The system needs types, not stronger adjectives. --- ## Completion contract Every work order should resolve to a completion contract: ```text C = ( authoritative_system, exact_target_object, requested_predicate, admissible_evidence, acceptance_authority, required_graph_closure ) ``` Where: - **authoritative system** is the system that owns the requested state: GitHub, a release registry, deployed service, package repository, durable database, or explicitly local filesystem; - **exact target object** is the branch ref, commit, pull request, issue comment, review, workflow run, release, deployment, file blob, endpoint, or other object named by the request; - **requested predicate** is the exact state requested: `prepared`, `submitted`, `verified`, `accepted`, `merged`, `published`, `released`, `operationally_verified`, etc.; - **admissible evidence** is the minimum receipt set capable of proving that predicate; - **acceptance authority** is the actor/system empowered to decide the predicate when external authority is required; - **graph closure** is the required provenance, dependency, supersession, credit, and interlock state. A local patch can complete a request to **prepare a patch**. It cannot complete a request to **fix the PR**, **push the branch**, **post the review**, **merge the change**, or **verify production**. Formally: ```text Complete(C) iff target_exists_in_authoritative_system AND target_was_read_back_after_mutation AND evidence_is_bound_to_exact_target_version AND evidence_proves_requested_predicate AND required_acceptance_authority_is_satisfied AND required_graph_edges_are_closed ``` --- ## Completion is a state vector, not one green word A single linear status cannot represent repository truth. A PR can exist and be exact-head green while unreviewed and unmerged. A release can exist but remain operationally unverified. A fully tested historical PR can be superseded. | Axis | Representative states | Governing question | |---|---|---| | Materialization | `absent`, `local_only`, `target_present` | Where do the bytes or state actually exist? | | Integrity | `unverified`, `locally_verified`, `read_back`, `exact_object_verified` | Which exact object was checked? | | Governance | `unreviewed`, `reviewed`, `accepted`, `rejected` | What authority evaluated which version? | | Integration | `not_submitted`, `open`, `closed_unmerged`, `merged`, `released` | How far did the object enter the repository/release channel? | | Operation | `not_exercised`, `hermetic_verified`, `operationally_verified` | Was delivered behavior tested on the real execution surface? | | Lineage | `active`, `blocked`, `superseded`, `retracted`, `abandoned` | Is this still canonical, and why? | The completion claim is the exact conjunction required by the contract. It may be weaker than intended. It may never be stronger than the receipts. --- ## Predicate-to-receipt matrix | Predicate claimed | Minimum receipt | What it does **not** prove | |---|---|---| | `prepared` | artifact path + content digest | target mutation, review, CI, merge | | `locally_verified` | command + exit status + exact input digest | remote submission or target state | | `submitted` | target URL/object ID + post-write read-back | acceptance, merge, release, runtime behavior | | `exact_object_verified` | immutable/versioned target identity + checks bound to it | maintainer acceptance or integration | | `accepted` | designated authority verdict on the exact verified object | merge, release, deployment | | `merged` | merge commit/default-branch reachability | release or production behavior | | `published` / `released` | immutable release identifier + digest | successful real-world operation | | `operationally_verified` | real-surface receipt bound to release/deployment identity | universal correctness outside tested conditions | | `blocked` | failed operation + exact error + boundary owner | completion | | `superseded` | typed edge to canonical successor + retirement state | that the historical object should merge | ### Exact-object rule for CI For target object version `v` and workflow receipt `r`: ```text CIValid(v, r) iff target_head(v) == workflow_head(r) ``` The following are useful diagnostic context but are not evidence for this predicate: - parent success; - merge-base success; - prior-head success; - sibling-PR success; - nearby-main success; - a green synthetic merge candidate for a different head. **Green is not hereditary.** --- ## Exact-object verification requirements A target object is exact-object verified only when all applicable requirements hold: 1. **Authoritative existence** — the object exists in the target system, not only in a local workspace or narrative. 2. **Stable identity** — URL plus object ID, commit SHA, blob hash, release digest, workflow-run ID, review ID, or equivalent. 3. **Post-write read-back** — the target is retrieved after the attempted mutation. 4. **Version binding** — every check, review, or receipt identifies the exact version it evaluated. 5. **Predicate match** — the receipt proves the state claimed, not a weaker adjacent state. 6. **Authority match** — the actor making an acceptance/merge/release decision actually owns that transition. 7. **Graph closure** — provenance, dependency, credit, and supersession edges required by the work are present. 8. **Temporal honesty** — later success does not rewrite an earlier failed mutation, and an earlier blocker does not erase later valid state. --- ## Concrete case study: the webhook publication record The supplied Task Completion Verification record captured two real repairs and one real authority boundary. ### Task 7 — named-profile configuration The prepared patch made `resolve_effective_webhook_config("worker")` read the requested profile's own `config.yaml` through Hermes' context-local home override, then restore the prior override before the next default-profile read. Historical local patch: ```text SHA-256 9c5d2cb4e3a2e17a114caee171eac53459700a94ae307d9fb671387142b92cf0 ``` At the recorded execution boundary: ```text materialization: local_only integrity: locally_verified integration: not_submitted lineage: blocked ``` ### Task 10 — HTTP/intake contract The prepared patch closed five concrete contract holes: - idempotency key includes `(profile, route, provider, delivery_id)`; - rate limiting is isolated by profile and route; - valid JSON arrays/scalars fail cleanly as non-object envelopes; - `original_bytes` and caps use UTF-8 byte accounting; - the default prompt uses the same valid raw-payload envelope as `{__raw__}`. Historical local patch: ```text SHA-256 62c158b8d1860edebe54002fc34e0cdc95b5b59743a3cd531f349929f6c135a5 ``` At the recorded execution boundary it had the same state vector: locally prepared, locally structurally verified, remotely blocked, not submitted. ### The authority boundary Three independent GitHub mutation routes were attempted against the fork: 1. Contents API; 2. blob/tree/commit construction; 3. direct tree/ref publication. Every route returned: ```text 403 Resource not accessible by integration ``` No branch moved. No public repository object changed. The correct result was **blocked after local verification**, not “fixed” or “completed.” The `403` is a valid blocked-state receipt because it proves the attempted object class, target system, rejection, and authority boundary. It is not a completion receipt. --- ## Temporal reconciliation: the graph later moved The dated blocker remains true. Later repository work created new source-of-truth objects. Both truths belong in the mutation journal. ### Task 7 canonical object - PR: #85002 - exact head: `355b50a30c184f1c70df172e018dedd240bd7400` - state at reconciliation: open, non-draft, mergeable - exact-head CI: success - exact-head Docker: success - exact-head Nix: success The later PR does not retroactively turn the earlier `403` into a successful write. It is a later materialization event with its own identity and receipts. ### Task 10 supersession Historical PR #85523 is: - closed; - unmerged; - explicitly retained as provenance; - superseded by #90236. Canonical successor #90236 is: - open; - non-draft; - mergeable at the observed reconciliation; - exact head `416c5e48aefcccfe945f7d4118415a3b992e017a`; - exact-head CI/Docker/Nix successful at the recorded head. The graph is: ```text #85523 --superseded_by--> #90236 #90236 --canonical_for--> Webhook Task 10 ``` Supersession preserves authorship, review history, and requirements without letting stale topology masquerade as the active delivery object. --- ## Refinement of the original `SHIPPED` standard The original paper deliberately defines a god file as `SHIPPED` when every agreed slice has been extracted, blind-reviewed to agreement, and landed as an individually interlocked open PR. That remains a valid campaign-specific definition. It must be namespaced: ```text KAG_SHIPPED ``` `KAG_SHIPPED` means the exact state defined by the Kill All Gods ledger. It does **not** entail: ```text MERGED PUBLISHED RELEASED DEPLOYED OPERATIONALLY_VERIFIED ``` This preserves the original paper's auditability standard while preventing a downstream system from inheriting a stronger lifecycle claim from the word “shipped.” --- ## The same architecture applies to papers and pull requests | Pull request concept | Paper concept | Shared invariant | |---|---|---| | working tree | manuscript draft | mutable local work is not a submitted object | | commit SHA | release digest | evidence binds exact bytes | | CI run | reproducibility/source/format checks | checks identify the exact release evaluated | | review | independent technical/semantic witness | author is not sole acceptance authority | | merge | accepted integration | acceptance and publication remain distinct | | release | immutable paper version | later refinement creates a successor, not silent mutation | | superseding PR | successor edition/amendment | lineage remains explicit and machine-readable | | production verification | replication/operationalization | publication alone does not prove real-world behavior | The August 2026 68-page PDF remains immutable v1.0. Amendment I is independently sourced. The composed v1.1 release is a successor artifact: ```text All Gods Must Die v1.0 --refined_by--> Amendment I: Task Completion Verification --composed_as--> All Gods Must Die v1.1 ``` No v1.0 page is silently replaced. --- ## Source-controlled doctrine surfaces The implementation/publication contribution is PR #80551 at exact source head: ```text 048606e79810a42fcc243e2ae30373c91eacf574 ``` | graph | `0c5f34693c8309e8c5798d339237e968c28baf37` | ### Generated release outputs The following outputs were built, PDF-preflighted, rendered, and visually inspected locally. Their binary presence in the GitHub tree is **not** asserted by the source publication. | Output | Pages | SHA-256 | Current predicate | |---|---:|---|---| | Amendment I PDF | 14 | `1a8f46528faf10339e7d0cdeb3cf0b8035b341a23ffbde2b0b7aa19e361505f5` | `locally_verified` | | Composed All Gods Must Die v1.1 PDF | 83 | `be5f9c912025eb2fbbcbcef2a497eb76f041db7ecfa6637550fe7bbae1fb805b` | `locally_verified` | | Source-and-release package | — | `51275dfa4fa7d55f4f14addfeceb1a665b567e0a9806c50ef105100f5d4cc126` | `locally_verified` | Publishing those binaries to GitHub is a separate object-class predicate requiring its own commit/tree read-back. --- ## Exact current PR state at filing PR #80551: ```text head: 048606e79810a42fcc243e2ae30373c91eacf574 state: open ready: non-draft mergeable: yes at last read-back merged: no ``` Exact-head workflows: - Docker `32437208692`: **success** - Nix `32437208780`: **success** - CI `32437209235`: **failure** The connector-exposed CI job page showed its visible jobs green or skipped, including Docusaurus, attribution, supply-chain, E2E, Windows/macOS, ruff, and exposed Python slices. The run-level aggregate nevertheless remained red, so an unexposed later-page/aggregate job failed. Therefore the current claim is deliberately bounded: > The amendment sources are submitted and exact-object read back at `048606e…`; Docker and Nix are exact-head green; PR #80551 is open, non-draft, mergeable, unmerged, and CI-red. No all-green, accepted, merged, published-binary, or released claim is made. --- ## Machine enforcement The JSON Schema and ledger are not illustrative appendices. They are the first executable expression of this architecture. A completion verifier must reject a record when any of the following is true: 1. the requested predicate is stronger than the observed evidence; 2. a remote predicate has no target locator or post-write read-back; 3. CI/review evidence binds a different SHA/version than the claimed object; 4. a local path or patch digest is offered as proof of remote mutation; 5. an object marked active has a live `superseded_by` edge; 6. a historical PR is presented as canonical after a successor owns the contract; 7. required provenance, dependency, credit, or interlock edges are missing; 8. generic `done`, `fixed`, `shipped`, or `green` appears without a namespaced predicate; 9. a write failure is omitted from the mutation journal; 10. a target-state claim cannot be reproduced by a third party from durable receipts; 11. a manifest or producer narrative attempts to certify its own publication; 12. an exact-object receipt is transferred to rebuilt or otherwise different bytes. ### Required repository integration The architecture should ultimately provide: - a canonical completion-record schema under repository ownership; - a validator with positive and negative fixtures; - a standard way for engineering agents to emit completion records; - exact-head workflow receipt ingestion; - typed supersession and blocker edges; - lint pressure against unqualified completion words in automation outputs where a stronger object state is required; - read-back verification after every GitHub mutation; - object-class capability preflight before an engineering workflow promises executability; - mutation-journal preservation of both failed and successful attempts. --- ## Adversarial regression matrix At minimum, permanent tests should cover: - [ ] local patch exists but no branch/ref changed; - [ ] comment/review write succeeds while Contents/ref write fails; - [ ] branch push succeeds but PR creation fails; - [ ] PR exists but the expected head SHA is not present; - [ ] prior-head CI is green while current head has no receipt; - [ ] parent/sibling/main CI is green while target head is red or untested; - [ ] workflow receipt names a different SHA than the completion record; - [ ] write returns success but post-write read-back disagrees; - [ ] timeout leaves remote mutation ambiguous; - [ ] historical PR is closed and a successor is active; - [ ] superseded object is incorrectly marked active; - [ ] accepted object remains unmerged; - [ ] merged source has no release artifact; - [ ] released artifact has no operational receipt; - [ ] generated PDF exists locally but is absent from the Git tree; - [ ] manifest self-claims publication without authoritative read-back; - [ ] late success does not rewrite the earlier blocked attempt; - [ ] earlier blocker does not erase later exact-object success; - [ ] `KAG_SHIPPED` cannot be parsed as `MERGED` or `RELEASED`; - [ ] removing any required graph/credit edge prevents campaign-complete status. Every negative test must assert that the stronger state transition does **not** occur. --- ## Acceptance criteria This issue is complete only when: ### Doctrine and publication - [ ] The sixth law is accepted as part of the Hermes architecture doctrine. - [ ] The original v1.0 publication remains immutable and the amendment/release lineage is explicit. - [ ] `KAG_SHIPPED` is documented as campaign-specific and not a release synonym. - [ ] The architecture guide, formal amendment, schema, ledger, release manifest, and interlock remain one contribution graph. - [ ] Generated release binaries, when published, receive exact Git blob/commit receipts; local hashes alone do not count as publication. ### Runtime and automation contract - [ ] Completion predicates have a shared typed vocabulary. - [ ] Every remote mutation path performs post-write read-back. - [ ] CI/review receipts bind the exact target version. - [ ] Stale, partial, blocked, ambiguous, and superseded states remain first-class rather than becoming success. - [ ] GitHub capability preflight distinguishes metadata, Contents, refs/Git Data, PR creation, Actions, checks, and workflow authority per repository. - [ ] A successful metadata write cannot satisfy a code-publication contract. - [ ] A target object cannot inherit green/acceptance/release state from an adjacent object. - [ ] Completion records are machine-validated and failure injection proves the verifier rejects overclaiming. ### Graph and provenance - [ ] PR #80551 and this issue are linked in both directions. - [ ] #90049 links this issue as the doctrine/publication layer without losing runtime implementation ownership. - [ ] #90200 links this issue as the authority-boundary case study without being closed by documentation. - [ ] #85002, #85523, and #90236 preserve the dated event sequence and typed supersession. - [ ] #78647 and the sibling campaign/skill nodes carry the publication edge. - [ ] Axl Ibiza's authorship of the doctrine and publication remains explicit; contributor, reviewer, agent, and source-project credit is preserved at its exact boundary. ### Exact current contribution - [ ] PR #80551 reaches exact-head CI green at its final head. - [ ] No green is inherited from `048606e…` if the head changes. - [ ] Maintainer acceptance, merge, binary publication, and release are reported as separate later predicates with their own receipts. --- ## Interlocks / topology ### Doctrine and campaign graph - #80551 — implementation/publication PR for the paper, guide, skill, amendment, schema, ledger, manifest, and interlock. - #78647 — Kill All Gods / graph-gated engineering EPIC. - #79609 — god-file kill campaign / 5×2×3 decomposition skill. - #79779 — KILL LOCK operations and bidirectional audit. - #79898 — Feature Parity & Alignment campaigns. - #80391 / #80392 — cross-language documentation germination implementation and EPIC. - #60535 / #63660 — French seed request and contributor provenance. ### Completion architecture series - #90049 — false success / typed completion proofs. - #90200 — GitHub split-authority capability model. - #90144 — proof scope equals mutation scope. - #90145 — generation-fenced mutation/recovery. - #90150 — delivered realization is part of the proof boundary. - #90866 — proof-carrying observable state. ### Webhook case-study graph - #84834 — Webhook Feature Package EPIC. - #85002 — Task 7 canonical effective-config object. - #85523 — closed/unmerged Task 10 historical provenance. - #90236 — canonical Task 10 successor. - #85644 — terminal partial/per-target delivery truth; intake acceptance is not delivery completion. Part of #78647 Related #80551 Related #90049 Related #90200 Related #90144 Related #90145 Related #90150 Related #90866 Related #84834 Related #85002 Related #85523 Related #90236 --- ## Attribution **Axl Ibiza, MBA** authored the doctrine, architecture, campaign design, source selection, editorial direction, completion-state refinement, and acceptance standard. Attribution remains typed rather than collapsed: - Axl conceived, directed, selected, corrected, and approved the argument and architecture; - agents generated, inspected, implemented, compressed, or verified artifacts under that direction; - original contributors retain their code, translation, review, test, issue, and provenance edges; - a negative receipt, truthful blocker report, audit proving no change, ledger repair, test, or supersession correction remains a first-class contribution. Attribution is not decoration. A repository that cannot preserve who produced, audited, corrected, or verified a defense cannot fully explain the provenance of its own safety system. --- ## Non-goals - Replacing #90049 or the concrete runtime fixes it interlocks. - Treating all work as incomplete until merge; the requested predicate controls the contract. - Redefining the original paper's campaign ledger retroactively without namespacing it. - Claiming that exact-head CI proves maintainer acceptance, release, deployment, or universal correctness. - Requiring one universal physical completion class across Python, TypeScript, GitHub, papers, and deployments. - Publishing the locally generated PDFs by assertion rather than creating and reading back exact Git objects. - Erasing historical failed attempts after a later success. - Letting historical provenance retain active implementation authority after typed supersession. The goal is narrower and stronger: > **Every completion claim names its predicate, authority, exact object, exact version, evidence, and graph state. Hermes may report what happened—no weaker and no stronger.**

signal.title: fix(cron): persist interrupted shutdown output
signal.text: ## Summary - Writes a minimal cron output artifact when gateway shutdown marks in-flight cron jobs interrupted after killing tool subprocesses. - Keeps the existing fail-closed `last_status=error` guard, but now preserves a durable `# Cron Job Interrupted` markdown file even when `run_one_job` never reaches its normal output-save step. - Adds shutdown-interrupt tests for the output artifact and for save-output failure not blocking the status mark. ## Verification - RED before implementation: `PYTHONPATH=. /Users/anton/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/cron/test_shutdown_interrupt.py::TestMarkRunningJobsInterrupted -o 'addopts=' -q` failed with `mock_save.call_count == 0`. - GREEN focused: same command passed (`5 passed`). - Regression: `PYTHONPATH=. /Users/anton/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/cron/test_shutdown_interrupt.py tests/gateway/test_update_cron_drain.py -o 'addopts=' -q` passed (`20 passed`). - Syntax/diff: `/Users/anton/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python -m py_compile cron/scheduler.py tests/cron/test_shutdown_interrupt.py && git diff --check` passed. - Real readback helper against a temp cron store wrote one `# Cron Job Interrupted` markdown artifact and updated the fixture job to `last_status=error` with the shutdown reason. signal.title: fix(update): self-heal broken Git-for-Windows trampoline on Windows
signal.text: ## Summary Fixes the Windows update breakage reported in #87876 where a Git-for-Windows **trampoline launcher** (the ~46KB `bin\git.exe` / `cmd\git.exe` shim) fails to re-exec the real git-core binary and refuses every git call with a `BUG (fork bomb)` guard instead of running it. Complementary to #88046 (which falls back to ZIP download when `git fetch` reports the trampoline error): this PR detects the broken trampoline **up front** and keeps the normal git update path alive. ## Approach - `_git_is_trampoline()`: probe `git --version` for the trampoline's "fork bomb" guard output (never raises; unknown states report False so a probe failure can't block an update). - `_locate_real_git()`: search standard Git for Windows locations (`C:\Program Files\Git\mingw64\libexec\git-core\git.exe`, `(x86)`, and the Hermes-managed PortableGit under `<HERMES_HOME>/git`) for a binary that runs and does NOT print the trampoline guard. - `_ensure_non_trampoline_git()`: rebuild `git_cmd` with the real binary when a trampoline is detected; when no real binary is found, leave the command untouched so the existing fetch-failure path (and #88046) still falls back to ZIP on Windows. ## Test Plan - 4 new unit tests (`TestGitTrampolineSelfHeal`): healthy git unchanged / trampoline swapped to real git / trampoline with no real git keeps command / non-Windows no-op. All pass. - `ruff check` clean on both files. - Full `test_cmd_update.py` run: 2 pre-existing failures are environment-only (local node v24.15.0 + npm 11.12.1 fail the repo's engines range with EBADENGINE during `_update_node_dependencies`; unrelated to this change — the affected tests pass the git fetch/pull phases before reaching npm). ## Risk / Exclusions - Windows-only behavior; off-Windows it's a strict no-op. - Candidate paths are conservative; finding nothing degrades to the existing ZIP fallback exactly as before. - No changes to the ZIP update path, fetch-failure handling, or venv logic. References #87876

signal.title: Windows: Desktop update hand-off hangs forever when gateway stays resident (windows.ps1 waits on ReadToEndAsync that never sees EOF)
signal.text: Summary Updating Hermes from the Desktop app on Windows can hang indefinitely at the "Updating Hermes" screen when a WeChat/Feishu gateway is configured to stay resident. The update pipeline itself completes (git pull, deps, rebuild), but the background hand-off script never finishes, so the result file is never written, the .hermes-update-in-progress marker is never cleared, and the Desktop stays on "Updating Hermes" until manually recovered. Environment - Hermes Agent 40.10.2, upstream main ad889540f - Windows 11, git install, Desktop app (Electron) - Weixin platform configured; gateway kept resident (this is the trigger) Root cause scripts/desktop-update/windows.ps1 — Invoke-HermesStep starts the updater with RedirectStandardOutput/RedirectStandardError and waits via: $outTask = $proc.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync() $errTask = $proc.StandardError.ReadToEndAsync() ... $proc.WaitForExit() ... $outTask.Result # never returns The updater is invoked as hermes update --yes --gateway --force --branch main. On the last step the updater spawns the resident gateway (gateway run --replace). The gateway inherits the updater's stdout/stderr pipe handles, so the pipe never reaches EOF, ReadToEndAsync never completes, and the hand-off script blocks forever on .Result. The hand-off then never writes .hermes-update-result.json, never removes .hermes-update-in-progress, and never relaunches the Desktop. Confirmed by inspecting scripts/desktop-update/windows.ps1 in main at ad889540f. Log evidence - logs/desktop-update-handoff.log stops after the step banner with no exit code line, while the updater itself had already completed (Hermes.exe rebuilt, desktop-build-stamp updated). - Killing the gateway immediately unblocks the script; the script then finishes the hand-off cleanly. - After manual recovery, logs/desktop.log shows detached update finished OK (branch main) and the gateway reconnects ([Weixin] Connected). Suggested fixes 1. Detach the gateway so it does not inherit the updater's pipes. Launch it with CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP/a separate job object, or otherwise close/repoint the inherited stdout/stderr handles so the parent pipe can reach EOF (e.g. redirect to NUL before spawning the resident child). 2. Don't block the hand-off on the updater's live descendant. In windows.ps1, avoid $proc.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync().Result as an EOF wait; use an explicit timeout plus WaitForExit, or spawn the updater with a detached console. 3. Stale-marker watchdog. If the hand-off script or updater makes no progress for > N minutes, write a failed result and clear .hermes-update-in-progress, so the Desktop never shows a dead-end "Updating Hermes" screen. Related Similar symptom family but different root cause: #87772 (stale marker after hung cua-driver installer). #90205 fixed a different hand-off hang (stdin treated as tty → "Restore local changes?" prompt) and is already in main; it does not address this pipe-EOF deadlock.

signal.title: [Architecture] GitHub automation has split authority: metadata writes succeed while repository-object writes fail
signal.text: ## Summary Our GitHub automation currently exposes a dangerous **split-authority state**: issue/PR metadata mutations succeed, while repository-object mutations fail with `403 Resource not accessible by integration`. This is bigger than one blocked patch or one connector session. It creates a system where an agent can successfully review, comment, retitle, reopen, relabel, and otherwise advance the *control-plane representation* of work while being unable to mutate the *source-of-truth repository objects* required to actually complete that work. The failure mode is especially deceptive because the GitHub App itself advertises the relevant permissions (`contents: write`, `pull_requests: write`, `actions: write`, `workflows: write`), so capability discovery says the operation exists and is writable. The missing dimension is **installation/repository scope**. Observed 2026-08-19 while closing Hermes obligations across #85523, #90048, #88764, #88551, and related PRs. ## Observed authority matrix ### Working The same connected GitHub surface can successfully mutate repository metadata: - create/update issue comments; - submit PR reviews; - update PR title/body; - close/reopen PRs; - update issues and topology. Those writes are live on `NousResearch/hermes-agent`. ### Failing Repository-object and Actions mutations return: ```text 403 Resource not accessible by integration ``` Verified against both `NousResearch/hermes-agent` and `andrexibiza/hermes-agent` where applicable: - Contents create; - Contents update of an existing file using its live blob SHA; - Contents delete of an existing file using its live blob SHA; - branch/ref creation and ref update; - Git Data blob/tree/commit publication paths; - PR creation from a new branch; - Actions rerun / failed-job rerun. The failures are not explained by a missing API wrapper: the Contents, Git Data, branch, PR, and Actions operations are all exposed. ## Installation evidence The connected GitHub App reports permissions including: ```text contents: write pull_requests: write issues: write actions: write workflows: write checks: read statuses: read ``` But installation discovery reports: ```text installations: [] installed accounts: [] installed repository search for hermes-agent: 0 repositories ``` That explains the otherwise contradictory behavior: the connector has a metadata-capable authority path, but there is no repository-installed GitHub App principal backing source/ref/Actions mutations. ## Why this is an architecture problem ### 1. Capability ≠ authorization ≠ installation scope Today these states are easy to conflate: ```text operation exists ≠ app permission includes operation ≠ app is installed on account/org ≠ repository is selected for installation ≠ current principal may mutate this repository object ``` Any agent harness that collapses those layers will produce false capability conclusions in both directions: - **false negative:** “Contents writes are unavailable” when the operation exists but authorization is incomplete; - **false positive:** “I can commit this repair” because the schema says `contents: write`, despite no installed repository principal. ### 2. Metadata success can masquerade as task progress An agent can leave the repository looking increasingly complete: ```text issue updated PR body corrected review posted CI interpretation recorded tracker topology reconciled ``` while the implementation itself remains uncommitted. For autonomous engineering, that is a serious completion-integrity hazard. A packet, issue comment, PR body, or review receipt is not equivalent to a branch/commit/merge receipt. ### 3. The failure arrives too late The current architecture discovers the missing repository principal only when a mutation is attempted. By then an agent may already have: - prepared a patch; - promised a rebase; - classified a task as executable; - updated tracker state; - spent substantial review/implementation effort. Installation scope should be discoverable as a first-class preflight capability. ### 4. Different GitHub object classes can have different authority paths The observed system is not simply “GitHub connected” or “GitHub disconnected.” It is closer to: ```text issue/PR conversation authority: writable repository content/ref authority: unavailable Actions control authority: unavailable public repository read authority: available ``` That needs to be represented explicitly. A single boolean connection state cannot model it. ## Required architecture ### A. First-class effective-capability report Before repository mutation, expose the effective authority tuple: ```text account / organization repository installation id repository selected by installation: yes/no operation class app-declared permission installation-granted permission object-level effective verdict ``` Example: ```json { "repository": "andrexibiza/hermes-agent", "installation": null, "operation": "contents.write", "declared_permission": "write", "effective": false, "reason": "app_not_installed_for_repository" } ``` Do not reduce this to generic `connected: true`. ### B. Distinguish operation classes At minimum model independently: - repository metadata/read; - issues/comments; - pull-request metadata/reviews; - Contents; - Git Data / refs; - PR creation; - Actions control; - workflow mutation; - checks/statuses. ### C. Typed authorization failures Translate GitHub’s generic 403 into the strongest locally provable reason: ```text app_not_installed repository_not_selected permission_not_granted branch_protection_denied organization_policy_denied resource_not_accessible_unknown ``` Preserve the raw GitHub status/message as evidence, but do not make every 403 look identical to the agent. ### D. Mutation preflight For engineering workflows, preflight the actual object class before claiming executability. Examples: ```text "rebase this PR" → verify ref/commit write authority on the head repository "implement this issue" → verify branch + Contents/Git Data + PR creation authority "rerun CI" → verify Actions write authority ``` A successful comment write is not evidence for any of those. ### E. Completion receipts must be object-class specific Completion should require receipts from the layer that owns the requested result: ```text code task → commit SHA + branch/PR/source diff rebase → new head SHA based on required base CI repair → exact-head workflow result review → posted review URL/id issue topology → live issue mutation ``` Metadata-only receipts cannot satisfy code-publication obligations. ### F. Recovery path should be actionable When the only missing prerequisite is installation scope, return the exact boundary: ```text GitHub App is connected but is not installed for andrexibiza/hermes-agent. Install/select that repository for the app before Contents/ref/Actions writes can succeed. ``` Do not tell the user merely to “check permissions,” and do not claim the API itself is unavailable. ## Required regression matrix 1. App schema exposes `contents: write`, no installation exists → preflight says `app_not_installed`, no mutation attempted. 2. Installation exists but repository is not selected → `repository_not_selected`. 3. Repository selected with read-only Contents → `permission_not_granted`. 4. Contents succeeds but Actions permission is absent → code publication allowed, CI rerun denied independently. 5. Issue comments writable while Contents unavailable → authority matrix represents both facts simultaneously. 6. Fork writable but upstream not writable → implementation can publish to fork and open cross-repo PR without assuming upstream source authority. 7. Upstream writable but fork not installed → do not automatically target the fork because the PR head happens to live there. 8. Branch protection rejects a write despite installation + permission → distinguish policy rejection from installation failure. 9. A generic GitHub 403 with insufficient evidence remains `resource_not_accessible_unknown`; never invent the cause. 10. Task-completion logic refuses to mark a code obligation complete from comments/reviews alone. ## Hermes incidents exposing the class This surfaced while processing several otherwise unrelated obligations: - #85523 — implementation patch exists, but code publication cannot occur through the current repository-object authority; - #90048 — exact current-main repair is prepared and locally verified, but no branch/PR can be published; - #88764 — semantic rebase contract is known, but refs cannot be rewritten; - #88551 / #88740 / #88758 — composed repair is specified, but no proof-preserving rebase can be published; - CI rerun attempts returned the same integration-level 403 even though issue/PR metadata remained writable. The common root cause is not any of those codebases. It is the authority model between the agent harness, GitHub App installation scope, and repository object classes. ## Design invariant > **Never infer repository mutation authority from tool presence, declared app permissions, successful metadata writes, or repository readability. Prove effective authorization for the exact object class and repository that owns the requested outcome.** This is the GitHub equivalent of the broader Hermes identity rule: do not discard exact authority information and reconstruct it later from weaker proxies. ## Acceptance criteria - Effective GitHub capabilities are queryable per repository and operation class before mutation. - Installation/account/repository-selection state is represented separately from declared app permissions. - Generic 403s are classified when evidence permits and remain explicitly unknown otherwise. - Engineering workflows preflight the mutation surface they actually require. - Completion logic requires source-of-truth receipts from the owning object class. - Split-authority states are visible and test-covered. - The UI/agent response gives an exact recovery action when repository installation/selection is the missing boundary. - No regression where comment/review success is treated as evidence of Contents/ref/Actions authority. ## Interlocks - #85523 — code-publication blocker that exposed the distinction repeatedly. - #90048 — prepared repair blocked at branch/commit publication. - #88764 — rebase blocked despite complete semantic rebase contract. - #88551 / #88740 / #88758 — proof-preserving compression repair requiring real repository-object mutation. This issue is intentionally about the **authority architecture**, not those individual implementation obligations.

signal.title: [Architecture]: make false success a first-class defect class with typed completion proofs
signal.text: ## Summary Hermes has a recurring cross-system defect class that is broader than any one protocol, UI, updater, or delivery path: > **An earlier lifecycle event is promoted into proof of a later one.** A payload exists. A function returned. A promise resolved. An event was emitted. Source moved. One fan-out target succeeded. A protocol turn ended. All of those can be true while the operation the caller actually cares about **did not complete**. This is **false success**: a system reports terminal success without proof of the authoritative postcondition at the mutation boundary. The same shape is now visible across unrelated Hermes surfaces: - **ACP — #89948, adjacent #72439:** the conversation loop already knows a provider turn failed (`completed: false`, `failed: true`, `error: ...`), but `acp_adapter.server::prompt()` drops that verdict, emits the error summary as ordinary assistant text, and returns `stopReason: end_turn`. Protocol termination is laundered into successful model completion. - **Quick Entry — #89920 / #85590:** the original fire-and-forget path could clear/hide the draft before authoritative session creation and prompt delivery were acknowledged. #89920 is moving this surface toward an explicit ack contract; it is an implementation node for this architecture, not evidence that the class is closed elsewhere. - **Updater / deployment — #88251, #86443, #83846, #79678, architecture #88683:** source/version movement can be reported as a successful update while the packaged Desktop executable is stale, missing, rebuilt from stale source, or destroyed before replacement succeeds. Source correctness is not shipped-artifact correctness. - **Desktop preview activation — #89272:** `open_preview` can return `{success:true}` when an event is emitted even though renderer normalization/activation is asynchronous and may fail or be clobbered. Producer emission is not route/tab publication. - **Webhook fan-out — #85523:** aggregate success can conceal per-target failure. One successful target does not prove the fan-out completed; every target must be accounted for with an honest result. There are additional instances of the same contract failure already tracked elsewhere, including result/fallback races, recovery markers, and delivery claims. They should interlock here when their failure is specifically “terminal success projected before the owning boundary proved the promised effect.” This issue is the shared architecture node. Linked incident issues and PRs remain the implementation/provenance nodes and retain their original reporters, evidence, and component ownership. --- ## The defect: completion laundering The deeper failure is **completion laundering**: a weaker lifecycle fact crosses a boundary and is reinterpreted as a stronger one. Examples: ```text request emitted → “opened” request accepted → “created” promise resolved → “published” source updated → “application updated” one target delivered → “fan-out succeeded” turn terminated → “model answered successfully” marker written → “recovery completed” ``` The left-hand events are often real and useful. The bug is treating them as proof of the right-hand claims. The general anti-pattern is: ```text caller intent ↓ intermediate operation ↓ weak success signal ───────────────┐ ↓ │ promoted async / remote / durable mutation │ without proof ↓ │ authoritative postcondition │ ↓ │ observable completion ◀─────────────┘ ``` The system becomes especially dangerous when the intermediate layer has enough information to sound authoritative: a normal assistant message, `end_turn`, `{success:true}`, exit 0, a resolved promise, “Already up to date,” or a green aggregate response. --- ## Design principle > **Completion requires a typed verdict and proof at the mutation boundary. A payload, return value, resolved promise, emitted event, progress message, source transition, or partial target success is not sufficient.** The component that owns the authoritative mutation must also own the evidence that allows the operation to advance to terminal success. A caller may observe earlier phases, but those phases must remain typed as earlier phases. --- ## Canonical lifecycle Not every surface needs every phase, but asynchronous/mutating operations should distinguish the semantic equivalents of: ```text attempted → accepted → started → committed → published / delivered / observable → verified / reconciled ``` Failure can occur between any two phases. A useful shared vocabulary is: ```ts type CompletionState = | 'accepted' // request admitted; effect not proven | 'started' // execution began | 'committed' // authoritative local mutation committed | 'delivered' // external consumer/provider accepted the effect | 'verified' // declared postcondition observed | 'partial' // aggregate operation has mixed terminal outcomes | 'failed' // definite failure | 'ambiguous' // effect cannot be proved present or absent | 'stale' // verdict belongs to a superseded generation ``` This is a semantic contract, not a requirement that Python, TypeScript, Rust, adapters, and provider SDKs share one physical type. --- ## Completion must be bound to identity and generation A verdict without identity is not enough. Async work can finish late, retries can overlap, routes can switch, sessions can be replaced, and fan-out targets can diverge. The completion proof therefore needs to bind to the exact operation and the exact mutation it claims to certify. Conceptually: ```ts type Completion<T> = { operationId: string generation: string | number requestedIdentity?: unknown authoritativeIdentity?: unknown state: CompletionState authority: string observedGeneration?: string | number result?: T receipts?: unknown[] failures?: unknown[] proof?: { kind: string value: unknown } error?: { code: string message: string retryable?: boolean } } ``` The representation can vary. The invariant cannot. A delayed completion for generation N must not acknowledge, clear, hide, replace, finalize, or release generation N+1. --- ## `ambiguous` is a first-class terminal verdict A timeout is not necessarily a failure. If Hermes dispatched a mutation and then lost the acknowledgement, there are at least three possibilities: 1. the mutation definitely did not occur; 2. the mutation definitely occurred; 3. the mutation may have occurred, but Hermes cannot prove either outcome. Case 3 is **ambiguous**, not success and not failure. This distinction matters because blindly retrying an ambiguous mutation can create duplicate sessions, duplicate messages, duplicate webhooks, duplicate external side effects, or destructive double execution. Therefore: - timeout/lost acknowledgement must not be normalized to success; - timeout/lost acknowledgement must not automatically be normalized to safe retry; - retries across ambiguous boundaries require stable operation identity/idempotency or an authoritative read-back/reconciliation step. This is directly relevant to Quick Entry correlation and any remote/provider mutation path. --- ## Aggregate operations require total accounting Fan-out exposes another common laundering path: one child result becomes the parent verdict. For N targets, aggregate success requires an accounted-for terminal result for all N targets. ```text 3 succeeded + 1 failed = partial 3 succeeded + 1 unknown = partial/ambiguous 4 succeeded = success ``` A warning attached to a success response does not make the result honest if callers branch on the success bit. For #85523 specifically, fan-out results must preserve per-target identity and outcome. No target may disappear behind a truthy aggregate. --- ## Incident-specific authoritative postconditions | Surface | Weak signal currently/previously mistaken for completion | Authoritative postcondition | |---|---|---| | ACP (#89948) | assistant text emitted + `end_turn` | Provider turn verdict is propagated; a failed provider turn remains typed failed/error to the ACP client and cannot be recorded as an ordinary successful answer. | | ACP model selection (#72439) | `session/set_model` returns success | Requested/effective model is valid for the selected provider, or the request returns a typed rejection before poisoning the persisted session. | | Quick Entry (#89920 / #85590) | submit emitted / renderer accepted work | Exact correlated submission is acknowledged after the requested session is authoritatively created and the prompt is bound to that session; only that acknowledgement may clear/hide the matching draft. | | Desktop preview (#89272) | tool event emitted / promise resolved | Renderer acknowledges the requested preview target/generation is actually published according to the active-surface policy; readiness may be a separate later phase. | | Desktop update (#88251 / #86443 / #83846 / #79678) | Git/source/version step succeeded or process exited 0 | Required packaged executable exists at the target generation, passes the declared probe, and the last known-good artifact is not destroyed before replacement verification. Managed runtime generation must be handled by #88683's deployment transaction. | | Webhook fan-out (#85523) | at least one target succeeded / aggregate truthy result | Every intended target has an explicit terminal result; only all-success is success, mixed results are `partial`, and unknown remote outcomes remain explicit. | --- ## Invariants ### 1. Admission is not completion Emitting an event, queueing work, accepting input, spawning a subprocess, resolving a route, or starting a provider call may return `accepted` or `started`. It cannot return the terminal state promised to the caller unless that is genuinely the caller's contract. ### 2. Success requires proof owned by the mutation boundary The layer that can know whether the effect happened must return the receipt/proof used to advance the operation. Upstream layers must not reconstruct completion from circumstantial state. ### 3. Verdicts are monotonic in meaning A downstream compatibility layer may translate representation, but it may not silently strengthen: ```text accepted → committed committed → delivered partial → success failed → success ambiguous → success ``` Nor may it discard a failure/result field and retain only a generic terminal marker. ### 4. Operation generation is mandatory where stale completion is possible Late completion from an older operation is a deterministic no-op against successor state. This applies to draft clearing, route publication, session activation, destructive replacement, retry bookkeeping, and any async state machine where multiple generations can overlap. ### 5. Result-bearing completion beats generic fallback completion A generic “done” hook cannot race with and overwrite/pre-empt a richer result for the same operation. Fallbacks must preserve the strongest authoritative verdict, not win by timing. ### 6. Aggregate success requires total accounting Every declared child operation must appear in the parent result. Missing children are not success. ### 7. Destructive replacement is stage → verify → switch → clean The previous working artifact/state remains recoverable until the candidate is verified. No updater/recovery path may destroy the last known-good state and then report success because an earlier source step completed. ### 8. Markers record achieved postconditions, not intentions A “settled,” version, recovery, migration, or completion marker is written only after the state it represents is verified. ### 9. Ambiguity survives the boundary If the owner cannot prove present or absent, the caller receives `ambiguous` (or equivalent). It must not receive a fabricated certainty. ### 10. User-visible success cannot outrun machine-verifiable success UI clearing, green banners, “Update complete,” normal assistant rendering, route transitions, and success HTTP responses are consumers of the typed verdict. They cannot be independent authorities. --- ## Relationship to qualified identity This contract is the temporal/outcome counterpart to Hermes' qualified-identity work. The two rules are structurally parallel: > **Identity:** once identity becomes more specific, no downstream layer may make it less specific and later infer the missing dimensions. > **Completion:** once outcome evidence becomes more specific, no downstream layer may discard it and later infer success from a weaker lifecycle signal. A correct mutation proof therefore binds both: ```text WHO / WHAT connection + profile + provider + route + resource/session/target AND WHAT HAPPENED operation + generation + verdict + receipt/postcondition ``` Preserving identity without completion evidence still permits coherent false success against the correct resource. Preserving completion without qualified identity permits a valid receipt to be attached to the wrong resource. Both dimensions have to survive end-to-end. --- ## Required adversarial tests Each adopting surface should test the applicable failure modes, not merely steady-state success: - delayed generation-N acknowledgement after generation N+1 starts; - timeout after the mutation may already have committed; - retry after ambiguous completion; - duplicate acknowledgement; - consumer/event handler absent after producer admission; - promise resolves but publication/read-back fails; - provider returns a definite error with a normal-looking payload; - fallback completion races result-bearing completion; - one fan-out target fails while others succeed; - one fan-out target never returns while others succeed; - per-target result serialization drops a failure; - candidate artifact build fails after source update; - candidate artifact build fails after cleanup begins; - process exits 0 but required artifact/postcondition is absent; - crash/restart between intent, commit, verification, and marker write; - stale completion attempts to clear newer UI/user state; - compatibility facade drops `failed`, `partial`, `ambiguous`, generation, target identity, or proof. The important test shape is not “did this function return?” It is “can any weaker intermediate event still produce terminal success while the authoritative postcondition is false?” --- ## Acceptance criteria This architecture issue is complete when: 1. Hermes has a documented shared completion vocabulary covering at least success, failure, partial, ambiguous, and stale/superseded outcomes. 2. Async mutation boundaries carry operation identity/generation where stale acknowledgement is possible. 3. The linked ACP path cannot convert a known provider failure into ordinary assistant text plus an unqualified successful turn. 4. Quick Entry clears/hides only on the acknowledgement for the exact requested submission/session generation; timeout ambiguity cannot erase the draft or blindly duplicate the mutation. 5. Desktop preview/tool activation distinguishes event admission from renderer publication and returns an authoritative acknowledgement for the requested target/generation. 6. Updater/deployment success is gated on required packaged/runtime postconditions, not source movement or exit status alone; #88683 remains the broader deployment transaction owner. 7. Webhook fan-out exposes honest per-target outcomes and returns `partial`/equivalent for mixed results rather than aggregate success. 8. Compatibility/facade layers preserve typed verdict, identity, generation, and proof instead of collapsing them to booleans, normal payloads, or generic terminal markers. 9. Stale completions are deterministic no-ops against successor state. 10. Failure-injection tests prove that no linked surface can manufacture terminal success from an earlier lifecycle phase. --- ## Interlocks / topology ### Direct implementation nodes - #89948 — ACP drops `failed/error` and reports failed provider turns as normal answers. - #89920 — Quick Entry acknowledgement + atomic new-session submission; concrete repair of one false-success path from #85590. - #89272 — Desktop preview active-tab desync; includes the `open_preview` fire-and-forget success boundary. - #85523 — webhook Task 10; requires honest per-target fan-out outcomes. ### Deployment/update class - #88683 — authoritative deployment plan + transactional activation; broader owner for installation/update/bootstrap topology. - #88251 — source can advance while packaged Desktop remains stale. - #86443 — destructive Desktop rebuild/update ordering can remove the last working artifact and still project success. - #83846 — ZIP fallback can remove packaged Desktop while later updates report “Already up to date.” - #79678 — updater can successfully pull and then restore stale detached HEAD while printing success. ### Adjacent ACP contract - #72439 — `session/set_model` accepts an invalid model and the next provider failure is surfaced as a silent/normal `end_turn`; complements #89948 by moving rejection to the mutation that introduced the invalid state. ### Existing architecture relationship This issue does **not** replace the narrow incident fixes or #88683. It supplies the shared completion invariant they should compose with. When another incident is found, interlock it here only if its core failure is: ```text weaker lifecycle fact ↓ projected as terminal success ↓ without authoritative mutation proof ``` That keeps this issue a real defect-class node rather than a generic reliability tracker.

signal.title: docs: canonize All Gods Must Die doctrine and exact-object completion amendment
signal.text: ## What this contribution is This PR canonizes **All Gods Must Die: Adversarially Verified Transformation** as a first-class Hermes publication, guide, reusable production skill, and versioned architecture doctrine. The original paper unifies god-file decomposition and multilingual documentation parity under one rule: > Make critical claims mechanically falsifiable, separate production from adjudication, and refuse hidden debt. Hermes is the system under study: a stateful, self-regulating cybernetic agent whose LLM layer supplies neural plasticity and whose deterministic skeleton — CI gates, cryptographic hashes, graph checks, seam identity, manifests, approval boundaries, memory/profile isolation, and adversarial witnesses — makes that plasticity answerable to structure. Hermes is explicitly framed as a **weapon for sovereignty, not war**: an instrument for preserving user agency over model choice, context, memory, tools, execution, provider routing, and technical records. Cyber defense is an internal function because Hermes lives inside the CLI, gateway, tool, memory, provider-egress, desktop-auth, documentation, and CI surfaces she defends. ## Amendment I — Task Completion Verification This PR now embeds a successor architecture refinement derived from the concrete `Task Completion Verification` execution record. The original five laws gain a sixth: > **No task is complete until the requested state exists at the authoritative target and is verified on the exact object.** Derivative rule: > **No receipt may be inherited from a local draft, previous head, adjacent commit, parent object, superseded artifact, or intended write.** This closes the **activity-completion collapse** failure class: a prepared patch is not a changed branch; a changed branch is not a pull request; a pull request is not approval; approval is not merge; merge is not release; release is not operational proof. Completion is represented as a typed state vector across: - materialization; - integrity; - governance; - integration; - operation; - lineage. The amendment preserves the original god-file campaign's `SHIPPED` definition as the namespaced predicate `KAG_SHIPPED`. It does **not** imply `MERGED`, `PUBLISHED`, `RELEASED`, or `OPERATIONALLY_VERIFIED`. The webhook case study preserves both time-bounded truths: - the supplied Task 7 and Task 10 patches were locally prepared and structurally verified, but three GitHub write routes failed with `403 Resource not accessible by integration`; no public state changed in that execution; - later repository reconciliation identifies #85002 as the current Task 7 object, #85523 as closed/unmerged historical Task 10 provenance, and #90236 as its canonical successor. The later target objects do not retroactively turn the earlier 403 into a successful write. The earlier blocker does not deny the later target state. Both events remain in the mutation journal. ## Publication surfaces ### Original v1.0 contribution - `website/docs/guides/all-gods-must-die.md` — long LLM-readable guide, registered in the Guides & Tutorials sidebar. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation.pdf` — immutable 68-page compiled publication. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation.tex` — reproducible LaTeX source. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation.bib` — merged bibliography. - `skills/research/long-document-production/SKILL.md` — reusable long-document production skill. - `website/scripts/generate-llms-txt.py` — curated `llms.txt` inclusion. ### Task Completion Verification source-controlled surfaces - `website/docs/guides/task-completion-verification.md` — exact-object completion architecture guide. - `docs/research/task-completion-verification-amendment.md` — canonical source-readable Amendment I. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-adversarially-verified-transformation-v1.1.tex` — successor composition source preserving immutable v1.0 and appending Amendment I. - `docs/research/task-completion-record.schema.json` — machine-auditable completion-record contract. - `docs/research/task-completion-verification-ledger.json` — dated local-blocker and current GitHub reconciliation records. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-v1.1-release-manifest.json` — source digests, generated-output digests, typed lineage, and packaging-time truth. - `docs/research/all-gods-must-die-interlock.md` — contribution graph and lifecycle boundary. ### Generated release outputs The amendment PDF and composed v1.1 PDF were built, preflighted, rendered, and visually inspected locally. signal.title: fix(desktop): make Windows package rebuild transactional and self-healing
signal.text: ## Summary Closes #44225 and #90829. Addresses the destructive packaged-app loss in #86443 and the split-Node `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` path in #90134. This PR composes the two missing halves of the Windows Desktop rebuild contract: 1. **Acquire a trustworthy candidate realization** — if the active dependency tree contains the exact reported `get-windows@9.3.0` missing/unresolvable package-root failure, realize that pinned package in an isolated temporary npm prefix and stage it through the existing native-binding authority. 2. **Settle replacement transactionally** — preserve the last-good packaged app under a generation-owned rollback identity, verify the replacement executable as a structurally valid PE, and restore the previous generation on builder failure or false success. The result is one bounded transaction rather than two disconnected repairs: ```text active dependency tree → canonical native staging → exact missing-package verdict only → isolated pinned dependency realization → canonical binding/binary gates → generation-bound package build → PE verification → commit replacement OR restore last-good app ``` ## Root causes closed ### Persistent corrupt dependency tree — #90829 An interrupted/in-place Windows npm extraction can leave `node_modules/get-windows` present but unresolvable. Re-running install or staging against the same active tree makes every later Desktop rebuild fail identically. The recovery path now: - recognizes only the canonical missing/unresolvable package-root verdict; - realizes exact `get-windows@9.3.0` outside active `node_modules`; - enables only that pinned package's lifecycle script; - verifies the recovered package root and version; - stages through `stageGetWindows()` / `stageGetWindowsInto()` and their existing binding gates; - removes the temporary realization on success or failure; - never rewrites, deletes, or retries inside the damaged active tree. ### Destructive or false-success package replacement — #44225 / #86443 The package wrapper owns one explicit pack-generation UUID across every `beforePack` call and the terminal builder outcome: - repeated targets cannot overwrite the original rollback generation; - interrupted valid rollback material can be adopted by a retry; - another generation's rollback material is never mutated; - non-zero builder exit removes partial output and restores the last-good app; - exit zero is not success unless the replacement contains a valid DOS header and PE signature; - rollback is discarded only after verified success. ### Split package-script Node authority — #90134 On Windows, npm may run under Hermes-managed Node while a package script's bare `node` resolves through stale fnm/system PATH. The builder wrapper selects npm's exact `npm_node_execpath`, performs one bounded self-reexec, and fails early unless the runtime is Node >=22.22 with working `require(esm)` support. ## Composition lock `desktop-pack-recovery-composition.test.mjs` asserts that the pieces remain one ownership chain: - `package.json` routes build staging and electron-builder `beforePack` through the recovery wrappers; - recovery wraps the canonical `before-pack.mjs` transaction owner rather than replacing it; - the canonical `beforePack(context)` invocation precedes the exact bounded-recovery invocation; - the explicit builder verdict precedes the exact `settleDesktopPack()` commit/restore invocation. This prevents a future edit from preserving both implementations while accidentally disconnecting them. ## Guarantees - Supported native targets remain fail-closed. - win32-arm64 retains its existing explicit degraded contract; no unsupported binding is fabricated. - Recovery is accepted only for a matching native host architecture. - Unrelated platform, version, package, and binding failures remain failures. - The active repository dependency tree is never the recovery destination. - Failed recovery leaves no persistent state that can poison the next update. - A failed or false-success package build leaves the previous verified `Hermes.exe` launch path intact. - One pack generation cannot adopt or destroy another generation's rollback material. ## Files - `apps/desktop/scripts/stage-native-deps-recovery.mjs` — isolated exact-package realization and one bounded retry through canonical staging. - `apps/desktop/scripts/before-pack-recovery.mjs` — wraps the canonical `beforePack` owner and handles only its exact missing-package verdict. - `apps/desktop/scripts/desktop-pack-transaction.mjs` — rollback identity, PE verification, commit/restore settlement. - `apps/desktop/scripts/desktop-builder-runtime.mjs` — npm-selected Node authority and capability gate. - `apps/desktop/scripts/run-electron-builder.mjs` — owns the pack generation and terminal settlement. - `apps/desktop/scripts/before-pack.mjs` — preserves/adopts rollback material under generation identity. - `apps/desktop/scripts/desktop-pack-recovery-composition.test.mjs` — locks recovery and package settlement into one transaction at the actual invocation sites. - Focused Node/Vitest regression suites cover recovery isolation, exact-version pinning, cleanup, unrelated-error preservation, architecture refusal, multi-target fencing, cross-generation refusal, interrupted retry adoption, PE verification, rollback, false success, Node-runtime selection, and end-to-end wiring. ## Exact source-of-truth receipt Current head: [`1b89359ab09773cad7003be1ada10c319b0cade3`](https://github.com/andrexibiza/hermes-agent/commit/1b89359ab09773cad7003be1ada10c319b0cade3) The implementation commit is based directly on current `main` [`8794e5a21c980a0f26532cb4883284b786cb3f25`](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/commit/8794e5a21c980a0f26532cb4883284b786cb3f25); the final commit corrects only the composition regression's invocation-site matching. No status is inherited from the previous head. Fresh workflows attached directly to this head: - [CI run 32432886338](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32432886338) - [Docker run 32432885577](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32432885577) - [Nix run 32432885604](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32432885604) ## Contributor topology - Builds on #88233 by @helix4u, which remains the native-binding repair and provenance owner. - Builds on rollback preservation from #44234 by @AIalliAI and the `.bak` mechanism on main through #69179. - #76088 by @RelaxJonh and #38170 / #34327 by @liuhao1024 remain complementary updater-wide npm-tree work. - Supersedes the separate transport PR #91063 by composing its exact-package recovery into this transaction owner without erasing its implementation chronology. - Interlocks #88683's transactional deployment architecture. This closes the Desktop package-realization transaction; it does not claim the repository-wide source/venv/process deployment plan is complete.

signal.title: Freemaxxing: authenticated proven-free local failover router
signal.text: ## What Ships **Freemaxxing** as a first-class Hermes model-provider plugin with one stable route: ```text provider = freemaxxing model = freemaxxing ``` An authenticated loopback router owns concrete model selection, backend health, bounded failover, and credential refresh. Hermes core keeps the opaque provider/model identity. This is a clean one-commit restack on current `main`; the pre-hardening head is preserved at `archive/85631-pre-hardening-0502d095` and is no longer in this PR. ## Cost authority: proven free or excluded Freemaxxing does not treat “an API token exists” as proof that a route is free. | Tier | Backend | Admission rule | |---|---|---| | 0 | Nous Portal | Only the explicit free DeepSeek Flash allow-list is admitted | | 1 | OpenRouter | Only model IDs ending in `:free` are admitted | Hugging Face is deliberately removed from automatic routing. Routed HF inference can consume credits and become pay-as-you-go; unknown or ambiguous pricing therefore fails closed. There is no silent paid fallback. ## Profile isolation The current loopback router is explicitly single-profile-only. When `gateway.multiplex_profiles` is active, Freemaxxing rejects initialization before reading Nous, OpenRouter, or fallback credentials. A safe multiplex implementation needs a profile-addressed capability mapped to a per-profile pool. Until Hermes has that wire, native providers remain the correct route for multiplexed gateways. Tests exercise two distinct profile scopes and prove neither can inherit the process capability or establish shared pool authority. ## Local capability and lifecycle - Listener binds only to `127.0.0.1`. - Every operational endpoint requires a random per-process bearer. - Blank tokens and token-mode changes are rejected; an unauthenticated listener cannot be reused or upgraded in place. - `GET /v1/healthz` exposes only a minimal liveness marker. - Provider discovery opens the authenticated listener but does not resolve upstream secrets, catalogs, or pool state. - Upstream authority is constructed lazily after the first authenticated runtime request. - Static picker discovery returns only the opaque `freemaxxing` model and cannot establish runtime authority. ## Failure and resource authority - `429`: bounded `Retry-After` cooldown, then fail over. - `5xx`, timeout, reset, DNS, and pre-status connection failure: short cooldown, then fail over. - Model-not-found: skip without poisoning general backend health. - `401/403`: one serialized credential refresh where supported, then skip. - Other `4xx`: return a client error without replaying a malformed request. - HTTP 200 with truncated, oversized, non-UTF-8, malformed, or non-object JSON: classify as transient and fail over before committing a response. - Streaming: first-line preflight before downstream `200`; bounded SSE lines/events; failover only before commit. - Downstream client cancellation does not cool down a healthy upstream backend. - Bounds: request 1 MB, catalog 2 MB, non-streaming response 10 MB, SSE line 1 MB, SSE event 2 MB. - Credentialed upstream requests use Hermes’ redirect-safe `open_credentialed_url` path. ## Code shape The implementation is split by authority: - `policy.py` — free-route admission, shared limits, typed failures - `pool.py` — backend state, strict tiering, round-robin, catalog single-flight - `upstream.py` — bounded credentialed HTTP and response-integrity classification - `handler.py` — authenticated OpenAI-compatible request/stream surface - `server.py` — immutable loopback listener lifecycle - `proxy.py` / `router.py` — stable public composition surfaces - `__init__.py` — lazy provider registration and profile-scope gate No Hermes core files are changed. ## Verification ```bash python -m pytest -q \ tests/plugins/model_providers/test_freemaxxing_proxy.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_freemaxxing_routing.py ``` Focused result on the exact implementation assembled for this head: ```text 31 passed ``` The tests import only the canonical production package module and cover the generic runtime credential resolver, listener authentication, profile isolation, proven-free admission, failover, refresh serialization, response bounds/integrity, streaming pre-commit behavior, and downstream cancellation attribution. ## Scope hygiene The PR is one commit ahead of current `main`, zero commits behind, and contains only the Freemaxxing plugin, its documentation/manifest, and focused tests.

signal.title: Desktop: mic fails with "runtime does not support microphone recording" when UI is loaded over HTTP (DEV_SERVER / remote dist)
signal.text: ## Summary Pressing the desktop voice/mic control shows: > This runtime does not support microphone recording. This happens when the desktop renderer is loaded from a **non-secure HTTP origin** (e.g. `HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER` pointing at a remote/Tailscale host serving `apps/desktop/dist` over plain HTTP). It is **not** tied to a specific model/provider, and it happens even when voice/STT are enabled in settings. ## Environment - Hermes Desktop (Electron) with renderer loaded from remote HTTP dev/dist server - Also reproducible by opening the same desktop `dist/` in a normal browser over `http://<host>:<port>` (non-localhost) - Voice/STT enabled in config - OS: macOS client + remote Linux host serving the UI (also applies to any HTTP origin) ## Steps to reproduce 1. Serve `apps/desktop/dist` over plain HTTP on a non-localhost address (e.g. LAN/Tailscale IP). 2. Point Electron at that URL via `HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER` (or open the URL in a browser). 3. Open a chat and press the mic / voice control. ## Expected - Mic capture works on the **client** machine (getUserMedia in the renderer), or - UI disables the control with a clear message: "Microphone requires a secure context (HTTPS/localhost) or the native desktop app." ## Actual ```ts // apps/desktop/src/app/chat/composer/hooks/use-mic-recorder.ts if (!navigator.mediaDevices?.getUserMedia || typeof MediaRecorder === 'undefined') { throw new Error(copy.microphoneUnsupported) } ``` On insecure HTTP, Chromium leaves `navigator.mediaDevices` / `getUserMedia` unavailable, so the generic "runtime does not support…" string is thrown. Permission handlers in `electron/main.ts` never run because the API is missing at the document origin. ## Why this matters Remote-agent setups commonly load the desktop UI from a headless host over Tailscale HTTP. Chat works; voice looks enabled in settings but is dead. The error reads like a missing binary feature rather than a secure-context / packaging issue. ## Suggested fix (product) 1. **Detect insecure context** before start: `!window.isSecureContext` or missing `mediaDevices`, and show a specific i18n string (HTTPS / native app / localhost), not "runtime does not support." 2. **Docs**: state that desktop mic requires native package, `file://`, localhost, or HTTPS — plain remote HTTP will never get getUserMedia. 3. Optional: for `HERMES_DESKTOP_DEV_SERVER` remote workflows, document HTTPS or SSH/local port-forward to `http://127.0.0.1`. 4. Related: browser-side voice capture work in #20765 / #54352. ## Workaround - Use the packaged native desktop app (local renderer), or - Load the UI from `https://` or `http://127.0.0.1` (port-forward), or - Use gateway voice messages (e.g. Telegram) for STT.
