signal.title: state.db corruption recurs on SQLite 3.53.1 — WAL sidecar unlink under a concurrent writer
signal.text: ## Summary `state.db` has corrupted multiple times on this host across two profiles. The first three traced to a known-vulnerable SQLite build (WAL-reset #69784, vulnerable ≤3.51.2, via a `pysqlite3` shim bundling 3.51.1). The most recent recurrence hit **both** the builder and reviewer profiles on a **current SQLite 3.53.1**, which #69784's fix line does **not** cover — so the earlier "remove the vulnerable build" closure is incomplete, and a residual corruption mechanism remains. ## Evidence (forensic, read-only) - On the affected DBs, ~20 of ~40 tracked open fds pointed at already-unlinked `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars. - Builder `state.db` page 1 clobbered by a `compression_locks` holder (`pid=4157689 tid=124375474894528 agent=711e8afb2650 nonce=ae12c5e0`); the reviewer DB showed interior b-tree damage (`btreeInitPage error 11`) with an intact header. ## Leading hypothesis (seeking confirmation) Under concurrent connections, a WAL (re-)initialization unlinks the `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars while a writer still holds them open; the next checkpoint then writes to offsets no longer backed by the file → page corruption. Whether the unlink originates in hermes-agent's connection management or is SQLite-level under concurrent WAL re-init is the open question. ## Workaround holding for us **The load-bearing step is a manual exclusive `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` on an idle DB** — not the config pin. `apply_wal_with_fallback()` in `hermes_state.py` returns early for an already-on-disk WAL DB (it never reaches the `configured == "delete"` branch), so a config pin alone leaves an existing DB in WAL with its sidecars intact. The pin only governs a *future* freshly-created DB. Procedure that actually held here (both profiles): 1. Stop the gateways; confirm **zero** live `state.db` fds, including already-deleted `-wal`/`-shm` descriptors. 2. Exclusive `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` on each DB (checkpoints, truncates the sidecars, rewrites the header to write-version 1). 3. Pin `database.journal_mode: delete` in `config.yaml` (affects new DBs only). 4. Restart; verify on-disk header byte 18 == 1 and no `-wal`/`-shm`. Corrected after @jackulau's source read in the discussion below. ## Gap that made this hard The live `WAL → DELETE` downgrade path refuses to run while connections are open, forcing a manual two-step (exclusive `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` on an idle DB, then a config pin). A safe live-downgrade — or a WAL-init that never unlinks active sidecars — would help other operators. ## Related upstream issues (cross-linked from the discussion) - **#85609** — surfaced warning when a `journal_mode` config pin is ignored on an existing WAL DB (our "operator-signal" gap). - **#90871** — skip automatic FTS rebuilds when another process holds the DB or its sidecars (our `~20/40` deleted-fd fingerprint). - **#90837** — second recurring-corruption report; FTS disabled for the last three of eleven incidents. - **#90892** — `synchronous` never executed on Linux; we measured `synchronous=2` (FULL) here, ruling NORMAL out. ## Questions 1. Is the WAL-init sidecar unlink under concurrent connections a known hermes-agent connection-management issue, or SQLite-level? 2. Would it help to attach the preserved corrupt DB copies for a repro? ## Environment - Linux (ext4), Discord + desktop gateways, both profiles. - SQLite 3.53.1 at occurrence time; earlier occurrences ranged the 3.7.0–3.51.2 vulnerability line.

signal.title: refactor(webhook): establish canonical intake authority
signal.text: Refs #90989. ## Purpose This is the first implementation slice of the webhook surface-convergence issue. It creates the domain authority that the existing webhook campaign lanes can compose onto instead of continuing to derive provider, delivery identity, event identity, and intake provenance independently. ## Exact topology - base: `5e32e3aecd2070e8245d9ae2c9ee257f547fcb71` - head: `a9af5efcfeb6d81ae7be04421c7fcc8e872440fa` - tree: `f174a69ead1a509be956207581eaccf927fe6665` - one commit - two files - no campaign receipts, contributor churn, UI/router spillover, or `webhook.py` god-file rewrite The branch was rebuilt after `main` advanced during PR creation. The current head overlays only the two webhook-authority blobs onto the exact new main tree; no intervening upstream files are dropped. ## What this establishes ### Canonical provider registry `gateway/platforms/webhook_contract.py` owns provider namespaces and the wire facts required by intake: aliases, provider-native delivery-ID headers, event headers, compatibility-detection headers, payload identity keys, allowed verifier modes, and default verifier mode. Provider identity and cryptographic verifier identity are related but deliberately not conflated. For example, an explicitly declared Chatwoot route can remain in the `chatwoot` provider namespace while using a registered generic HMAC verifier. Impossible provider/verifier combinations fail closed. ### One route/provider binding decision `WebhookRouteConfig.bind()` normalizes profile, provider, signature mode, enabled state, and event allowlist once. Explicit route authority cannot subsequently be replaced by attacker-controlled request headers. Undeclared historical routes retain one explicit compatibility bridge (`infer_legacy_provider`) so migration can be staged without silently breaking existing installs. The compatibility result is recorded as provenance and is not a downstream authorization mechanism. ### Provider-native retry identity `resolve_delivery_identity()` consumes only the already-bound provider namespace: - GitHub: `X-GitHub-Delivery` - Svix: `svix-id` - GitLab: event/webhook/idempotency UUID headers - Standard Webhooks: `webhook-id` / `Idempotency-Key` - Chatwoot: declared delivery header, then declared payload ID - Stripe: declared payload ID - generic: `X-Request-ID` There is **no timestamp fallback**. If no stable provider identity exists, deduplication authority is absent and the envelope receives a unique trace/session identity instead. Payload `id` is accepted only for explicitly declared providers, so an attacker cannot turn an undeclared/generic route into Stripe or Chatwoot by shaping the JSON body. ### Immutable intake envelope `WebhookEnvelope` carries the facts that downstream execution should consume exactly once: - normalized route/profile - provider + verifier/auth provenance - provider-scoped event type - stable delivery identity when one exists - unique trace identity - SHA-256 of the exact raw body - recursively immutable payload - profile/route/provider-scoped idempotency key This creates the intended HTTP/domain boundary: later composition can move from `aiohttp.Request` to `WebhookEnvelope` without re-deriving security or identity facts. ## Focused verification surface `tests/gateway/test_webhook_contract.py` covers immutable registry behavior, alias normalization, unknown provider/verifier rejection, provider/verifier disagreement, valid provider + generic-verifier composition, attacker-header resistance, provider-scoped event extraction, bounded legacy inference, provider-native identity precedence, absence of dedupe authority without a stable ID, timestamp non-identity, explicit-only payload IDs, scoped idempotency keys, profile mismatch, raw-body provenance, and recursive envelope immutability. Fresh hosted CI/Docker/Nix is required on `a9af5efc...`; no sibling or historical green is inherited. ## Composition boundary This PR intentionally does **not** rewrite the current `WebhookAdapter` handler yet. Doing that before the current Task 10/auth/session candidates converge would recreate the same multi-owner conflict #90989 is intended to eliminate. - #90236 remains the canonical executable Task 10 intake/idempotency/raw-body owner. - #85318 remains the exact-head-green explicit signature-verifier authority. - #90304 owns session/interaction policy. - #85640 remains the sole terminal integration owner. The next convergence slice should wire current intake/auth onto this contract, preserving #90236's body-hash/idempotency semantics and consuming #85318's verifier rather than copying either implementation again.

signal.title: fix(cli): map Shift+<symbol> under xterm modifyOtherKeys=2
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Fixes shifted punctuation being untypeable in the interactive CLI on terminals that speak xterm `modifyOtherKeys`. `_enable_extended_enter_keys()` pushes modifyOtherKeys level 2 (`CSI >4;2m`) to Ghostty, iTerm2, WezTerm, VS Code, tmux and Windows Terminal. Those terminals then re-encode modified keys as `ESC[27;<mod>;<codepoint>~`. `install_modify_other_keys_aliases()` maps Shift+letter but not Shift+symbol, so on Ghostty 1.3.x pressing <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>/</kbd> inserts the literal text `^[[27;2;63~` into the prompt instead of `?`. Same for `!` `:` `"` `_` `+` `<` `>` `(` `)` `~` — i.e. most punctuation is unusable while the mode is active. This is the same class of bug as #87711, which fixed it for letters only. The symbols were skipped deliberately, with this comment: > `Shift+digit symbols are layout-specific (US: '!', AZERTY: '¹', etc.) so they > are NOT mapped here — if the terminal sends those under modifyOtherKeys, they > will leak, but that's better than wrong input.` That reasoning holds when deriving a shifted character from an **unshifted** codepoint. But the modifyOtherKeys encoding reports the codepoint **already shifted by the terminal**, which has applied the user's real keymap — Shift+/ on a US layout arrives as `63` (`?`), not `47` (`/`). So echoing `chr(codepoint)` is not a layout guess; it is exactly what the terminal says was typed, and is correct on every layout. There is no "wrong input" risk to trade against here. ## Related Issue Related to #87711 (same leak, letters only). No separate issue filed. ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) ## Changes Made - `hermes_cli/pt_input_extras.py` — in `install_modify_other_keys_aliases()`, register `ESC[27;2;<cp>~` → `chr(cp)` for every printable ASCII codepoint (0x20–0x7E) that is not already mapped. Removed the now-obsolete "symbols are layout-specific" note and documented why the shifted-codepoint encoding makes this layout-safe. - `tests/cli/test_cli_shift_symbol_keys.py` — new, 6 tests. **Deliberately scoped to the modifyOtherKeys (tilde) spelling only — not CSI-u.** The Kitty protocol reports the *unshifted* codepoint plus a shift bit, so registering `ESC[47;2u` → `chr(47)` would type `/` for Shift+/. Kitty-protocol terminals deliver printable keys as plain text anyway, so there is nothing to map. A test pins this so a later "make it symmetric" refactor cannot silently break it. Letters and Space are registered earlier in the same function and are skipped by the `if seq not in ANSI_SEQUENCES` membership check, so this only fills genuinely unmapped codepoints. Codepoints 9/32/127 keep their dedicated `BackTab` / `" "` / `ControlH` meanings. ## How to Test Reproduce (before this patch), in Ghostty: 1. Start the interactive CLI: `hermes` 2. Press <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>/</kbd> — the prompt shows `^[[27;2;63~` instead of `?`. 3. Same for <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>1</kbd>, <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>;</kbd>, <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>'</kbd> … With the patch, each inserts the expected character. Headless equivalent: ```python from prompt_toolkit.input.vt100_parser import Vt100Parser from hermes_cli.pt_input_extras import install_modify_other_keys_aliases install_modify_other_keys_aliases() events = [] Vt100Parser(events.append).feed_and_flush("\x1b[27;2;63~") print([e.key for e in events]) # ['?'] (was: Escape + 9 literal chars) ``` Test suite: ``` pytest tests/cli/test_cli_shift_symbol_keys.py -q # 6 passed pytest tests/cli/test_ctrl_enter_newline.py \ tests/cli/test_cli_shift_enter_newline.py \ tests/cli/test_cli_terminal_shortcuts.py -q # 21 passed, 2 skipped ``` The new suite covers: the shifted-symbol table; an exhaustive no-leak sweep over all printable ASCII; Shift+letter non-regression; Space/Tab/Backspace not being clobbered; CSI-u spellings left untouched; and installer idempotency. Verified end-to-end on Ghostty 1.3.1 / macOS with prompt_toolkit 3.0.52.

signal.title: fix(gateway): make Windows Scheduled Task install work on workgroup machines
signal.text: ## Summary `hermes gateway install` fails on Windows workgroup machines with "Windows gateway install failed". Two root causes in `hermes_cli/gateway_windows.py`: 1. **`_resolve_task_user()` returns `WORKGROUP\user` on workgroup machines.** Task Scheduler cannot map that principal to a security ID, so `schtasks /Create /XML` rejects the generated task at the `<UserId>` element: ``` (17,8):UserId: ERROR: No mapping between account names and security IDs was done. ``` Reproduced on Windows 11 build 10.0.26200 (workgroup machine, local account). 2. **The `/RU` create variant combines `/NP` with `/IT`.** On newer Windows builds schtasks rejects the pair (`/IT switch cannot be used with /NP`), and `/NP` alone makes schtasks prompt for a run-as password, which hangs non-interactive installs. ## Changes - `_resolve_task_user()`: return the bare username when `USERDOMAIN` is unset or a workgroup sentinel (`WORKGROUP` / `MICROSOFTACCOUNT`), so the task principal is a valid local account. - `_install_scheduled_task()`: drop `/NP` from the `/RU` variant. The generated task XML already declares the principal (`InteractiveToken`), so `/IT` alone keeps the task interactive without a stored password. The XML-only fallback variant is unchanged. ## Verification On Windows 11 build 26200 (workgroup machine, Hermes v0.18.2): - Before: `hermes gateway install --start-now --start-on-login` exits 1 with `RuntimeError: Windows gateway install failed`; no task is created. - After: install exits 0, creates the `Hermes_Gateway` ONLOGON task (Logon Mode: Interactive only), and the gateway starts. schtasks variant matrix on the affected machine: | XML `UserId` / CLI flags | Result | | --- | --- | | `qiaoa` (bare) | success | | `helen_redmi\qiaoa` | success | | `WORKGROUP\qiaoa` | fail — no mapping between account names and security IDs | | `.\qiaoa` | fail — no mapping between account names and security IDs | | `/RU user /IT` | success | | `/RU user /NP` | prompts for a run-as password | | `/RU user /NP /IT` | rejected — `/IT switch cannot be used with /NP` | Unit tests added for `_resolve_task_user()` (workgroup / domain / unset-domain / missing-username / pre-qualified username cases) and verified against the patched code in the Hermes venv on the affected machine. Fixes #89807

signal.title: fix(tui): re-read profile .env on every interactive turn
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Desktop and `hermes serve` keep a long-lived backend whose process environment is loaded from `.env` at startup. Interactive turns for the launch/default profile never installed a per-turn secret mapping (`profile_home` is None, so `set_secret_scope` was skipped). `get_secret("HASS_TOKEN")` therefore kept the startup snapshot: adding a token to `.env` and restarting the gateway still left Home Assistant tools returning HTTP 401 until a full app quit-and-relaunch. This installs `build_profile_secret_scope(_session_home(session))` on every interactive turn, and on compute-host agent builds, so `.env` is re-read each turn without mutating process-global `os.environ`. The compute-host `finally` resets that mapping even when there is no `profile_home` override. ## Related Issue Fixes #91147 ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [ ] 📝 Documentation update - [ ] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - `tui_gateway/server.py` — `_install_session_secret_scope` re-reads `<session home>/.env` on every interactive turn, including launch/default sessions with `profile_home=None`. - `tui_gateway/compute_host.py` — same mapping when building an agent without `profile_home`; `reset_secret_scope` runs whenever a mapping was installed, not only when a home override exists. - `tests/tui_gateway/test_launch_profile_secret_scope.py` — launch-home fallback and `.env` re-read without reloading `os.environ`. - `tests/tools/test_homeassistant_tool.py` — `_get_config()` still sees a stale process env until the mapping is installed. ## How to Test 1. signal.title: Feature: canonical unified sessions across WebUI and Telegram
signal.text: ## Problem Hermes currently treats WebUI and Telegram as separate conversation surfaces. A user may talk to the same profile from both surfaces, but the conversations are stored and displayed as separate session transcripts. Sharing a profile, chat ID, or routing key does not make the history or live turns unified. This makes a WebUI/Telegram workflow unreliable for users who want to start a task in Telegram, continue it in WebUI, and receive WebUI replies back in the same Telegram conversation. The existing delivery mirror path is useful for one-off outbound notifications, but it does not provide a canonical conversation session or reliable bidirectional synchronization. ## Proposed behavior Add a supported cross-surface session attachment or unified-session mechanism: - A WebUI session can attach to an existing Telegram-origin session without creating a second transcript. - User and assistant messages from both surfaces appear in the same history. - Replies are delivered exactly once to the originating Telegram chat and topic. - Starting a new WebUI conversation has an explicit, predictable attachment policy; it must not silently bind to a stale session. - Session resets, model changes, tool calls, streaming, and errors preserve the same routing identity. - The behavior works with Telegram topics and normal private chats and remains profile-isolated. ## Acceptance criteria - A message sent from Telegram is visible in the attached WebUI session. - A message sent from WebUI is visible in the same Telegram chat/topic. - The two surfaces show the same ordered user/assistant transcript after refresh. - No duplicate assistant replies are produced during reconnects or retries. - A service restart does not create a new detached transcript. - Existing independent WebUI and Telegram sessions continue to work unchanged when no attachment is requested. ## Scope note Hermes-Relay's Android app can consume upstream Hermes sessions, but the canonical session/routing behavior belongs in hermes-agent. Relay can then display or select the unified session through its existing session APIs.

signal.title: fix(update): restore a Desktop build wiped by an earlier Windows update
signal.text: ## Summary Closes the residual self-concealing recovery gap in #83846 and supersedes stale/conflicting PR #87879 while preserving its exact implementation and author identity. After an earlier Windows ZIP-fallback/update failure deletes `apps/desktop/release/`, every later update can incorrectly conclude that Desktop was never installed: - the current run sees no packaged executable; - the normal rebuild gate returns early; - an up-to-date checkout short-circuits before Desktop repair; - the user remains permanently stranded behind “Already up to date!” and a dead shortcut. This current-main rebase uses `$HERMES_HOME/desktop-build-stamp.json` as the durable evidence that Desktop existed before the prior destructive run. The up-to-date repair path now invokes the existing Desktop rebuild owner; content-stamp checks keep the no-op path cheap, and users who never installed Desktop still do not pay for an Electron build. ## Provenance This is the exact #87879 commit rebased cleanly through GitHub onto current `main`; the original Git author is preserved: - [`531e465eeafc6386ba8414d3dc652f0674c8f447`](https://github.com/andrexibiza/hermes-agent/commit/531e465eeafc6386ba8414d3dc652f0674c8f447) ## Exact-head verification All hosted workflows attached directly to `531e465e...` are green: - [CI 32433513487](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32433513487) - [Docker 32433512086](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32433512086) - [Nix 32433512092](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32433512092) No status is inherited from #87879 or its former base. ## Interlock - #91079 makes the *current* package replacement transactional and self-healing. - This PR repairs machines already damaged by an earlier generation, including the “artifact absent, source current” state. - #87878 / #87304 remain the source-tree ZIP-fallback safety owner; this PR does not duplicate that broader guard. - #88683 remains the repository-wide transactional deployment architecture owner.

signal.title: fix(update): restore a Desktop build wiped by a previous update run
signal.text: ## Summary A Desktop build deleted by a previous update run is now rebuilt by the next `hermes update`, instead of being stranded forever behind "Already up to date!". Fixes the two residual gaps of #83846 (partially addressed by 4aa9f738ce, which only covers loss during the *current* run). ## Root cause After a ZIP-fallback run wipes `apps/desktop/release/` (#83846, #87304): 1. `_rebuild_desktop_after_update` gates on `had_desktop_app_before_update or _desktop_app_present(...)` — both False on every LATER update, so the rebuild is silently skipped. 2. Post-wipe updates land on the `commit_count == 0` "Already up to date!" short-circuit, which never called the desktop rebuild at all — the failure is self-concealing (shortcuts point at a deleted Hermes.exe while updates report success). Only a manual `hermes desktop --force-build` recovered. ## Changes - `_desktop_build_stamp_recorded()`: `$HERMES_HOME/desktop-build-stamp.json` lives outside the checkout and survives the wipe — it is the durable "this user had Desktop" signal, and now satisfies the rebuild gate. - The "Already up to date!" path (`_repair_node_deps_on_current_checkout`) now calls `_rebuild_desktop_after_update`. Cheap for everyone else: the in-process content-hash stamp check short-circuits when the app exists and is current; users who never built Desktop return immediately (no stamp, no app, no npm spawn). ## Validation | Check | Result | |---|---| | New: prior-run wipe + stamp present → rebuild fires | pass | | New: no stamp, no app → no Electron build imposed | pass | | New: up-to-date path calls the rebuild with the right args | pass | | Full `tests/hermes_cli/test_cmd_update.py` | 38 passed |

signal.title: fix(install): fail clearly before PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mutates anything
signal.text: ## Summary Refs #89857. Supersedes stale/conflicting PR #90128 while preserving its exact implementation and original author identity. This does **not** make Hermes install under PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage Mode. The current installer performs more than forty method calls on non-core .NET types; a partial conversion would only move the failure deeper into a mutating install. The correct bounded behavior today is fail-before-mutation with an accurate diagnosis. This current-main rebase adds a CLM-legal preflight before script-scope environment normalization, explaining: - that AppLocker/WDAC/application-control policy imposed the restriction; - why `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` cannot change language mode; - which policy/path changes can make the script trusted; - how to verify `FullLanguage` before retrying. The test suite creates a real constrained child runspace, proves the restriction is active, and locks the preflight's placement ahead of the first forbidden .NET call. Installer workflow coverage runs under both Windows PowerShell 5.1 and pwsh 7. ## Provenance This is the exact #90128 commit by @jackulau rebased cleanly through GitHub onto current `main`. The original Git author is preserved: - [`11599ccf28a39b0b062944d4023d71df3c7405eb`](https://github.com/andrexibiza/hermes-agent/commit/11599ccf28a39b0b062944d4023d71df3c7405eb) ## Exact-head verification All hosted workflows attached directly to `11599ccf...` are green: - [CI 32433654721](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32433654721) - [Docker 32433654284](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32433654284) - [Nix 32433654286](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/32433654286) No status is inherited from #90128 or its former base. ## Scope and follow-on This closes the misleading/raw-failure class and prevents partial installation under an unsupported policy context. A true CLM-compatible installer remains a separate product decision because PATH broadcasts, folder resolution, process capture, and BOM-free writes have no behavior-identical CLM replacements. This PR does not claim that capability.

signal.title: fix(install): refuse ConstrainedLanguage with a reason instead of a .NET error
signal.text: ## Read this first: it does not make the install work `Refs #89857`, not `Fixes`. This does not let anyone install under Constrained Language Mode. It makes the failure legible, and it stops the installer from dying in a way that points the operator at the wrong thing. Whether Hermes should support CLM at all is a maintainer decision, and I have put the measurements for it at the bottom rather than deciding it in a PR. ## What does this PR do? `install.ps1` makes more than forty method calls on non-core .NET types. Constrained Language Mode refuses every one of them. The first is at **script scope**, so it fires before the script has looked at a single parameter: ```powershell $script:NormalizedProfilePaths = Set-LongProfileEnvVars # line ~327, runs on load -> foreach ($name in @('TEMP','TMP','LOCALAPPDATA','APPDATA','USERPROFILE')) { $current = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable($name) # line 312 -- refused ``` That is why the report's log shows `stage=__manifest__`: `-Manifest` is a read-only query that touches nothing on disk, and it still cannot answer. Same for `-ProtocolVersion`. The bootstrap gets exit 1 and forwards a raw .NET error, localized into the host language, naming line 312 of a file in `AppData\Local\hermes\bootstrap-cache\` that the operator did not write. Nothing in that output contains the words "language mode". This adds a preflight at the top of the script that detects the mode and says so. Every construct in it is CLM-legal: a property read on an automatic variable, string concatenation, `Write-Host`, and `Write-Error`. `$host.UI.WriteErrorLine` is **not** legal there, and neither is `[Console]::Error.WriteLine` (which `Write-PathDiag` uses) -- both are method calls on non-core types and would throw the exact error the block exists to explain. ## Related Issue Refs #89857 ## Type of Change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] Security fix - [ ] Documentation update - [ ] Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - `scripts/install.ps1` - a language mode preflight immediately after `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"`, before the UTF-8 console block and well before the 8.3 normalization that currently kills the run. Fires on anything that is not `FullLanguage`, prints an explanation, and exits 1. **57 lines added, 0 changed** - no existing line is touched. - `scripts/tests/test-install-ps1-language-mode.ps1` - new, following the `Assert-Equal`/`Assert-True` shape of the three tests already in that directory. - `.github/workflows/installer-tests.yml` - runs the new file on pwsh 7 and Windows PowerShell 5.1, the same pair the 8.3 test already uses. ### What the operator sees now ``` [X] Hermes cannot install in PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mode. This session is restricted by an application control policy (AppLocker, WDAC, or Windows Defender Application Control). In this mode PowerShell refuses the .NET calls the installer needs to read environment variables and locate profile folders. -ExecutionPolicy Bypass does not help. Execution policy and language mode are separate controls; bypassing the first leaves the second exactly as it was. PowerShell applies the restriction because this script sits in a user-writable directory that the policy does not trust. Ask whoever administers the policy to either: * allow-list the installer's path, or * let you run it from a directory the policy already trusts (typically %ProgramFiles% or %SystemRoot%). Confirm the fix worked before re-running: $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode must print FullLanguage. ``` The `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` sentence is there because it is the reporter's own step 2. They tried it, it did not help, and nothing told them why. It is the sentence I would most want kept if the message gets trimmed. ### Three decisions worth a maintainer's eye **1. It refuses rather than degrades.** A partial port that made line 312 CLM-safe would move the crash to the next blocked call and leave a half-configured tree behind. I would rather the installer stop while it can still explain itself. If you would prefer best-effort-then-fail, the guard becomes a warning and the mutation table below tells you which test to expect to flip (M3). **2. Exit code 1, not a new one.** The stage protocol documents `0` success, `1` generic failure, `2` unknown stage. A distinct code (say `3`) would let the Rust bootstrap render this specially instead of forwarding text, but that extends a documented contract and drivers would need to learn it. I used `1`. Say the word and I will add `3` plus the protocol doc entry. **3. No override flag.** There is deliberately no `-IgnoreLanguageMode`. Anything that got past the guard would fail ~200 lines later with the original error, so the flag's only real effect would be to restore the confusing failure. ## How to Test ```powershell powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\tests\test-install-ps1-language-mode.ps1 # 12/12 powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\tests\test-install-ps1-stage-protocol.ps1 # unchanged, passes powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\tests\test-install-ps1-longpath.ps1 # unchanged, passes ``` No AppLocker or WDAC policy is needed on the runner: the test drops a **child** runspace into `ConstrainedLanguage` with `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode = 'ConstrainedLanguage'`, which is the same restriction the policy applies, and runs `install.ps1` inside it as a real subprocess. To see the old behavior, revert `scripts/install.ps1` and re-run the first file: five assertions fail and the raw error comes back. ## Verification **The failure reproduces exactly, on a real Windows 11 box.** Against pristine `upstream/main` in a constrained child: ``` Cannot invoke method. Method invocation is supported only on core types in this language mode. At C:\Users\jackl\AppData\Local\Temp\install-pristine.ps1:312 char:9 + $current = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable($name) + ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ + FullyQualifiedErrorId : MethodInvocationNotSupportedInConstrainedLanguage ``` Same line, same character offset, same error id as the report -- in English rather than the reporter's Spanish, which is itself the point: the text an operator gets is host-localized, so it cannot be searched for. **Mutation proof - 6 mutations, 6 caught:** | # | Mutation | Caught by | |---|---|---| | 1 | guard removed entirely (the reported bug) | 5 assertions | | 2 | condition inverted, fires on `FullLanguage` instead | 9 assertions, including every FullLanguage regression check | | 3 | `exit 1` removed, so it warns and continues | 2 - the run reaches line 312 and the raw error resurfaces | | 4 | stderr via `$host.UI.WriteErrorLine` instead of `Write-Error` | 1 - the guard itself throws under CLM | | 5 | the `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` sentence dropped | 1 | | 6 | guard moved after the 8.3 normalization block | 5 - placement, not presence, is what makes it work | Mutation 6 is the one worth looking at: the guard is only useful *before* `Set-LongProfileEnvVars` runs at script scope, and nothing about the code's appearance says so. That assertion is what stops a future reshuffle from silently reverting this. **The test cannot pass vacuously.** Its first two assertions check the harness itself: that the child reports `ConstrainedLanguage`, and that `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable` really is refused inside it. Without those, a host where the mode assignment silently did not take would run every remaining assertion against FullLanguage and report green. **Platform:** Windows 11, Windows PowerShell 5.1. **I could not run pwsh 7 locally** - it is not installed on this machine - so the pwsh 7 job added to `installer-tests.yml` is the first real execution of this file under 7. Flagging that rather than implying I tested both. `scripts/install.ps1` stays pure ASCII with CRLF endings, as its own header requires. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate: no open or merged PR names #89857, and a search for `ConstrainedLanguage` / `LanguageMode` across open PRs returns nothing - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix (no unrelated commits): one commit, one added block, one new test, one workflow wiring - [x] I've run the tests and all pass: all three installer suites above, on 5.1 - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes) - [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows 11 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation or N/A: the block documents itself and names why each construct in it was chosen - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys or N/A: no config keys - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows or N/A - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact per the [compatibility guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#cross-platform-compatibility): Windows-only file. On any host reporting `FullLanguage` (which includes every non-Windows PowerShell) the guard is a single string comparison and does nothing - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior or N/A ## What a real CLM port would cost, if you want one I measured this before choosing to refuse, and the answer is not "impossible", it is "a decision with trade-offs": | construct | count | CLM-legal replacement | cost | |---|---|---|---| | `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable($n)` (process scope) | 5 | `(Get-Item "Env:$n").Value` or `$env:$n` | none - the file already uses `Set-Item "Env:$name"` for the *write* one line below the read that fails | | `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User"\|"Machine")` and the matching `SetEnvironmentVariable` | 18 | `Get-ItemProperty`/`Set-ItemProperty` on `HKCU:\Environment` and the machine key | loses the `WM_SETTINGCHANGE` broadcast .NET does, so open shells keep a stale PATH | | `[Environment]::GetFolderPath(...)` | 4 | no cmdlet equivalent | already fallback-only in `Get-LongProfileRoot`; the shortcut sites at ~4131 have no equivalent | | `New-Object System.Diagnostics.Process` | 2 | `Start-Process` | changes stdout/stderr capture semantics | | `[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($p,$s,$utf8NoBom)` | 3 | `Set-Content -Encoding utf8` | **behavior change on 5.1**: it writes a BOM, and these sites pass `UTF8Encoding($false)` deliberately | | `Add-Type` P/Invoke for `GetLongPathNameW` | 1 | none | already wrapped in try/catch with two fallbacks, so it degrades today | I verified each replacement in a constrained runspace rather than reasoning about it -- `Get-Item Env:`, `$env:`, `Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\Environment` and `ConvertTo-Json` are all allowed; `[Environment]::*`, `[Console]::*` and `$host.UI.WriteErrorLine` are all refused. The two rows that make it a decision rather than a chore are the PATH broadcast and the BOM. Both are silent behavior changes on hosts that are working fine today, in exchange for supporting a locked-down configuration. Happy to do the port as a follow-up if that trade is one you want to make, but it should be its own PR with its own argument, not smuggled in behind an error message.
signal.author: jackulau

signal.title: architecture(desktop): make route identity immutable, generation-bound, and resource-owned across multi-gateway Desktop
signal.text: ## Summary Desktop now has real multi-gateway routing, but the architecture still treats route identity as reconstructible metadata rather than an immutable authority proof. #89719 successfully shipped registered-gateway switching and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation across REST, WebSocket, sessions, messaging, cron, projects, settings, and status state. Background gateways retain sockets and continue work. That is the correct product direction. However, one review finding crossed into `main`: `resolvedConnectionId()` can take a descriptor that already corresponds to an exact registry route and reconstruct a weaker identity from URL or `user@host`, selecting the first match. Legal duplicate registrations can therefore alias: - identical URLs with different auth mode, headers, credentials, Cloud organization, or account; - identical SSH user/host pairs with different port, key path, remote Hermes path, or remote profile. Because the rest of the new source-aware machinery then follows that reconstructed ID consistently, the result is a particularly convincing split-brain: the system can be internally coherent under the wrong source identity. That concrete defect should be fixed, but it exposes a deeper class that needs an architectural contract rather than another matcher patch. ## Core design principle > Once identity becomes more specific, no downstream layer may make it less specific and later infer the missing dimensions from foreground, endpoint, transport, or mutable registry state. Exact route identity must be **sticky, monotonic, generation-bound, and resource-owned**. ## Current evidence ### 1. Exact route provenance already exists before transport details are lost The existing `desktop-remote-route` planner resolves registry provenance before URL normalization, OAuth, SSH tunnelling, or other transport steps discard distinguishing information. Its identity matcher includes the dimensions that actually distinguish legal registrations: - auth mode; - headers; - token envelope; - Cloud organization; - SSH host/user/port; - key path; - remote Hermes path; - remote profile. For non-primary matches it accepts only a unique result. This is the right place in the pipeline to freeze route ownership. ### 2. `resolvedConnectionId()` weakens that proof after the fact The compatibility helper added by #89719 reconstructs identity from: - normalized `baseUrl` for remote/Cloud; - normalized `user@host` for SSH. It uses the first registry match and its descriptor type does not make an already-resolved `connectionId` authoritative. This can overwrite the exact identity already established by the route planner. ### 3. Source scoping is broad, but ownership is still ambient in many consumers `hermesApi()` injects the renderer's currently active source into requests. That works for foreground-global actions, but existing resources such as sessions, cron jobs, projects, approvals, OAuth flows, artifacts, and files should execute against their **owning route**, not whatever route happens to be foreground when an asynchronous callback finally runs. This becomes load-bearing now that background gateways remain live across foreground switches. ### 4. Some namespaces are source-aware at transport boundaries but still bare internally Gateway event dispatch now compares composite source/profile scope, which is correct. But many downstream stores and transient maps still key by bare runtime/session IDs, with source provenance kept separately or inferred from the active route. Copied/restored Hermes homes can reproduce IDs exactly. Multiple registered gateways make those duplicate namespaces concurrent. ### 5. Source switching still relies on manual global-state invalidation `wipeSessionListsForGatewaySwitch()` explicitly clears sessions, cron, messaging, unread paint, transcript tails, artifacts, and other gateway-bound state. This works only as long as every new source-owned store is remembered in the wipe list. That is an omission-prone correctness mechanism. Multi-gateway state should be partitioned by route identity so switching changes the visible partition instead of destructively reusing one global namespace. ## The deeper class issues ### A. Identity proof is not monotonic A registered route and an unqualified legacy descriptor should not share one loose shape. Suggested direction: ```ts type ResolvedRoute = | { identity: { kind: 'registered' connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } | { identity: { kind: 'legacy-unregistered' provenance: 'environment' | 'profile-v1' | 'settings-v1' } profile: ProfileKey transport: TransportDescriptor } ``` Only the legacy-unregistered branch may enter compatibility inference. A registered descriptor must never have its identity overwritten by a weaker downstream guess. ### B. Registration identity, physical backend identity, principal, and locator are conflated Desktop needs explicit equivalence relations for concepts that are currently easy to treat as interchangeable: - **registration identity** — saved `connectionId`; - **registration generation** — which endpoint/credential envelope that ID currently denotes; - **physical runtime identity** — backend installation / `installId`; - **authorization principal** — account, Cloud org, credential set, permission envelope; - **locator** — URL, SSH host, tunnel endpoint. These answer different questions. Two registrations may share a locator but represent different principals. Two locators may reach one physical installation. A registry ID can be edited in place to point at a different runtime. Physical sameness does not prove authorization equivalence. Callers should explicitly choose the relation they require instead of using a generic "same connection" test. ### C. The route algebra overloads omission, `local`, `primary`, and legacy fallback These are semantically distinct: - omitted / null connection selector; - explicit `local`; - registry `primary`; - `lastUsed`; - unknown or removed ID; - legacy profile-routed fallback. V2 routing should represent this structurally rather than through magic-string normalization. Suggested direction: ```ts type ConnectionSelector = | { kind: 'registered'; id: ConnectionId } // including `local` | { kind: 'legacy-primary' } ``` `primary` and `lastUsed` should resolve user intent into a concrete registered route **before** an operation begins. They should not be consulted later as fallback authority for an already-started operation. ### D. Gateway activation is coordinated but not one transaction A foreground switch currently spans independently changing facts: - registry entry and credential envelope; - resolved descriptor; - WebSocket URL; - opened socket; - active gateway pointer; - active profile pointer; - renderer connection descriptor; - ambient REST connection/profile; - cache invalidations; - `lastUsed`; - new-chat ownership. Descriptor resolution and socket activation should not be independent proofs. The activation path that actually prepares the socket should return the exact descriptor and identity used to establish it. The outcome should be typed and explicit: ```ts type ActivationReceipt = | { status: 'activated' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number connection: HermesConnection socketInstanceId: string } | { status: 'already-active' route: RouteKey activationEpoch: number } | { status: 'superseded' | 'removed' | 'offline' | 'ambiguous' | 'cancelled' requested: RouteIntent current: RouteKey } ``` Only an exact successful receipt may authorize success side effects. This directly interlocks with #89586 / #89609: a declined activation must not resolve indistinguishably from a successful one, especially for same-source profile switches where comparing only `connectionId` proves nothing. ### E. A connection ID identifies a mutable slot, not an immutable route A registry entry can be materially edited while retaining the same ID. For example, `homelab` can change from endpoint/credential A to endpoint/credential B while stale callbacks, sockets, caches, and resources still carry only `homelab`. Material edits already trigger backend/socket recycling, which is necessary but not sufficient as the architecture grows. Introduce a monotonically increasing registration generation: ```ts type RouteKey = { connectionId: ConnectionId connectionGeneration: number profile: ProfileKey } ``` Every descriptor, socket, request, response, event, cache entry, persisted resource handle, and activation receipt should carry the generation. Results from an obsolete generation may finish but must not commit into the new generation's state. This closes ABA-style edit/remove/re-add races and makes descriptor/socket agreement provable. ### F. Ambient active-route state must not authorize mutations on existing resources Foreground-global actions can use the current route. Existing resources should carry their owner. Instead of: ```ts archiveSession(sessionId) ``` prefer: ```ts archiveSession({ owner: session.route, sessionId: session.id }) ``` The same principle applies to: - session mutations and hydration; - cron jobs and runs; - projects and repo/worktree operations; - approvals and input requests; - OAuth flows; - artifacts; - filesystem and Git operations; - background/tile/window actions. This directly interlocks with #89916: filesystem and Git facades need the same route identity as the resource/session that owns them, not merely the current foreground gateway. ### G. Resource namespaces must be source-qualified, not just transport-qualified The canonical resource identity should include route ownership: ```ts type ResourceKey = { route: RouteKey resourceId: string } ``` At minimum, audit and qualify: - runtime session IDs; - stored session IDs and lineage aliases; - unscoped stream pins; - approvals and input requests; - provider-wait / compaction / drafting state; - transcript tails; - unread/read watermarks; - pin mirrors; - cron job and run IDs; - project IDs and project scope; - artifacts; - OAuth flow/session IDs; - query and capability cache keys; - window/HUD/quick-entry session references. Unscoped events should be pinned per socket or `RouteKey`, never through one renderer-global ref shared by multiple retained gateways. ### H. Manual cache wiping should stop being a correctness boundary Gateway-owned state should be partitioned by route identity. Foreground switching should select another partition rather than globally clearing one namespace and hoping every source-owned store was included. Generation revocation can explicitly retire obsolete partitions after connection edits/removals, but ordinary switching should not require destructive global wipes. This also aligns state lifetime with the already-shipped behavior where background gateway sockets remain alive and continue work. ### I. Compatibility needs a versioned protocol and retirement path Absence of `connectionId` can currently mean too many things: - older Electron main; - environment-provided unregistered route; - genuinely local legacy route; - ambiguous registry match; - accidentally dropped exact identity; - failed lookup. Optional fields are not a sufficient compatibility protocol. Prefer an explicit versioned IPC contract: ```ts type ConnectionProtocol = | { version: 1; route: LegacyRouteDescriptor } | { version: 2; route: RegisteredRouteDescriptor } ``` A v2 registry-scoped call must produce a v2 registered route. Legacy compatibility should remain explicitly unregistered unless a unique, full-fidelity pre-dial match proves ownership. Compatibility paths should also expose diagnostics/telemetry so they can be retired rather than becoming permanent alternate authority models. ### J. Multi-window and registry-write concurrency need explicit semantics Desktop supports multiple full renderer windows while `lastUsed` and registry entries are global persisted state. Define and test: - whether `lastUsed` is installation-global, window-specific, or primary-window-owned; - what happens when one window removes/edits a connection another window is activating; - how concurrent registry mutations are serialized; - whether writes use a registry revision / compare-and-swap contract. A monotonically increasing registry revision should make stale write rejection explicit. ## Required invariants The architecture should eventually be able to state and mechanically test all of these: 1. Once exact registered identity exists, no downstream layer can replace it with inferred identity. 2. Registry ordering cannot affect route resolution. 3. Zero or multiple compatibility matches fail explicitly. 4. Socket route, descriptor route, REST route, UI route, and activation receipt agree on one `RouteKey`. 5. A same-source profile activation decline produces no success side effects. 6. Edit/remove/re-add during dial cannot publish an obsolete generation. 7. Old-generation responses/events cannot commit after generation replacement. 8. Identical resource IDs on two gateways remain independent. 9. Unscoped events on simultaneous retained sockets cannot cross-pin. 10. Explicit `local` never aliases omitted legacy-primary routing. 11. One stalled activation cannot permanently wedge later user intent. 12. Multi-window activation and registry edits produce a serializable result. ## Diagnostics / observability Every routed operation should be traceable without logging secrets. Include a correlation tuple such as: ```text connectionId connectionGeneration profile activationEpoch socketInstanceId requestId resourceId ``` A split-brain should be diagnosable from one trace rather than inferred from contradictory UI symptoms. ## Implementation sequence ### Phase 1 — immediate shipped defect - Treat an existing descriptor `connectionId` as authoritative. - Never overwrite it through post-dial inference. - Restrict compatibility inference to genuinely unqualified legacy descriptors. - Reuse the full-fidelity pre-dial identity contract from #88922 / #88697. - Fail closed on zero or multiple matches. - Add duplicate URL/auth/org/header and SSH port/key/path/profile witnesses. ### Phase 2 — canonical route identity - Introduce structured `RouteKey` with connection generation. - Distinguish registered routes from legacy-unregistered routes at the type boundary. - Make explicit `local` a real registered identity, never omission. ### Phase 3 — activation transaction - Return a typed activation receipt from the prepare/dial/publish path. - Return the exact descriptor used by the activated socket. - Consume activation verdicts at all callers before any success side effects. - Bound activation leases / unresolved IPC so one operation cannot wedge the switch coordinator indefinitely. ### Phase 4 — resource ownership - Add `RouteKey` ownership to sessions, cron, projects, OAuth flows, artifacts, FS/Git resources, and other durable/background objects. - Remove ambient foreground routing from mutations against existing resources. ### Phase 5 — route-partitioned state - Source-qualify cache/store keys. - Replace broad switch-time wipe correctness with route-owned partitions and generation revocation. ### Phase 6 — compatibility and concurrency hardening - Version the Desktop IPC routing contract. - Add compatibility diagnostics and retirement criteria. - Add registry revisioning / serialized write semantics. - Define multi-window ownership of `lastUsed` and route mutations. ## Acceptance / adversarial matrix The closing test matrix should include at least: - two URL registrations with the same normalized URL but different auth mode; - same URL with different token/header envelopes; - same Cloud URL under different org/account identity; - two SSH registrations with same user/host but different port; - different key path; - different remote Hermes path; - different remote profile; - exact descriptor `connectionId` survives all of the above; - ambiguous legacy descriptor returns no registered identity; - `(homelab, default)` -> `(homelab, research)` decline leaves route/caches/preferences unchanged; - edit connection generation while activation is in flight; - remove and recreate a connection ID while old work is still completing; - two gateways with identical stored/runtime session IDs; - copied Hermes home with identical project/job/session IDs on two active sources; - simultaneous unscoped stream events from two retained sockets; - explicit local operations while registry primary is remote; - two Desktop windows switching different sources and mutating registry state concurrently. ## Interlocks / provenance - #89719 — shipped registered-gateway switcher and broad `(connectionId, profile)` propagation; this issue is the architectural follow-through from the merged residual. - #88325 / @dokterdok — substantive source of #89719's fifteen-commit salvage; provenance remains preserved. - #88307 — product request implemented by #89719. - #88922 / #88697 — exact pre-dial route identity architecture that must remain authoritative rather than being weakened post-dial. - #89586 / #89609 — activation-verdict work: completion must prove publication, not merely promise resolution. - #89483 — adjacent atomic-publication work that exposed the need to distinguish prepared, activated, superseded, and declined states. - #89622 — lifecycle race witness around activation leases / target disposal. - #88095 — complementary foreground session/profile ownership work. - #89916 — resource facade ownership: FS/Git must follow the owning route, not ambient foreground state. ## Non-goals This is not a request to replace all compatibility code immediately or to break single-source Desktop behavior. The goal is to establish one canonical identity/ownership model so compatibility code is explicitly fenced and cannot weaken exact v2 identity. It is also not sufficient to solve this by expanding `resolvedConnectionId()` with more matcher fields. That repairs the current witness but leaves the defect class open anywhere identity can later be erased and reconstructed. ## Definition of done This issue is complete when Desktop can prove, by type contract and adversarial tests, that: - exact route identity never becomes less specific downstream; - mutable registrations are generation-bound; - successful activation returns an authoritative receipt; - every durable/background resource carries its owning route; - source-qualified resources cannot alias across gateways; - foreground switching does not determine ownership of already-existing resources; - compatibility inference is explicit, ambiguity-safe, observable, and retireable; - multi-window and registry mutation semantics are serializable and documented. The target architecture should make the current #89719 split-brain impossible to represent, not merely unlikely to reproduce.
